Fail-functional systems are increasingly vital in safety-critical areas like automotive control, where they enable safe roadside stops upon detecting subsystem failures. This paper formally validates a real-world, real-time control architecture implementing this capability for vehicle driving. Adopting a component-based approach, the system transitions between operating modes via a mode machine, and this paper provides rigorous proofs of liveness and safety properties concerning these mode machine transitions.

We introduce a novel data-driven clustering approach for dynamical systems that influences global system behavior. This method reformulates traditional clustering as an optimization task that maximizes the minimal impact of each subsystem on the total system, employing Riemannian optimization to evaluate impact curves of individual components. A specific kernel-based Riemannian metric is developed to quantify the relationship between individual subsystems and the aggregate system, with its curvature and associated Riemannian distance derived and experimentally verified. Furthermore, an $O(N)$ data-efficient update algorithm accelerates this metric's computation significantly. Experimental results across both synthetic datasets and real-world applications, such as gene regulatory networks and power grids, demonstrate the method's superior performance in achieving high clustering quality with enhanced computational efficiency.

This paper explores the various approaches to classifying the methods underlying Leibnizian calculus, a foundational aspect of the foundation of calculus. The study of these historical categorizations is not merely an academic exercise; it provides essential insight into the development of calculus and offers a fresh perspective for addressing modern issues in the history and philosophy of mathematics, specifically the concept of continuity and continuous change. By examining how different historians and philosophers have organized these Leibnizian techniques, the work sheds light on the evolution of mathematical thought and provides a renewed understanding of continuous transformation. Analyzing the diverse ways these methods have been categorized by past scholars not only advances our historical comprehension but also reinvigorates the exploration of continuous change. In conclusion, this investigation into historical categorizations of early calculus methods offers both a deeper historical analysis and a fresh philosophical angle on continuous change.

Disturbance theory offers a promising framework for intensity mapping of cosmic structures, particularly neutral hydrogen (HI). In the radio frequency band, foregrounds vastly overpower the faint cosmological background signals, necessitating their removal. We evaluate the efficacy of foreground rejection using the disturbance theory model through numerical simulations. Our results indicate that, unlike the previous assumptions of ideal background-only data, real simulations show that foreground subtraction can introduce significant residual biases in power spectrum estimates. We further demonstrate that the magnitude of these biases is sensitive to the specific characteristics of the simulation volume. Consequently, accurate modeling of realistic simulation data becomes essential for achieving high-precision intensity maps via disturbance theory.

In this paper, we define a self-contained operator as one where the closure of its span, together with that of its adjoint's span, forms the entire algebra of bounded operators on the underlying Hilbert space. For any separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, we demonstrate the existence of nilpotent operators of arbitrary order whose indices are defined by these self-contained properties. Additionally, we establish that any operator which is both nilpotent and self-contained automatically falls into the class of operators with a cyclic multiplicity of one.

Hybrid recommender systems have become popular for addressing the limitations inherent in individual recommendation methods. This study introduces a novel hybrid architecture designed to integrate the strengths of both document-based and behavioral-based systems. The system prioritizes recent user interactions to suggest items, utilizing a dual approach: (1) a hybrid method combining Local Collaborative Filtering (LCF) and Text Ranking (TR) that leverages both historical and item textual data, and (2) a purely TR system relying solely on item content. By incorporating both temporal context and textual information, the TR component enhances recommendations with items featuring similar attributes, while the LCF maximizes accuracy by utilizing past rating behaviors. Experimental results across two real-world datasets demonstrate that the combined proposed hybrid outperforms TR-only systems, achieving superior accuracy, recall, and diversity scores.

This study investigates conditions under which random matrices exhibit freeness of type $B$ and explores their independence conditional on trace zero. We establish that for $2$-periodic GUE matrices, freeness of type $B$ holds conditionally given trace zero. Additionally, we demonstrate two other scenarios where freeness of type $B$ arises: these cases involve Hermitian matrices that are either uniformly distributed over the general linear group or drawn from a rotation-symmetric distribution. In all instances, the moments of the resulting sums correspond to the conditional moments of standard Gaussian matrices, restricted to trace zero. The paper further analyzes the moments of sums involving Hermitian matrices drawn uniformly from orthogonal groups or according to a rotation-symmetric distribution. Finally, the conditional moments regarding trace zero are derived for Hermitian matrices selected uniformly from either the unitary or the orthogonal group.

This study introduces a novel observational semantics for Timed Automata (TA) with the specific goal of capturing the system's timed behavior through its execution traces. To this end, it defines an original minimal region-based semantics that refines traditional minimal regions to more accurately model a trajectory's maximal domain of validity within the region structure. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the supremum of a trajectory can be computed in constant time relative to the number of clock constraints. The paper concludes by proving that using maximal regions yields the coarsest minimal semantics and that the distance between standard minimal regions and this new maximal region-based approach is bounded by a factor of the number of clock constraints.

The LHCb collaboration reported measurements of the branching fraction for the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0\eta$ decay, which is approximately $1.5 \times 10^{-6}$ with an uncertainty of around $0.3 \times 10^{-6}$. This paper provides the initial theoretical framework for this process, utilizing the $s$-wave $B_s^0 \to \eta V$ mechanism along with the $\eta \to \pi^0\gamma\gamma$ transition to model it. The findings indicate a branching fraction of roughly $1.2 \times 10^{-6}$ with uncertainties of $0.2 \times 10^{-6}$, closely aligning with LHCb observations. This study further explores the decay amplitude across the kinematic phase space to investigate the underlying $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ mixing phenomenon.

The GRAVITY instrument on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) merges light from four Unit Telescopes and their auxiliary instruments into a dual-beam configuration. It utilizes four beam combiners that operate across the spectral range of 1.3 to 24 micrometers, delivering astrometric precision sufficient to resolve the angular diameters of nearby stars. This study details the characteristics of GRAVITY's new imaging detector, designed to capture astrometry and measure fringe visibility. We evaluated the detector's performance through laboratory tests and on-sky observations of bright calibrator stars. Results indicate that readout noise is negligible, with a dark current of 0.0002 e-/s, and full well capacity reaching 1.1 x 10^6 electrons. While the effective quantum efficiency averages 40%, it varies between 15% and 55% across the observed spectrum. In terms of linearity, deviations remain below 0.1% for exposures under 10 seconds. We also assessed readout speed, timing stability, and pixel-to-pixel uniformity, confirming that these metrics are adequate for high-precision interferometry.

The $k$-center problem seeks the minimum radius required to cover a set of points using $k$ balls. For general metric spaces, this problem is NP-hard, yet approximation schemes exist for linear radii when considering large values of $k$. To better understand the complexity of such coverings, Hailperin et al. introduced the concept of freeway dimension, which they defined as the smallest radius $R$ such that every subset of points can be covered by $R$ balls using only $O(f(k))$ balls of radius $R/k$ for some function $f$. They demonstrated that in Euclidean spaces of dimension $d$, the freeway dimension scales as $O(d^{\lceil \log d \rceil})$. Conversely, spaces with high Doubling dimension—meaning they can be covered by $O(n^\log_2)$ centers of half their original radius—are expected to exhibit significantly different covering behaviors. In this paper, we prove that any metric space with Doubling dimension $d$ can require a radius as high as $O(n^{1/2})$ to achieve efficient coverage with $k$ balls, thereby establishing a substantial gap between the efficiency of freey dimensions in Euclidean settings and the necessary radius in Doubling spaces.

This study investigates the shared Shiffuer (or shift) admissible value for an entire function $f$ in the form $f(z+c_1+kT), f(z+c_2+kT),$ where $k \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $c_1$ and $c_2$ are fixed non-zero complex constants, and $T$ is a positive real number. Under the assumption that the Nevanlinna counting function $n(r,f)$ is of order 1, the authors present a unification of several theorems established by the first author, Li, and their colleagues, demonstrating the unicity of $f$ in $f(z+c_1+kT), f(z+c_2+kT)$ for $k=0,1,2,\ldots$. Additionally, the paper establishes a unicity theorem concerning an entire function $f$ and its exponential shift $f(e^c z)$, where $c$ is a non-zero complex constant.

This study addresses the task of solving $m$-variable linear equations with polynomial coefficients, where access to each term is probabilistic and may yield incorrect results. We establish lower bounds for the sample size of queries required to determine a solution across three specific co-randomness frameworks: bounded error ($\mathsf{C}\mathsf{-R}\mathsf{-E}$), constant error ($\mathsf{C}\mathsf{-R}\mathsf{-C}$), and error-free ($\mathsf{C}\mathsf{-R}\mathsf{-Z}$) models. Within these settings, we introduce novel lower bounds for the $\mathsf{C}\mathsf{-R}\mathsf{-E}$ and $\mathsf{C}\mathsf{-R}\mathsf{-C}$ cases, demonstrating that query requirements scale at least linearly with $m$. In contrast, we show that existing algorithms operating under the $\mathsf{C}\mathsf{-R}\mathsf{-Z}$ assumption can function with a sublinear number of queries. Finally, we present a new method for determining a solution using an early stopping strategy, even in scenarios involving erroneous responses.

This study introduces an innovative method for generating chiral molecules in bulk form by utilizing a chiral photocatalyst. The proposed photochemical bundle emission mechanism is governed by the catalyst's inherent symmetry and parity, a principle that can be experimentally validated through the observation of photoluminescence polarization.

A simple, precise, and rigorous analytical model for calculating thermodynamic properties of high-precision alkali metals in equilibrium is developed. This approach avoids any approximations regarding inter-alkali interactions, which are often the source of errors in standard theories like Saha-Eggert. Instead, it treats these interactions as a hard-sphere system, with the effective hard-sphere diameter determined by maximizing the entropy of the resulting fermi-gas correction. This method yields direct and exact expressions for thermodynamic variables based on just two parameters: the ionization energy and the effective diameter. Treating ionization as a one-body process, the resulting theory provides a robust framework for describing alkali metals under equilibrium conditions.

This study investigates the spectral properties of vector mesons within a medium exhibiting chiral asymmetry caused by fermionic vacuum condensates. Within the framework of the Holographic Massive Vector (HMVM) model, we derived two five-dimensional action formulations to compute both the spectral function and the mass of the mesons. Our results indicate that chiral asymetry modifies the mass spectrum, causing the separation between even and odd-parity states. Furthermore, we analyzed the quenching effects on even-parity vector mesons, observing that their velocities increase with rising temperature and fermion chemical potential.

Accurately estimating the size of a network is fundamental to numerous network management tasks. In this paper, we investigate the Byzantine failure model during a proposed network size estimation protocol. Our findings indicate that estimating size is impossible when even a single Byzantine node exists within the network. We further demonstrate that in small-world graphs, the presence of Byzantine nodes can drastically inflate estimation time, potentially scaling it up by a factor of $O(\log^2 n)$. To address this delay, we present an accurate estimation method based on counting two-hop neighbors, which remains robust even with Byzantine agents. Our approach leverages counting protocols established in prior research to achieve both high precision and efficiency.

Numerical relativity simulations of binary neutron star (BNS) mergals typically commence with data generated by "evolution-from-scratch" methods, which involve integrating Einstein's equations forward from an initial configuration. This evolution is highly sensitive to minor errors, often resulting in undesirable artifacts like excess energy or angular momentum that distort the BNS system. To mitigate these issues, a common strategy is to perform a lengthy pre-evolution period to erase the errors before the actual merger begins. However, this introduces further complications: the necessary cleanup time consumes valuable computational resources, and prolonged evolution can amplify certain flaws rather than fully eliminating them. We propose a new approach that bypasses these drawbacks by initiating merger simulations with data derived from a "time-reversal" method. In this scheme, we evolve a BNS system backward in time from a known state characterized by minimal energy and angular momentum, a state easily identified within a short backward integration. This strategy offers multiple advantages: it eliminates evolution artifacts, drastically reduces the required computational time, and avoids error accumulation associated with long-duration pre-evolution. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method using the "CTTK" code, a tool designed specifically for this time-reversal integration. Simulation results show that merging systems constructed via this time-reversal technique exhibit significantly improved data quality compared to traditional approaches.

The structure of the neutrino's flavor mixing is defined by the mass matrix, which JUNO aims to probe. This experiment involves a 20-meter-diameter liquid scintillator sphere, JUNO, designed to detect solar and reactor neutrinos. To achieve the necessary energy resolution, JUNO relies on high-performance photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) with a 20-inch diameter, which will be fully instrumented within the detector. These 20-inch PMTs, sourced from various manufacturers, must undergo rigorous uniformity testing to ensure JUNO's precision neutrino measurements. This study details the comprehensive evaluation of 20-inch PMTs, covering initial screening, aging protocols, and detailed characterization. Initial screening involved measuring spectral response and quantum efficiency using JUNO's dedicated setup, while characterization focused on optical and particle detection efficiency, along with timing and spatial resolutions. Furthermore, we assessed the consistency of these 20-inch PMTs across different manufacturers to establish their suitability for JUNO's scientific objectives.

Graph-based methods have proven highly effective for modeling multidimensional time series (MTS), particularly when the series exhibit long-range dependencies. Although existing solutions often rely on a static global graph fixed at training time, this rigid structure proves insufficient for scenarios where the data's inter-variable relationships shift over time. To address this limitation, we introduce AGCN, a novel adaptive framework that dynamically constructs graphs based on the specific task and data. This approach features two primary innovations: (1) a multi-level adaptation strategy that dynamically learns the graph topology for each subsequence of the training data, and (2) a time-varying graph mechanism that synthesizes these static levels into a single dynamic model, enabling the graph structure to evolve chronologically. Experiments across six real-world MTS datasets demonstrate that AGCN significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a suite of atmospheric simulation models designed to analyze direct imaging data from the high-contrast system HD 169142 b, obtained via the VLT/UVES instrument. The atmospheric models were developed and tuned using a Bayesian inference framework, specifically the EXTRA-POL code, to ensure their consistency with emerging observational capabilities. We detail the development of these models and evaluate the characteristics of the derived parameter sets. Results indicate that HD 169142 b exhibits a temperature of 1300 K, a surface gravity of 4.0, and metallicity matching the solar value, with an estimated 68% confidence interval.

Pre-trained models (which we refer to as the "super-teacher") have emerged as a significant breakthrough in computer vision, enabling the creation of superior models with relatively modest effort through knowledge transfer to student networks. However, these large-scale architectures are often computationally demanding, making their deployment in real-world scenarios impractical due to high computational costs. Knowledge Distillation (KD) offers a solution by training a streamlined student model to mimic a super-teacher, yielding both efficiency and effectiveness. In this paper, we introduce a super-teacher of unique composition: a group of diverse, specialized networks, each possessing distinct knowledge. The core challenge lies in aggreginating these varying capabilities into a unified student model. We propose the Pairwise Iterative Logits Aggregation method (PILE), an innovative distillation strategy designed to facilitate this Multi-Teacher Learning process. PILE achieves a refined balance among conflicting teacher objectives through iterative pairwise interactions, effectively capturing both individual characteristics and collective knowledge of the teacher ensemble. Experimental results demonstrate that the PILE framework substantially boosts performance in KD settings, surpassing existing state-of-the-art approaches.

The prospect of detecting ultralight bosonic dark matter (DBM) fields, which oscillate at ultra-low frequencies, has garnered significant attention. This study proposes employing an atom interferometer to identify such ultralight DBM through strength interferometry. As the DM-induced oscillation causes variations in the coupling strength between the DM field and atoms, this modulation alters the interaction-mediated repulsive force (specifically, the Yukawa force) acting on atoms within the interferometer. By measuring the interference pattern resulting from this oscillatory coupling variation, we can detect the presence of ultralight bosonic DM. Our analysis indicates that with current technology, this method can constrain or detect DM masses up to $10^{-13}$ eV, a sensitivity that surpasses existing approaches for detecting fields of comparable mass.

We investigate Basis Pursuit (BP) within a continuum framework, focusing primarily on establishing conditions for the unique sparse solution. By examining how feasible solutions evolve as an $\ell_1$-norm constraint bound varies continuously, we derive a general theoretical result proving that, under specific prerequisites, the BP problem admits a unique sparse solution, with these requirements met in most scenarios. Furthermore, by linking this continuous evolution to the Euler derivative of the convex function representing BP's optimal value, we establish additional sufficient conditions for sparsity uniqueness. Finally, we introduce a novel condition by analyzing the behavior of Lagrange multipliers associated with BP, which further guarantees a unique sparse answer.

The P4 language has emerged as a prominent choice for specifying programmable data plane processors, yet current implementations generally restrict users to a maximum of 1,024 bits for the match section and 64 bits for the action section within table entries. This limitation hinders the utilization of advanced features like complex header parsing, extensive metadata, and intricate actions, which are often necessary in modern network and service chain architectures. This paper introduces an open-source P416 compiler tailored for P1MS switches, a flexible, reconfiguration-capable system featuring match-action table capabilities. P16 offers switch operators the freedom to dynamically adjust both individual entry sizes and the overall number of tables. We also present a backend utilizing address-dependent dynamic reconfiguration to enhance the performance of match-width adaptation. Experimental findings indicate that this proposed solution delivers superior space and temporal efficiency compared to alternative strategies for width adaptation.

This study examines a standard second-order-accurate, central-difference-based discretization of the vector transport equation on unstructured quadrilateral and hybrid quadrilateral-meshes, utilizing Raviart-Thomas finite elements of lowest order. The scheme is fully flux-conserving, monotone, and preserves both divergence and $L^2$ norms. The research analyzes how enhancing the approximation of the directional component—specifically through higher-order schemes or pre-computation—impacts performance. Numerical experiments demonstrate that pre-computing the direction significantly boosts accuracy and computational efficiency with minimal added overhead, whereas higher-order approximation schemes yield only negligible improvements.

Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a robust privacy framework for machine learning, enabling decentralized data training while ensuring privacy through mechanisms like Differential Privacy (DP). FL and DP are often utilized in tandem to address the differential risks associated with specific user data leakage. However, recent studies indicate that achieving meaningful FL performance requires low noise levels, which inherently risks compromising the privacy guarantees of the users. This paper investigates the trade-off between equity (fairness) and privacy within FL systems, specifically examining how varying degrees of privacy noise impact data equity across diverse client groups. We identify that FL systems burdened with heavy DP noise exacerbate imbalances in user data, thereby skewing model performance. To mitigate these disparities and foster more equitable outcomes, we propose two novel personalized modeling strategies designed to reduce bias toward minority clients with data that is less balanced under strict privacy constraints. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets confirm that our proposed approaches not only enhance equity but also maintain or improve overall model accuracy and robustness.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a standard for solving complex problems, yet their massive scale necessitates hardware acceleration. Model-parallel DNN training across GPU clusters is a prevalent technique for this purpose; however, it often suffers from inefficient resource usage and communication bottlenecks. We introduce a new approach called Regional Training, which partitions a model into finer sub-components than model-parallel training and groups them by functional region. These sub-components are then distributed across GPU regions using an all-reduce communication pattern optimized for network topology. By applying consistent abstractions for both training and inference, this method achieves simplified development workflows. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Regional Training through large-scale experiments involving a 1.7B parameter model trained on 256 GPUs, which outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques by 1.35x in training speed.

Recent research has uncovered that Wada fractals—boundaries sharing intricate, infinitely branching rims across multiple basins of attraction—can emerge in systems featuring both dissipation and chaos. These structures typically arise within the context of feeble, or weak, dissipation. This study investigates chaotic scattering involving Wada basins in three-dimensional (3D) dissipative systems, specifically focusing on the role of such dissipation. We identify novel Wada fractals separating the basins, observe that basins with higher fractal dimensions exhibit more extensive areas, and demonstrate that these regions expand as dissipation decreases. Furthermore, we uncover that energy loss rates are concentrated along the basins' boundaries, whereas the internal volumes of the basins remain largely free of dissipation. Our findings indicate that feeble dissipation not only fosters the emergence of these structures but also drives their growth and intensification, thereby offering significant implications for both theoretical frameworks and practical applications.

Although the Stueckelberg extension of the massive photon represents the leading minimal model exploring the long-standing phenomenon of flavor change flavor dependence (FCFI) in the electromagnetic field, previous claims suggested that the associated signal duration remains negligible, thereby hindering experimental verification. Contrary to this expectation, our study demonstrates that the activity duration of the bosons within the Stueckelberg framework can endure for extended periods under specific parameter conditions. This conclusion rests on a systematic analysis of both the temporal and spatial characteristics of the coherent states governing Stueckelberg photons. Furthermore, we examine the potential for experimental detection involving the photodisintegration of positronium and the resulting positron-acceleration processes.

Human action recognition in videos is a significant area of computer vision research. However, existing methods often struggle with the high computational demands and data sparsity inherent in videos, which typically consist of numerous frames containing redundant information. To overcome these hurdles, this paper introduces a Hierarchical Focus Network (HFN) designed to capture the essential spatio-temporal characteristics of actions efficiently. The HFN operates through a two-stage process: initially, it utilizes temporal focus modules to identify critical video segments, while subsequently, spatial focus modules extract the primary visual features from those selected frames. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed HFN surpasses current state-of-the-art performance on three major benchmarks—UCF101, HMDB51, and Kinetics-600—while achieving these results with significantly lower computational costs.

This work examines the emergence of stars within the context of emerging star theory. We analyze how stars form in the shadows, a metaphor for the philosophical and physical conditions required for their appearance. By exploring these conditions, we provide a mathematical framework for star generation and discuss their cosmological implications. Our findings indicate that stars arise when three specific criteria are met: (1) sufficient mass density, (2) low temperature, and (3) gravitational instability. When these factors converge, they facilitate the formation of stars. Our results also suggest that the universe may have produced its initial batch of stars during the epoch of recombination, marking a pivotal stage in cosmic history.

The information entropy of a discrete set quantifies the average uncertainty regarding which specific member belongs to that set. While often approximated by the Shannon entropy, calculating exact values can be computationally prohibitive due to the vast number of configurations involved in systems like those in cosmology. This study demonstrates that Nested Sampling (NS)—a technique originally devised for estimating multi-dimensional integrals and posterior densities in Bayesian inference—is capable of accurately and efficiently computing both the entropy of finite discrete systems and the partition functions required for continuous systems to determine Shannon entropy. By employing NS, we achieve precise and rapid calculation of partition functions and entropies for two standard test cases: the Ising model and the Knuth-Morris-prater random generator, yielding results that align perfectly with those obtained via Monte Carlo simulations.

This study addresses a nonlinear hyperbolic conservation law featuring non-Lipschitz continuous flux, introducing two solution concepts: fragile measure-valued solutions and fragile C-evidence solutions. Both are extensions of the corresponding standard solutions previously proposed for Lipschitz hypotheses. It is established that any fragile C-evidence solution qualifies as a fragile measure-valued solution. Furthermore, through an example demonstrating time-fractality in a specific solution, it was shown that the class of fragile C-evidence solutions forms a proper subset of fragile measure-valued solutions.

Network assault detection is a critical component of cybersecurity, a field that has seen significant advancements in recent years. While numerous detection systems exist, many are either too resource-intensive for devices with limited capacity or lack the ability to operate efficiently under strict constraints. This paper introduces NB coded, a novel technique designed to mitigate these limitations by leveraging a combination of the Naive Bayesian model and feature encoding strategies. Specifically, NB coded utilizes Naive Bayesian learning to train compact classifiers capable of distinguishing between normal traffic and various attacks. Furthermore, it applies entropy-based feature encoding to compress both the training datasets and the resulting model structures. The proposed NB coded classifier was evaluated using the NSL-KDD dataset under stringent limits of 250 KB memory for the model and 10 seconds of training time. Under these conditions, NB coded achieved an accuracy of 94.41% and a detection completeness of 94.41% across all attack classes, while remaining significantly smaller in size than existing network assault classifiers.

We investigate interval extensions of activities for elements within finite solvable groups, demonstrating that these expanded elements remain solvable. Furthermore, a solvable group's activity is shown to be solvable activity iff it maintains the commutativity property. Several necessary and sufficient conditions are identified regarding when these commutativity properties hold, and we introduce a criterion for this. Finally, we illustrate that it is sufficient to verify this condition on certain specific sub-structures rather than checking the whole structure.

Movement represents a fundamental biological trait, yet its detection within video footage remains a difficult challenge. This struggle stems from the difficulty in modeling general biological motion and the lack of extensive video datasets capturing such activity. This paper presents a new computational strategy for observing animals in footage, relying on a dual approach that combines traditional optical flow with a specialized "biology motion model." The latter utilizes a simplified representation of typical hierarchical movements to guide feature extraction and highlight areas of biological activity. Testing against diverse natural video sources confirmed that this method effectively identifies real-world biological motion.

This work demonstrates how quantum entanglement can be harnessed to improve pure-state quantum energy transfer. We introduce a novel protocol where a quantum agent, possessing knowledge of the environment and the ability to perform local operations, injects an entangled pair into the network. The agent then tailors the resulting multipartite state through local operations to maximize the non-local energy component. It is shown that this enhanced non-local component is not only superior in value but also more resilient to decoherence. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we prove that the agent can universally maximize energy transfer across any network topology and any initial state using an efficiently calculable strategy via Quantum Resource Theory.

A significant challenge in modern science involves extracting physical laws governing complex systems. While machine learning (ML) has become a popular tool for this task, its application is often limited by a lack of theoretical understanding of the learned principles and their practical deployment. This paper demonstrates how ML can uncover and differentiate between fundamental and emergent behaviors in complex systems, using the evolution of neurons in a spiking neural network as a case study. By applying a combination of unsupervised and supervised techniques, we show that although entropy maximization appears to drive the emergence of memory and computational abilities in these neurons, entropy itself is not a causal factor. Instead, inconsistencies in entropy calculations across different representations reveal that these apparent contradictions arise from representation flaws, not from the underlying physics. This work establishes a new framework for uncovering causal mechanisms in complex systems, a method that could be extended to other fields, including biology and climate science.

This study presents a search for the production of charged, long-lived particles with substantial specific ionisation ($dE/dx$) and extended track lengths within the ATLAS detector at the LHC. Utilising the complete Run 2 data set from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, the analysis targets particles with masses exceeding 1 GeV and lifetimes longer than 0.1 mm, identified through track length, specific energy loss, and timing criteria. The analysis covers the full phase space for these stable particles, resulting in 95% coverage of the model predictions for long-lived supersymmetry scenarios. Standard model backgrounds are simulated with a precision of 10%, and the analysis yields no significant excess over background expectations. These findings are interpreted in the context of simplified supersymmetry models involving a light charged Higgs, leading to exclusion limits for charged color-octet particles (gluinos) with masses surpassing 2.2 TeV, assuming lifetimes greater than 0.1 ms.

This study introduces an integrated ridge single-photon source that achieves near-unity effectiveness by directing emitted photons directly into a neighboring tapered fiber. The source relies on InGaAs quantum dots located within the ridge structure, which are excited via a coupled grating waveguide. The authors demonstrate experimentally that, under pulsed pump excitation, the efficiency reaches 0.72 ± 0.02, with a total system purities of 0.87 ± 0.01. The authors attribute the high effectiveness to precise alignment between the quantum dot emission and the tapered fiber mode, a result supported by finite-difference time-domain simulations. These findings present a promising pathway for creating highly effective single-photon streams suitable for scalable single-photon technologies.

The boson summit, a newly emerging peak in the small-angle regime, has recently attracted significant interest within the neutron scattering community. This work provides a comprehensive review of existing literature and presents new data aimed at clarifying the nature of the boson summit. Our data were acquired using the NG3 instrument at the UK's Inelastic Neutron Scattering Centre (NCNS), which offers superior resolution in the momentum transfer ($Q$) domain. By analyzing the summit through a Lorentzian profile, we derived its full width at half maximum (FWHM) as a function of $Q$. Furthermore, we examined the data using a damped harmonic model, interpreting the observed behavior as resulting from confined excitations.

In high-precision phenomenology, Feynman diagrams featuring complex topologies and multi-loop structures often arise, resulting in phenomenological predictions that depend critically on multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman integrals. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of current advances and unresolved challenges in calculating these integral types, particularly focusing on techniques grounded in differential equations, difference equations, and graph polynomials.

In scattering systems, an energy absorption eigenchannel (EAEC) represents a specific input channel that concentrates energy absorption while remaining invariant under system evolution. This study reveals two fundamental sum rules governing the EAEC weights $w_n$ associated with channels $\{c_n\}$. The first rule states that the sum of the squared weights vanishes, $\sum_n w_n^2 = 0$, while the sum of the weights themselves equals the total number of channels, $\sum_n w_n = N$. These sum rules remain valid regardless of whether the system operates in a coherent or incoherent mode and provide a precise framework for analyzing the distribution of weights across individual channels. Furthermore, the second sum rules offers a mechanism to significantly reduce measurement efforts: determining the weights requires accessing only a sparse subset of the full set of channels rather than every channel individually.

We introduce the discovery of the distant 3-kpc Arm, a newly identified spiral arm located approximately 15 degrees from the Galactic center. By analyzing H-alpha emission and CO data, we determined that this structure extends roughly 30 degrees in Galactic longitude and spans about 5 degrees in latitude. Our analysis of H-alpha and 13CO data indicates a spiral arm nature, supported by kinematic evidence derived from CO data at 115 GHz and 86 GHz. Kinematic studies suggest the structure is situated at a Galactocentric distance of roughly 17.5 +/- 2.5 kpc, with a width of approximately 2 +/- 0.5 kpc and a height of about 1 +/- 0.2 kpc. Additionally, we utilized CO data to map the local spiral arm pattern speed, finding Omega(r) = 27 +/- 3 km s^-1 kpc^-1 at a radius of r = 8.5 +/- 1 kpc.

The increasing application of optimization techniques across various fields has driven significant interest in developing methods to preserve solution diversity. Since these heterogeneous solutions offer distinct advantages for both end-users and decision-makers, researchers have designed numerous diversity-based objective functions. However, there is a lack of consensus on defining the attributes of diverse solutions and their advantages, with existing studies often deriving specific objectives from the assumptions of their individual sub-fields. This work presents a structured examination of diverse solution concepts and an analysis of their distribution within the phenotypic search space, utilizing landscape analyses across four distinct optimization problems. Our findings indicate that diverse solutions predominantly cluster in specific regions of the search space and the fitness landscape, with their actual benefits remaining problem-dependent. Furthermore, we evaluated the efficacy of state-of-the-art, diversity-focused algorithms; results suggest that while these methods succeed in continuous optimization tasks, they often fail in combinatorial contexts, producing inconsistent outcomes.

We present an efficient algorithm for the three-dimensional steady state roommates problem that accommodates preferences over how quantities are shared. In this setting, two agents with additive values distribute three commodities among themselves, seeking to maximize the sum of their achieved utility. Our method operates within a continuous flow of prices and allocations, where each agent continuously refines their demand based on current prices, while market equilibrium is reached through a supply-demand balancing mechanism. This approach extends the previously established two-agent, two-commodity model to this higher dimensionality.

Intrinsic valley polarization in two-dimensional (2D) materials stems from the distinct electron-phonon interactions specific to each valley. This study provides a foundational framework for modeling valley polarization by incorporating the unique nature of these valley-dependent electron-phonon mechanisms. Our model accounts for the non-adiabatic coupling between valley and phonon degrees of freedom, revealing that, unlike the conventional approach limited to longitudinal phonons, transverse phonons significantly enhance this effect. Furthermore, the proposed theory is validated through its accurate description of experimental valley polarization data in MoS₂ monolayers.

A cloud represents a specific family of metric spaces that are nearly isometric to one another with discrepancies no greater than a given $\varepsilon > 0$. In this paper, we demonstrate the completeness of the Gromov-Hausdorff cloud associated with any complete base space. Furthermore, for each such cloud, we establish the existence of a "hub"—a center metric space within that cloud which maintains a maximum "radius," defined as the largest Riemannian distance (within the $\varepsilon$-tolerance) to any space in the cloud. This radius is bounded relative to the individual radii of the cloud members. Our findings also confirm the existence of hubs possessing specific topological characteristics, provided the base cloud exhibits corresponding topological properties.

This paper introduces a millimeter-wave patch antenna featuring a wide bandwidth and an expansive spatial coverage. The wideband characteristic is achieved through a dual-layer stacked architecture, where the lower layer functions as an impedance-matching unit utilizing complementary frequency-selective surfaces (FSS). These complementary surfaces consist of two FRRs (complementary frequency-selective surfaces) that are separated by an impedance-matching layer, allowing for independent tuning of each FRR to enhance impedance matching across a broader spectrum. The antenna demonstrates a measured impedance bandwidth of 10.2% (5.2–5.725 GHz) and maintains stable radiation patterns within a broad operating angular range of ±45 degrees.

Developing error-correcting codes for fault-tolerant quantum computation is an exceptionally difficult challenge. We introduce a novel methodology that leverages reinforcement learning to automatically generate these codes. By employing a deep neural network to forecast a candidate code's performance, we employ an agent that iteratively selects binary codewords to maximize the agent's cumulative reward. Using this framework, we successfully derived several new high-quality binary linear error-correcting codes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed architecture can be generalized to discover non-linear codes and, crucially, to develop entirely new codes specifically tailored for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

We introduce a new scheme for precision displacement sensing that utilizes a dual-cavity network featuring an input-output quantum coupling. By employing balanced homodyne detection, we demonstrate that utilizing quantum vacuum fluctuations enables significant improvements in performance, surpassing both classical capabilities and previously known quantum strategies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that sensing accuracy can exceed the standard quantum limit and achieve the Heisenberg scaling.

Using data from Au+Au and d+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV, the PHENIX collaboration measured correlations between high transverse momentum ($p_{_{T}} > 5.5$ GeV/$c$) charged hadrons and direct photons. These photons serve as an ideal, non-fragmenting recoil partner. Comparisons between the Au+Au and d+Au systems reveal a suppression of high $p_{_{T}}$-$h$-$\gamma$ pairs within the central rapidity region in central collisions, whereas forward photon-hadron correlations remain largely unaffected by centrality. The observed modification in the central rapidity zone suggests that medium-induced mechanisms alter jet fragmentation specifically when balanced against non-fragmenting photons.

In quantum simulation, efficiently handling the encoding of Pauli matrices within digital-vortex (or hybrid digital-analog) quantum computing frameworks remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a strategy to encode three-dimensional Pauli vectors ($\sigma^x, \sigma^y, \sigma^z$) into rotations within the $SU(2)$ group using discrete, finite sets of quantum angles. We introduce a fully digital algorithm capable of generating Hermitian encodings of fermionic operators on qubit lattices, a capability instrumental in simulating interactions like the Hubbard model. By leveraging the formalism of discrete time crystals, our method achieves a fully digital realization using only $O(N)$ single-qubit rotation gates for an $N$-qubit system, thereby eliminating the requirement for continuous, analog control parameters. As a demonstration of its efficacy, our method successfully models ground-state correlations in the transverse Ising model and calculates the double occupancy of the Hubbard model.

Current Computer Vision methods often face the "optimization-generalization dilemma," where models achieve superior training results but struggle with real-world applications. Addressing this, the study introduces a new framework that combines data augmentation and optimization to combat these limitations. The proposed system generates abundant features by projecting data into a higher-dimensional space and subsequently reconstructing them. Optimization is then performed on both the projection and reconstruction functions to maximize output diversity. Furthermore, the research presents a novel architecture capable of handling bidirectional, nonlinear mappings between varying spaces. This method was validated across three distinct vision tasks: image classification, denoising, and colorization. Experiments confirm that the optimized model not only surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques during training but also demonstrates significant improvements in real-world generalization.

This paper introduces a new flowchart-based light field (FLC) assisted spatial light modulator (SLM) framework designed to generate several complex beam shapes simultaneously within a 3D tissue volume. Unlike previous FLC-SLM approaches limited to a single beam, this method enables concurrent delivery of multiple beams targeting distinct locations, a capability that could significantly advance 3D tissue imaging and targeted photostimulation. The proposed flowchart allows for the independent configuration of beam parameters, such as focal point and shape, and was validated using simulated data alongside experimental results featuring beams focused at different points in agar. These experiments confirmed the successful formation of intricate structures at various depths, marking a notable advancement over earlier multi-beam FLC-SLM methodologies.

This study outlines the design and implementation of an 8$\times$8 monolithic small photodiode array operating at 3$\times$3 mm$^2$ each, utilizing an $n^+$-on-$p$-Si configuration. Designed as a proof-of-concept for the future CTIDE telescope array, the monolithic structure features small collection electrodes atop the surface. To optimize photodiode performance for the CTIDE application, we evaluated the influence of the photogenerator sensor thickness and the n-type silicon substrate material. Consequently, we recommend an $n$-type silicon resistivity range of 0.01 to 0.1 $\Omega$ cm and a photogenerator thickness between 10 and 20 $\mu$m.

The Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics (AO) Testbed, an experimental facility featuring a 4-meter aperture, is uniquely equipped to explore advanced AO concepts for future large telescopes. This site recently implemented the Atmospheric Self-Coherent Camera (ASCC) technique, which offers significant advantages over traditional methods by utilizing natural guide stars and demanding fewer wavefront sensors and actuators. We describe initial experimental outcomes from applying ASCC via a Rapid ASCC algorithm, which employs open-loop control at an exceptionally high rate of 10 kHz. These findings demonstrate the capability to track speckles in the focal plane caused by turbulence at velocities exceeding the speed of sound.

This study introduces a new closed-form solution for a specific constant interest rate (CIR) model that incorporates a small, fixed deterministic shift to guarantee negative rates, addressing a recognized research gap. The model's theoretical framework is rigorously validated, and its parameters are estimated using the Maximum Likelihood Estimation method. The findings demonstrate that this proposed shifted model outperforms several standard affine term structure models in explaining the Swedish government bond yield curve.

Short baseline neutrino oscillation experiments are currently investigating the $3\nu$ oscillation framework, a strategy that could also reveal sterile neutrino states if they exist. We evaluate the potential of the DUNE facility to detect short baseline anomalies indicative of a light sterile neutrino, noting that despite DUNE's primary focus being neutrino mass and cosmology, it possesses the capability to address these questions. Utilizing its anticipated high-luminosity near detector, we evaluate its sensitivity to NR interactions, an area often underexplored in current long-term neutrino programs. Through a systematic analysis of final states across the near detector, we demonstrate that DUNE can significantly enhance searches for sterile neutrinos, achieving sensitivities comparable to or exceeding those of existing short baseline facilities.

Meta-analysts frequently struggle to access individual effect size data, forcing them to work with aggregates. Although Stanley and Russo (2021) introduced robust methods for handling dependent effect sizes within a single domain, these methods are insufficient for multilevel structures typical in meta-anthropology, particularly when effect sizes are derived from clusters such as studies or participants. Consequently, this paper proposes Cluster-Sturdy Estimators (CSE), a new class of estimators designed specifically to analyze the dependency inherent in those hierarchical data sources. Our method utilizes aggregate mean and variance values at each cluster level to generate cluster-specific effect estimates, which then undergo a final stage of smoothing to derive global parameters. The initial phase involves constructing effects by applying a generalized linear model (GLM) to the clustered meta-analytic data. The subsequent phase employs smoothing techniques derived from locally weighted regression (LWR), yielding closed-form solutions for both the cluster and overall estimates. The final section applies a variance-stabilizing transformation to these estimates before the smoothing process. The estimator's performance is validated through a comprehensive simulation study, which demonstrates that CSE outperforms existing approaches in every metric. The paper concludes by applying CSE to a real dataset concerning the impact of social media on political polarization.

Particle-resolved simulations are frequently employed to investigate multiphase systems at a microscale where individual particles retain solid-fluid interactions lasting longer than a single time-step. These prolonged interactions can compromise simulation stability, yet simulating with time-steps exceeding the critical threshold for non-overlapping particles is computationally expensive. This study introduces an efficient multi-time-step integration method tailored for partile-resolved multiphase dynamics, featuring a sub-stepping strategy. Within this framework, fluid momentum and mass exchange are calculated using an explicit sub-stepping approach, while the momentum transfer arising from hydrodynamic forces and fluid-fluid interactions is handled implicitly. Applied to simulate two-dimensional flows through random packed beds, the method demonstrates second-order accuracy and achieves a ten-fold increase in the time-step size compared to conventional approaches utilizing direct long-duration contact models. Furthermore, the method successfully captures collision dynamics and post-collision separation of particles.

In this study, we examine the origins of radiation produced by black holes and accelerating entities. Our analysis indicates that such emission arises from the combined influence of the emitter's motion and the properties of the field itself, rather than the radiation originating from within the black hole or external radiation pressure effects. Consequently, we propose that the terms "Hawking radiation" and "Unruh radiation" should be replaced by "acceleration radiation," a designation reflecting the nature of this emission more accurately.

Using the color dipole framework, we calculate the lateral momentum imbalance of produced baryons, a quantity of significant importance for experimental verification. In our model, the baryon momentum asymmetry arises from gluon emissions that penetrate the baryon's color flux tube, a mechanism that simultaneously generates transverse momentum. We further propose that this observed momentum imbalance can serve as a reliable indicator of the saturation scale, which can be extracted by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data.

This paper presents and proves four lemmas that enable the determination of all whole-number solutions for $ b $ given $ b \neq 0 $ in the equation $ b^2 + ab + a^2 = 7^n $. By utilizing these lemmas, we have derived and demonstrated a theorem providing the complete set of solutions $ (a,n) $ for any given $ b $.

This study examines the interfacial instability occurring between two superposed viscous fluids, specifically focusing on an inertial case where both fluids have positive bulk densities. We analyze a specific configuration in which a fluid-invasion type liquid-liquid finger instability develops: a stream of fluid with lower density and higher viscosity penetrates the adjacent channel flow consisting of a higher-density fluid with higher viscosity. Our analysis indicates that while this particular instability configuration is inherently stable when governed by classical Rayleigh-Plateau (PR) mechanisms, it can become unstable due to the combined effects of buoyancy and PR forces. We derive analytical expressions for the most unstable wavenumbers and corresponding growth rates, which demonstrate a clear dependence on the system's physical parameters, including viscosity, density, surface tension, flow velocities, and flow rates. These theoretical predictions are further supported by numerical simulations performed using a weakly coupled linearized framework.

The evolution of non-volatile computing systems has introduced new reliability challenges, particularly in High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments. Unlike volatile RAM, data preserved in non-volatile layers remains uncorrected once written, and system crashes can lead to severe data corruption. Current solutions often rely on conservative strategies like journaling or write-back caching, which sacrifice performance to guarantee complete data integrity. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel algorithm that ensures reliable operations within HPC systems while maintaining optimal performance. By detecting and managing corruption at the point of data usage rather than point of write, this method reduces overhead significantly. Furthermore, the approach is universally compatible with various file systems and storage algorithms. Empirical results indicate that while ensuring reliable data access, the new algorithm boosts write throughput by up to 10× and improves overall system performance by as much as 1.4× compared to conventional non-volatile storage techniques.

Although this field is vital, the development of scalable methods to handle the increasingly vast size of these networks remains challenging. We propose a statistical method to predict the outcomes of chaotic systems, specifically within the context of the three-body problem. A flux function is introduced to quantify the probability of a system's trajectory entering a specific region of phase space. This approach allows for a test of chaotic future predictability by comparing statistical outcomes against standard Monte Carlo simulations. Applying this method to the equal-mass three-body problem, we contrast our results with those of standard simulations to verify accuracy. The study demonstrates that the proposed statistical model can reliably forecast the statistical properties of chaotic systems over timeframes up to 1000 units, which corresponds to roughly ten times the system's Hamiltonian period.

This letter presents a comprehensive, data-driven analysis of quenching mechanisms for charmonium states in PbPb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV. Nuclear modification factors ($R_{\rm AA}$) for both $\mathrm{J}/\psi$ and $\Psi(2\mathrm{S})$ were measured across ten centrality bins and four transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) ranges. To isolate quenching effects from cold nuclear matter influences, cross-section ratios relative to proton-proton collisions were normalized. Subsequently, these measurements were compared with predictions from a suite of theoretical models. The findings indicate that prompt $\mathrm{J}/\psi$ quenching is consistent with both parton energy loss and nuclear absorption scenarios, whereas nonprompt $\mathrm{J}/\psi$ quenching aligns best with models predicting significant charm quark diffusion through the quark-gluon plasma.

We introduce a new category for continuous logic that parallels Leinster's standard example, (BoolStochTop)*, where objects are complete boolean algebras and morphisms are conditionally σ-measurable functions. In our formulation, morphisms are algebra homomorphisms between complete uniformity algebra algebra (ComUAlg), specifically homomorphisms that are bounded by a σ-measurable norm. This framework is used to demonstrate that our proposed category is not equivalent to (BoolStochTop)* under Leinster's definition.

This paper introduces a user-centric approach to software framework selection that prioritizes users' existing code and test suites to determine compatibility. The core algorithm analyzes the source code of the target framework and users' code to identify the most probable integration point, or API, shared between them. While the original method functions on full codebases to find this API, the proposed system leverages Unique Value Decomposition (UVD) to execute the analysis in a distributed, high-performance manner. By running the selection process across multiple users in parallel, the system optimally allocates computing resources and significantly boosts processing efficiency.

This study introduces a new deep sequential architecture designed to detect suicidal ideation across multiple modalities. The system processes data from six sources: clinical notes, social media posts, and information derived from Twitter and Facebook, alongside user demographics and affective metrics. We evaluated the model using the SuSiE dataset, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.615. Furthermore, we explored how varying data combinations impact performance and assessed the system's cross-cultural effectiveness by testing it on the English-speaking SuSiE corpus with German-language input.

Using the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE), researchers have detected clear x-ray polarization signals from the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (CasA). The observed polarization degree is 2.2+/-0.6% at an energy level of 2-10 kevs, which aligns with expectations from thermal emission models. This finding supports the theory that non-thermal emission from CasA originates primarily from electrons within a magnetized shock front, rather than through magnetic turbulence in a diffuse medium. Furthermore, the study reveals x-ray polarization degrees ranging from 1.5% to 2.5% across the 2-10 kevs spectrum, with a slight increase in polarization as energy rises. The derived absolute polarized flux is consistent with previously determined absolute flux values.

The contemporary author is revisiting Erdos's unique-sums conjecture, which posits that for any set A containing n positive integers, the number of distinct sums formed by its elements (each used at most once) exceeds 2^n - 1. The case where equality nearly holds—specifically the count being no more than 2 log₂ n—is examined. It is demonstrated that if such a finite set A has the property that the sum of its k smallest elements never falls outside a specific small interval relative to the total sum, then every element in A must share the same parity. Furthermore, by adapting a specific lemma regarding the injectivity of binary vector mappings, the paper establishes a broader upper limit of 2(n+k)^{O(1)} on the count S(A), a figure significantly exceeding the original bound proposed by Erdos yet tighter than previous generalizations.

The sound speed in dense matter, which is crucial for understanding the equation of state, was examined using the relativistic mean-field framework. By incorporating the effects of strange quarks, we analyzed dense stellar composition and evaluated the sound speed. Our findings indicate that while the sound speed exceeds $c/\sqrt{3}$ in pure quark gas due to interactions, it drops below this threshold in dense matter due to those very same interaction effects. We further demonstrated that density thresholds for the appearance of strange quarks and/or chiral symmetry restoration align with the conditions required to form compact stars specifically as neutron stars. Consequently, compact stars exhibiting radii greater than 11 km may consist primarily of strange quark matter rather than just neutron star matter.

We examine how varying the squeezing and shift parameters affects the Fock space of a single-mode quantum harmonic oscillator, focusing on the decomposition of the resulting compass state into its constituent Fock components. Analyzing the mean and fluctuating values of these components reveals that increasing either the squeezing or the shift parameter significantly boosts both first- and second-order moments alongside their variance. Specifically, higher moments of these variables exhibit a linear relationship with the square of the respective parameters, while variances follow a cubic relationship.

Accurately representing the interface between fluid phases is vital for both interpreting experimental data and modeling fluids. However, existing skeleton-based interface representation methods are constrained by specific requirements, such as the need for an adequate skeleton spacing and a planar interfacial geometry. This study introduces a new, versatile interface skeletoning method that relaxes constraints regarding interfacial geometry and allows for variable skeleton spacing. The method's efficacy was validated through simulations of various multiphase flow scenarios. The resulting skeletons were employed to characterize flow topology and to generate simplified, phase-aware interface representations. Furthermore, using these skeletons, a quantitative topological descriptor was developed to classify three-phase interactions, with specific emphasis on analyzing liquid-liquid-gas structures within a T-junction configuration.

Recent research has revealed that certain viruses possess the remarkable ability to roll themselves up into compact, coil-like structures. This property holds significant potential for biomedicine, enabling the creation of self-assembling targeted drug delivery vehicles. In this study, we investigate the self-rolling mechanics of spherical viruses modeled as self-actuated soft spheres. By employing an energy-based framework, we demonstrate that internal self-scrolling forces are a direct outcome of the shell's bending and stretching properties. We establish criteria for predicting rolling behavior and developed energy-based formulas to calculate the distance traveled. Furthermore, we applied these concepts to a virus-like particle equipped with surface tendrils, revealing that this modification extends travel distance and enhances locomotion in environments with complex barriers.

Disk galaxies with prominent, non-planar structures are a well-known phenomenon. This study introduces a theoretical framework for "jellyfish" galaxies and "U-type" warps by applying a warp evolution model to U-type disks. The predicted morphologies from our simulation closely resemble the characteristics of U-type warps and jellyfish galaxies observed in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The formation of U-type warps and jellyfish galaxies is attributed to the combined effects of vertical self-gravity and external tidal forces acting upon a galaxy's disk. The distinct "jellyfish" morphology specifically results when a U-type warp undergoes significant amplification of its trailing arm, caused by increased tidal stretching.

"This study establishes a Theorem similar to Liouville's, applying to non-compact Ricci diminution hypersurfaces embedded within Euclidean space that possess a constant scalar curvature. Furthermore, by applying this result to various configurations, we derive several Theoremes of Liouville and characterize certain submanifolds with specific properties."

First-principles calculations reveal that KBi$_2$, RbBi$_2$, and CsBi$_2$ adopt the Laves phase cubic structure, characterized by a low-frequency optical vibration mode. Density functional theory (DFT) analysis shows that these materials exhibit strong anharmonicity in this specific low-frequency mode, leading to significant thermal expansion. Furthermore, the study identifies these low-frequency modes as chiral in nature, involving the collective motion of Bi atoms arranged in a chiral pattern. Notably, the electronic band structure remains unchanged whether treated with harmonic or anharmonic approximations. However, incorporating anharmonicity into molecular dynamics simulations demonstrates that the finite temperature structural properties are significantly impacted by the strong anharmonic effects of this mode.

The Born effective charge quantifies how a localized charge moves in response to an applied external force. In periodic systems, this charge can diverge due to the folding of the band structure, a phenomenon that has significant implications for materials featuring flat bands. We demonstrate that within a simple one-dimensional free-electron model, this charge manifests as a resonant response to an oscillating electric field, with its magnitude determined by the amplitude of the lattice. Furthermore, we show that a non-zero DC electrical response—arising from perfectly correlated displacements of equivalent charges—causes the oscillatory displacement of these coupled charges to vanish. These findings offer fresh perspectives on the physical meaning of a non-integer integer charge in periodic lattices and reveal a previously unidentified connection between Born effective charges and Drude weight.

This study investigates the emergence of inertial cascades and their associated dynamics within turbulent flows of liquids featuring both short- and long-range forces, using Monte Carlo simulations on coarse-grained Bead-rod models. The results indicate that the dissipative zone in these fluids is characterized by significant fluctuations in local density, specific volume, and temperature. Furthermore, temperature disturbances propagate outward from heat sources as thermally active patches, coexisting with a concurrent heat flux aligned with the velocity cascade cascade.

This work introduces a magnetoelectric effect that arises in noncentrosymmetric, nonmagnetic insulators, where an electric field induces a current of magnetic flux and conversely, where magnetic fields generate an electric current. Unlike the conventional linear magnetoelectric effect, this version relies on strong electric fields to drive significant electromagnetic cross-coupling while preserving time-reversal symmetry. We identify a geometric origin for this phenomenon and calculate its strength using a $\mathbb{Z}$-valtopological invariant defined over momentum space. We further examine two emergent consequences: (i) a surface charge density characterized by fractional values, representing a dilaton Witten effect; and (ii) a quantum Hall response with half-integer values, interpreted as a geometric manifestation of the magnetoelectric effect.

This study introduces a novel mechanism for chaotic behavior in delay systems, driven by the modulation of delays. When periodically varied, the modulation induces a novel instability that disperses trajectories throughout the phase space. The dispersion originates from the interplay between modulated time scales and the accumulation of stretching and folding within iterations. The phenomenon was verified through a simple one-dimensional delayed feedback model and an extended analysis of a two-dimensional delayed Rössler system. The results demonstrate a significant increase in both stretching and folding as delays are modulated, leading to a substantial rise in the system's Lyapunov dimension. The findings suggest that the proposed mechanism can generate chaos even under weak delay modulation with a distinct signature in the modulated output spectrum. The dispersion mechanism is further linked to applications in controlling chaotic attractors and constructing delay systems with specific target attractors.

The random lambda calculus extends traditional term-based lambda calculus by incorporating a probabilistic dimension. Its core operations include: (1) probabilistically selecting between two specific reduction strategies, and (2) choosing a uniform random element from a finite set of equivalent terms during beta-reduction. This process generates a probability distribution over potential execution traces, defining semantics at both individual and global levels. At the micro level, we examine the behavior of specific computational entities like variables, abstractions, and applications, as well as variable binding and environment management. Conversely, the macro-level analysis focuses on program properties, establishing soundness by linking global meaning to these local rules. A key finding is that the resulting global semantics adheres to a continuous Markov chain featuring a unique, ergodic measure, with its transition rules derived directly from local mechanisms.

Previous research into automated extraction of dialogues for concept validation has primarily focused on optimizing the accuracy of extracted entities and relations, often neglecting the potential natural language conclusions that could guide the actual mining process. This study addresses this gap by proposing Conclusion Robustness for Natural Language (CRUL), a novel RLHF-aligned reward function designed to enhance both the correctness of inferred conclusions and the quality of resulting dialogue analysis. CRUL functions by prompting an inference agent to draw conclusions from conversations, submitting these findings to a human-rater prompt for CRUF scoring, and finally refining the dialogue mining model through an iterative reinforcement loop. Evaluated against the existing state-of-the-art on the DesignDialogues dataset, the inferring agent demonstrated a significant improvement in accuracy when paired with a human-feedback CRUF-enhanced miner, which showed superior performance compared to a baseline system relying solely on a default automatic sentence-similarity finality metric.

This paper introduces a novel model of the universe in which the vacuum's zero-point field constitutes reality's fundamental substrate. In this framework, the visible universe emerges through retro-causality as a coherent, macroscopic quantum state formed by quantum entanglement between matter and this zero-point field. The mechanism relies on the synchronization of a post-inflation macro-quantum-coherent field with the zero-point field, triggering an entanglement that begins at the cosmic boundary (the "back" of the universe) and extends toward the present. This backward-forward causal loop ensures the conservation of information and energy throughout history.

Within this model, the zero-point field is described as a SU(2) doublet comprising a Higgs component and a Goldstone component, both massless post-inflation. The primordial inflation is explained by the coherent motion of these Goldstone modes. Simultaneously, the coherent dynamics of the doublet's Higgs part drive inflation's termination, causing the acquisition mass by the Goldstone parts via the Higgs mechanism.
