We examine a class of sub-differentiable convex functions that enable the identification of Riemannian manifolds through the use of specific step sizes. This framework unifies and extends various existing approaches, encompassing Euclidean spaces equipped with standard Euclidean metrics, spaces with arbitrary convex constraints utilizing Euclidean metrics, spaces with general constraints and induced operator metrics, and spaces with custom sub-metrics. Within this unified model, we analyze Newton-type algorithms for zero-finding, demonstrating Newtonian convergence rates of order $Q$-linear for functions with Lipschitz continuous subgradients and rates of $Q$-cubic or better for those with bounded sub-Hessian.

In this study, we introduce the concept of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals of rings and examine their fundamental properties. Additionally, we explore the relationships between feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals and other related ideal theories, specifically covering primary, absorbing, feely absorbing, and absorbing prime categories. The relationships are explored alongside distinctions regarding the separation of feely and feebly absorbing prime ideals. We further investigate the characteristics of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals within commutative rings with multiplicity one, analyzing them under quotient rings and homomorphic images to define some relevant concepts. Finally, we present several examples and counterexamples to distinguish feely from feebly absorbing prime ideals and to develop the fields of feely and feebly 1-absorbing composite ideals of composite rings.

Although astrometric techniques have successfully mapped millions of stars across the Milky Way, creating extensive catalogs, accurately linking these entries to spectroscopic databases remains a major hurdle. This study examines four existing methods for such spectroscopic matching and highlights their inherent flaws. We then propose two remedial strategies: a spectral imaging technique and a new algorithm designed to mitigate these specific limitations.

Although recent advancements in neural relation extraction (NRE) have proven highly effective for extracting knowledge from biomedical literature, they frequently fail to capture the cohesive context surrounding individual medications. In this paper, we introduce a novel medication pair scoring framework that integrates cohesive medication representations into a relational deep learning architecture. We achieve cohesive drug modeling by aggregating embeddings of associated co-occurring drugs within a sliding window. Furthermore, we introduce MedPair, a comprehensive dataset containing 118,000 medication pairs and 118,000 negative samples to benchmark our approach. Our framework was evaluated using this newly curated dataset as well as an external corpus of medication interactions, demonstrating superior performance in medication pair scoring compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of our model's behavior regarding drugs with varying co-mention frequencies.

Identifying harmful roads, such as potholes, is vital for maintaining road networks and ensuring public safety. Although numerous algorithms have been developed for this purpose, most require extensive, carefully annotated datasets that are difficult and costly to assemble. This paper introduces a method to identify potholes across different countries by leveraging transfer learning to utilize pre-existing datasets. Our approach transfers the final layer of a pre-trained model onto new target datasets, using classification as a means to adapt the model. We evaluate our strategy on two datasets from distinct nations, analyzing results using various transfer approaches, including fine-tuning the entire network versus fine-tuning only specific components. Our findings demonstrate that effective identification is achievable even with limited labeled data in new target environments through this method.

Imitation learning (IL) seeks to transfer skills from an expert to a learner across various domains. However, traditional approaches often require paired data consisting of expert and learner actions, which are frequently unavailable in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces Cross-area Imitation from Observations (CI-O), a novel framework designed to master new tasks through IL without needing simultaneous actions from both expert and learner agents. By combining an implicit cross-domain feature extractor with an explicit cross-domain feature extractor, the method effectively mitigates domain shift issues inherent in both action and observation spaces. Experimental evaluations on complex tasks within the MULEVO gaming environment demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art observation-based IL methods.

A significant unresolved issue regarding the formation of the first stars in the early Universe is whether they develop as single massive objects or in small clusters of stars. We propose that a strong magnetic field could resolve this by promoting the growth of a single star. Using ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations, we modeled a protostar in the early Universe with an initial mass of 100 solar masses ($M_{\odot}$) and a rotation period of 100 days. Our results demonstrate that a moderately strong magnetic field can cause the fragmentation of a collapsing disk, leading to the birth of a massive Pop III star. We suggest that this process is universal and could account for the observed high masses of Population III stars.

Association rules are widely used to identify relationships among variables in data sets, and various frameworks have been proposed to define the conditions under which these rules hold. This work introduces two frameworks for deducing rules within rule systems and provides criteria to identify the minimal cardinality of rules necessary to establish valid relationships defined by any deduction system. These contributions include a repeat-by-deduction framework applicable to deriving both positive and negative association rules, offering minimum cardinality results that depend on the rule's support frequency and whether it is positive or negative.

This research examines how mandated mental health treatment influences recidivism within the criminal justice system. It begins by quantifying the pre-conviction mental illness prevalence among convicted individuals, finding rates of approximately 15% for outpatient care and 20% for inpatient care. Utilizing data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997, the study employs difference-in-discontinuity analysis to assess the recidivism effects of mandated therapy. Results indicate that access to this care reduces recidivism by roughly 10% over a three-year post-conviction period.

This paper introduces a parametric variant of the generalized Apostol–Bernoulli polynomials alongside the matching chi-paramedic polynomial, leveraging the parametric type of the generalized Apostol–multiple zeta function introduced by the second author. The study establishes several important properties for these polynomials and develops related properties via a parameter-paramedic type of the generalized Apostol–multiple Legendre polynomial function.

This study introduces a novel system for radio map assessment utilizing autonomous drones equipped with software-defined radios (SDR). The software architecture is designed to support a swarm of drones, enabling them to explore the spectrum cooperatively in aerial environments. This framework allows for a distributed measurement of signal strength across diverse locations, resulting in the creation of an extensive signal strength map. The paper outlines the end-to-end system, emphasizing its distributed nature and the measurement methodology. Additionally, the proposed system demonstrates superior energy efficiency when contrasted with current approaches that rely on a single mobile unit.

Identifying anomalies in industrial systems is critical for maintaining operational efficiency and preventing equipment failure. This paper introduces a novel approach for detecting irregularities in signal processing that utilizes Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). The proposed system first constructs HMMs representing the normal operational states of specific devices. Once established, these models evaluate the likelihood of incoming data; deviations marked by low probability likelihoods are classified as anomalies. An experimental assessment conducted on acoustic signals from a ball bearing system demonstrates the method's efficacy, with results indicating superior performance when compared to existing alternative methods.

This study examines multimodal individual authentication leveraging audio-visual-thermal data, driven by the rising prevalence of surveillance cameras equipped with triple infrared sensors that capture reflected visible light, emitted thermal energy, and audible waves. The research evaluates four distinct authentication workflows: (1) extracting speakers' voiceprint and subjects' demographic traits from thermal imagery, (2) generating a visual faceprint from thermal data while verifying voice from audible sound, (3) generating a visual faceprint from visible light while verifying identity via thermal demographics, and (4) creating standard voice authentication from audible sound while using visible imagery for face recognition. The analysis employs a dataset of 100 participants, each providing 100 utterances recorded across all four modalities. The findings indicate that visible imagery yields the most precise face recognition, whereas audible sound produces superior voice authentication. However, when combining modalities, voice verification based on thermal-derived demographic information surpasses using visible-derived face information for authentication tasks.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) face persistent hurdles, including the need for vast, high-quality training datasets and limited generalization capabilities. Although transfer learning has emerged as a viable solution, it demands extensive pre-existing labeled data for well-performing reference models. We introduce a contrasting strategy: small-effort data augmentation. This approach enhances model generalization by increasing the quantity of training information through the generation of multiple equivalent speech-translation pairs per sample using various granularities of speech enhancement and synthesis. We evaluated our method on the IWSPT 2020 and 2021 test sets using a base model pre-trained on 5,000 hours of speech and bilingual data. Results demonstrate that our technique outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving a reduction of 1.0 BLEOU on IWSPT 2020 (non-continuous) and 0.8 BLEOU on IWSPT 2021 (continuous) translations relative to a standard fine-tuned fine-tuning baseline.

This paper introduces a generalized maximum likelihood method for estimating the average of multiple parameters distributed across several groups. We develop both theoretical properties and an application of this estimator, specifically examining the average of true values in a setting of imperfect sampling.

Diff erential privacy (DP) provides a robust guarantee for private datasets, yet recent research indicates that its strength diminishes significantly when data exhibits dependencies, potentially allowing adversaries to deduce sensitive attributes entirely in extreme cases, or determining them nearly uniquely with only minimal additional privacy consumption by attackers reliant on specific dependent traits. Building on this insight, the current study investigates confidentiality risks arising from dependent features within DP frameworks through a novel dependency model. The author demonstrates that an adversary holding access to a single query result containing these dependent characteristics can nearly pinpoint sensitive attributes with near-perfect accuracy. Furthermore, the work quantifies the gain in inference precision achievable by leveraging such dependent features and introduces Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation as an effective tool for actively enhancing attack success rates.

The AS 209 system features a prominent outer gap in its CO emission, which has been variously interpreted as evidence for either gas depletion or chemical processing. This study utilizes ALMA observations of CO (J = 2–1) at an angular resolution of 0.22" to investigate the coexistence of silicate dust grains and gas-phase CO in the outer regions of the disk. We find that the observed CO distribution is consistent with a solid-state to gas transition of gas-phase CO (co) occurring between 30 and 50 au, aligning with the location of the water snowline. This study introduces an open toolkit designed for analyzing time-tagged data, developed using the open-source functional programming language Comb. The software enables the creation of complex data analysis pipelines by sequencing basic operations, a methodology that enhances both reproducibility and clarity. To demonstrate its capabilities, the article details the toolkit's implementation and its use in examining photon arrival patterns from three distinct experimental setups.

We demonstrate the presence of "mild" solutions to a specific control-constrained agent's limitation framework within a mean-field game context. By leveraging an optimization approach to a related fixed-point problem, our work establishes control feasible solutions that satisfy the agent constraints strongly, even without assuming their smoothness. Crucially, this result does not require the Nash equilibrium's payoff function to be differentiable, a requirement often found in prior research regarding control constraints. These findings offer a significant foundation for future investigations into first-order optimal control problems involving control constraints.

Recent high-precision data from the Gaia mission have revealed that many prominent stellar filaments, or "threads," in the Milky Way exhibit significant spatial curvature. This discovery has prompted a re-examination of the physical mechanisms proposed to explain these structures, particularly those rooted in spiral arm dynamics. We argue that even straight stellar filaments can emerge through the combined effects of spiral arm rotation and differential rotation alone, without invoking specific star formation processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the physical dimensions of these filaments align with the characteristics of the guiding center approximation, suggesting that they represent coherent entities traveling along the mean potential rather than being static formations fixed within the rotating frame. Consequently, we propose that the traditional physical interpretation associated with stellar threads may be misleading, and we offer an alternative framework to better describe their fundamental nature.

This study introduces VICTOR, a discrepancy detection system designed to identify visual inconsistencies such as impossible combinations or illogical attributes within images. Our approach relies on a dual mechanism: contrastive pre-training and discrepancy vector construction. To effectively capture the intricate relationships between disparate visual elements, we employ a contrastive pre-training strategy that utilizes part segmentation masks to separate tokens, ensuring the transformer encoder learns robust, fine-grained representations. Following this pre-training stage, we construct specialized vectors that encode the inherent logical violations to maximize detection accuracy. Empirical results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on the Synset256 benchmark, achieving an AUC score of 0.9466.

Quantum resource theory serves as a rigorous framework for distinguishing and quantifying nonclassical light properties. This introductory survey examines recent advancements, with a specific emphasis on single-mode resources such as coherence, entanglement, and magic. We investigate how these core resources can be defined, measured, and converted through various methods, utilizing both global and local operations. Particular attention is given to transformations involving random access memory constraints. By highlighting current open questions, this work aims to outline promising avenues for future research.

This paper introduces a new asynchronous buffering algorithm for federated averaging, where the server maintains a fixed-size queue and aggregates gradients only when filling it up, rather than stopping the client workflow. Our analysis demonstrates that this method avoids constrained gradients caused by premature optimization, thereby reducing communication rounds needed for convergence while introducing specific computational complexities. Under assumptions of bounded stochastic variance and smoothness, we establish theoretical upper limits for the expected error relative to the optimal model at each algorithmic step. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for this buffered approach and prove that it converges to the gradient's unconstrained limit during gradient accumulation, meaning the gradient estimate approaches the true global gradient as the buffer reaches capacity. Finally, numerical experiments across multiple trials show that this proposed method outperforms existing federated learning techniques in terms of both communication efficiency and final model accuracy.

This study introduces a calulculus that is jointly operational, developed within a specific domain of algebraic polynomial tempered distributions. This framework encompasses the multiplication by variables $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the Euler derivations defined as $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi_i}$, and the standard partial derivatives $\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$. This approach extends the concept of Laplace operational calculus, which is well-established in generalized functions and represents a natural extension of classical operational calculus.

The Shadow Dimension (SD) serves as a low-energy effective field theory designed to resolve fundamental conflicts between general relativity and quantum mechanics, a problem it addresses by enforcing compliance with various string theory swampland conjectures. By leveraging the SD's predictions, we re-examine the early universe dynamics, specifically investigating whether a significant portion of the total dark matter could consist of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our analysis indicates that, under the most favorable conditions, the fraction of dark matter comprised of PBHs formed at temperatures of approximately $10^{10}$ K is approximately 10\%.

This paper examines fractures within particle-based, two-dimensional layered structures known as atomically thin sheets or "atomic sheets" (AS). These fractures are governed by inter-particle forces, which we model using a simplified Hertzian framework. The study reveals that the geometry of the resulting cracks is highly sensitive to the magnitude of the normal compressive stress acting between layers. Specifically, we analyze how stresses concentrate around the tips of such tips, demonstrating that these concentrations scale with a power law of exponent 1/2 relative to the distance from the tip. We further present numerical results indicating that the ultimate strength of the sheet is governed by its largest flaw, analogous to the principles of Griffith fracture theory.

The anisotropic strain exerted by lattice-matched substrates significantly influences the electronic properties of GaN. This study investigates the band structure of GaN when grown on $c$-oriented ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$, utilizing the $p$-type acceptors P, Si, C, and B as dopants. Employing state-of-the-art $ab$-initio calculations, we examine valence band structures and analyze the mechanisms behind mobility variations. Our findings reveal that aligning the GaN layer with the $\langle 11\bar{2}0\rangle$ direction relative to the MgSiN$_2$ substrate yields a mobility increase of 100%, whereas alignment with the $\langle 10\bar{1}0\rangle$ direction offers a 60% boost compared to free-standing GaN. Furthermore, we determine the optimal doping strategies to maximize mobility for each substrate and dopant combination. Notably, P-doped GaN exhibits the highest mobility when oriented along the $\langle 11\bar{2}0\rangle$ direction on a ZnGeN$_2$ substrate, surpassing free-standing values by 120%. These results underscore the critical role of substrate-induced anisotropic strain in enhancing GaN hole mobility.

This study introduces a nonlinear regression approach designed to handle functionally significant tasks, specifically denoting them as Temporal Variation Learning (TVL). TVL is implemented using Sparse Gaussian Process (SGP) models, which partition a regression function into a time-invariant component and a time-dependent component. The former is shared by all functions within a dataset, whereas the latter evolves with time and is parameterized as a temporal function, the critical "temporal variation point" (TVP). By selecting only those time points where this evolution is most pronounced, TVL achieves significant model sparsification. A primary application of TVL lies in marine robot navigation, where it addresses position estimation amidst noisy sensor data. Furthermore, the proposed system supports active learning by determining the optimal locations for acquiring new data. Simulation results confirm that the proposed method yields superior learning efficiency and enhanced estimation accuracy.

A complex isothermal surface is defined as a conformal mapping $f: \Sigma \to \mathbb{C}P^1$ from a Riemann surface $\Sigma$ to the Riemann sphere, characterized by its associated data $(\lambda, \mu)$, where $\lambda$ represents the trace and $\mu$ the determinant of the associated linear ODE $u'' + (\lambda/2)u = 0$. Specifically, $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are meromorphic 1-forms of specific types. A primary finding of this work demonstrates that given any pair of meromorphic 1-forms $(\lambda, \mu)$, there exists an corresponding isothermal surface $f$, up to an automorphism of the domain $\Sigma$. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the group of isothermal surfaces for a fixed $(\lambda, \mu)$ and the multiplicative nonzero constants $\mathbb{C}^*$ that scale solutions of the associated ODE. Additionally, we detail transformations of $(\lambda, \mu)$ that yield new isothermal surfaces and explicitly provide the governing differential equations for these cases. Particular attention is given to instances where $(\lambda, \mu)$ are differential forms derived from Darboux or Calapso transformations acting on a standard flat metric on $\Sigma$.

This study introduces a class of semi-parametric estimators for conditional expectation functions within a univariate framework utilizing one covariate. The methodology combines a univariate kernel density estimator with a kernel regression estimator, whose bandwidth is optimized via data-driven selection. The bandwidth selection process relies on minimizing the integrated squared error of intermediate density and regression estimates, thereby eliminating the need for arbitrary manual tuning. Furthermore, the main estimator achieves the optimal minimax rate of convergence, demonstrating smoothness even with a bandwidth selected through this data-driven approach.

Identifying summation formulas is a key characteristic of any special number sequence. This work establishes several such identities for the $\lambda$-version of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We begin by establishing basic properties and deriving both recurrence relations and two distinct methods of computing these numbers. Furthermore, we utilize generalized binomial coefficients along with $\lambda$-factorials to formulate various identities.

Link prediction is a fundamental task within knowledge graph reasoning, while forecasting future entity links based on historical evolution presents a critical challenge in Temporal Knowledge Graphs (KGs). Although recent advances in deep learning have driven significant progress in this field, the methods remain largely underperformed by established deep learning models. This paper investigates the potential of static models, specifically those utilizing low-level embeddings, for link forecasting. We find that these simpler frameworks not only match the accuracy of top deep learning approaches but also offer distinct benefits: simpler design, greater interpretability, and efficient training. Furthermore, the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in a distributed training setting.

The study addresses the problem of deriving a Morita equivalence between $C^*$-algebras associated with graphs, given a known shift equivalence at the graph level connecting their underlying structures. Focusing on connected, undirected graphs with a row-finite constraint, the analysis establishes that a shift equivalence between them necessitates Morita equivalences among their corresponding $C^*$-algebras. Furthermore, this equivalence exhibits a robust characteristic: it remains valid even if undetermined isolated vertices are added to otherwise equivalent connected components, effectively allowing equivalence to be established across broader classes of graphs composed of such connected components.

Heavy quark fragmentation, which serves as a probe of the quark-gluon plasma, is examined within the general propagator framework under the influence of an intense external magnetic field. By calculating the anisotropic momentum distribution of charm quarks, we identify that the magnetic field not only suppresses their yield but also induces significant anisotropies in momentum distribution. This distinct anisotropy is found to depend on temperature, the strength of the magnetic field, and the degree of plasma anisotropies.

In knowledge-based question answering, integrating a knowledge graph (KG) into a large language model (LLM) enhances the generation of responses. However, directly injecting an entire KG is computationally expensive and often hinders the model's ability to infer critical information due to sparsity. To address this, we introduce an LLM-enhanced method tailored for free-form question answering that incorporates an inference layer. This layer enables the model to deduce missing facts by reasoning over a structured KG, thereby enhancing performance on KG-inclusive queries. We evaluate our approach using the ComplexWebQuestions dataset, which involves combining two natural language questions to form a KG-inclusive statement. Results demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms strong baseline LLM methods.

Expander graphs represent a highly significant concept within theoretical computer science and mathematics, finding applications ranging from computer science to combinatorics. A specific novel class, known as High Dimensional Expands Graphs (HDEGs), has recently emerged and is now utilized in diverse fields such as coding theory, theoretical computer science, and geometry. These graphs can be constructed by sampling vertices and edges from a high-dimensional grid under specific constraints. This paper introduces a new methodology for generating HDEGs by leveraging vertex covers on graphs. Our approach allows for the efficient construction of these structures even when the vertex count grows super-linearly. Effectively, our framework establishes a superset encompassing all currently existing High Dimensional Expands Graphs (HDEGs).

This paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation of 1,128 unique zero-shot prompting formulations, spanning seven distinct choice tasks, to identify the most effective instruction prefixes for each. We further investigate the relationships between these choice tasks and the underlying capabilities of zero-shot prompting, analyzing model performance using both GPT-3 and InstructGPT. Our findings reveal a significant overlap in abilities across different choice tasks and offer valuable insights into the connections between specific zero-shot prompting variants and task effectiveness. Ultimately, this research provides practical guidance for developing and refining similar high-performing prompt strategies.

This paper investigates the $\mathscr{L}$-invariants of motivic Artin $L$-functions defined over an $l$-adic field $\mathbb{K}$. We demonstrate that the invariants of a specific class of Artin $L$-functions can be expressed using $p$-adic Regisberger values of multiple zeta functions. Furthermore, we provide rationality conditions determining exactly when an $\mathscr{L}$-invariant is expected to be rational.

Detecting multiband microwave and terahertz radiation emitted by quantum devices is vital for characterizing their quantum states. However, conventional detection methods struggle with low signal-to-noise ratios when dealing with weak signals. In this study, we present an improved strategy for identifying weak Rydberg multiterahertz microwaves by employing a deep neural network to analyze audio data from a standard detector. This method enhances detection efficiency by approximately 40% compared to traditional approaches. We anticipate that this framework will facilitate more efficient spectroscopic analysis of future quantum systems.

The central region of UGC 8839, a nearby spiral galaxy, displays a strikingly uniform distribution of neutral hydrogen (HI) across its central 2.5 kiloparsecs, characterized by a flat velocity profile and negligible velocity dispersion. This unexpected behavior is modeled as a "hyper-constant" disk, a phenomenon attributed to a massive, centrally concentrated supermassive black hole that gravitationally dominates the dynamics of the inner disk. Our analysis indicates that UGC 8839's central HI mass is approximately $1.1 \times 10^9$ solar masses, while its central velocity curve rises sharply, reaching nearly 200 km/s within 100 parsecs. These observations imply a supermassive black hole with a mass of roughly $1.5 \times 10^9$ solar masses, based on a standard black-disk model. This finding represents the first observational evidence of a "hyper-constant" HI disk and provides the strongest current indication of a supermassive black hole in UGC 8839.

In quasiregular dynamics, the Hausdorff dimension of the Julia set is a pivotal attribute. While R\"{u}hkenm\"{u}lker established a lower bound of 2.5 for the Julia sets of all quasiregular mappings on ${\mathbb R}^3$, the author provides examples demonstrating that this dimension can exceed any given value and has no upper limit.

This study examines gravity wave dispersion and motion within Mars' lower thermosphere by analyzing neutral density observations from Mars Global Surveyor (MGS), Odyssey (ODY), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution (MAVEN) missions. These datasets were combined to generate a comprehensive set of horizontal horizontal wind velocities and density values. The analysis reveals that wave horizontal wavelengths typically range from 15 to 30 km, with vertical scales estimated between 5 and 10 km. Additionally, waves exhibit an outward radial movement from the polar regions toward the equator, displaying a latitudinal dependence in their group velocity. This specific polar outflow is interpreted as a consequence of wave propagation occurring in a wind field shaped by strong gravity wave drag and Coriolis forces.

Ultra-peripheral Pb--Pb collisions represent an ideal environment for investigating ultra-high-energy ultrahigh-energy photon-photon interactions. At the LHC, the ATLAS and LHC experiments have observed extensive spectra of lepton-antilepton pairs arising from these collisions. This paper details new findings from the ATLAS and LHC experiments concerning forward J/$\boldsymbol{\psi}$ production in Ultra-peripheral Pb--Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of 5.02 TeV. Measurements were conducted using data corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 1 nb$^{-1}$ collected by ATLAS and LHC experiments at a center-of-momentum energy of 5.02 TeV. This analysis covers transverse momentum ranges from 2.5 to 12 GeV/$\boldsymbol{\psi}$ and rapidity intervals from 2.0 to 9.0. Measured cross sections were compared against theoretical predictions derived from Ultra-peripheral Collision models.

This study addresses the challenge of generating sounds based on visual input, specifically focusing on creating meaningful audio for moving objects through a multi-modal framework. The system utilizes a visual feature derived from an image to regulate a base sound generator. We evaluate this approach across two distinct scenarios: first, mapping the orientation of a rotating object to rotation speed in a Moog Ladder filter, and second, using feature values from a walking person's imagery to adjust inter-partition times in a Markov model driven by a subtractive synthesizer. The research outlines two implementation pathways: a fully automated method employing deep learning to learn the visual-to-audio mapping, and a semi-automated method where human designers incorporate audio domain knowledge to constrain the resulting synthesis.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are renowned for their capacity to model sequential temporal data. Although the fundamental architecture of RNNs is straightforward, the mechanisms behind their ability to capture temporal dependencies remain elusive. This study investigates the inherent structure of Theoretical Hebbian Learning (THL) within the framework of recurrent networks to explain this capability. Specifically, we demonstrate that the internal state trajectory of an RNN functions as a dynamical representation of input sequences, where the dynamical features inherent to this state trajectory constitute the acquired sequential temporal knowledge. Crucially, we prove that the fundamental dynamical properties of this internal state trajectory are exclusively dictated by the weight matrices that connect hidden neurons. Consequently, the sequential temporal knowledge itself is determined solely by these inter-neuron weights. To identify a weight matrix configuration capable of representing specific temporal dynamics, we introduce a new, unsupervised, and computationally efficient unsupervised method. This approach constructs an approximate ordinary differential equation (ODE) using the acquired temporal dynamics by applying the vanishing gradient principle to recurrent networks. Finally, the newly proposed method is benchmarked against several standard supervised techniques using both synthetic data and real-world datasets.

This paper investigates the precise solution for minimizing total damages from a pandemic by combining economic and health models. By leveraging the accuracy of linearization techniques inherent in such problems, we derive closed-form expressions for the optimal control strategies. We apply a general theory to evaluate these solutions across various economic and epidemiological scenarios, revealing that total economic and welfare losses remain remarkably stable despite significant variations in model parameters. Furthermore, we examine the stability of this solution within the solution manifold using Lyapunov theory and demonstrate its robustness through numerical simulations. The findings indicate that the precise solution offers both robustness and reliability, making it a valuable tool for decision-makers.

Machine Learning (ML) has transitioned from experimental research to a standard methodology across numerous domains, enabling organizations to construct expansive systems that integrate vast data flows, extensive feature sets, and complex model architectures. Despite this widespread adoption, Shallow Data Analysis (SDA)—the practice of evaluating feature contributions to model outcomes—remains underdeveloped. Although features are central to ML, understanding their specific impact is crucial for effectively troubleshooting data issues. This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm for Feature Shapley Significance (FSS) tailored for such large-scale end-to-end pipelines. The proposed approach offers a comprehensive model-agnostic framework that accommodates end-to-end systems, including those relying on endogenous data. Empirical results validate the F-sa's accuracy in estimating feature contributions and highlight its computational efficiency when applied to extensive real-world data pipelines.

This paper examines the challenges and potential avenues in enumerative geometry, with particular attention to how cutting-edge theoretical physics influences these fields, followed by a specific analysis of tropical geometry and its application to enumerative problems.

The emergence of a quantized anomalous Hall effect in triangular antiferromagnetic materials like Mn$_3$Sn depends on the precise balance between the exchange-skiller, spin structure, and applied pressure. Under pressure, this system undergoes a transition from a Kagome antiferromagnetic state to a trimerized configuration, which eliminates the anomalous Hall signal. This specific magnetic reorganization is driven by the competition between the exchange-skiller and the trimerized structural distortion. Consequently, pressure can be utilized to control the exchange-skiller and fine-tune the anomalous Hall response.

This study offers a thorough review of recent deep neural network architectures used in relation extraction, alongside their applications and limitations. The examination begins by defining the relation extraction task and analyzing the evolution from traditional methods to deep learning models. It categorizes current systems into three groups: (i) those encoding sentences as vectors, (ii) those processing sentences as sequences, and (iii) those utilizing span extraction. The paper concludes by summarizing the most pressing challenges in this field and suggesting promising future research avenues.

This paper examines a Steklov-Robin type eigenproblem defined by the system $\Delta u + \lambda (1 + |u|^2) h = 0$ in a domain $\Omega$ subject to the boundary condition $\partial_{\nu} u + \mu |u|^q = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$. Under the conditions that $\Omega$ is either bounded with a $C^{1}$ boundary or extends to be unbounded, and that the parameters $\mu$ and $h$ satisfy specific constraints, the work establishes the existence of non-trivial bounded solutions.

Modern techniques for building 3D surface models from point clouds are highly efficient, yet they often fail to represent complex features like loops and multi-planar structures. To capture these details, we investigate hypergraph-based reconstructions, which can model both surfaces and higher-order topological elements. However, existing methods struggle with surface-adjacent hyperedges, frequently resulting in ambiguous or invalid edges. We introduce a new approach that utilizes a guided strategy to resolve this ambiguity. Specifically, we first build a rough "guidance graph" containing both faces and adjacent hyperedges from the point cloud; this rough model is then refined to create a precise canonical framework. Finally, we assign the hyperedges to either the surface or its neighboring area in a way that maximizes an energy function, ensuring global optimality. Our method was tested on various synthetic scenarios as well as real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to reconstruct complex structures that elude current state-of-the-art methods.

Automated systems for analyzing chest radiographs are increasingly vital for public health, especially given the necessity of rapid, large-scale screening during emerging infectious outbreaks. However, existing computer vision models often struggle to match radiologists in accuracy and reliability. Our study introduces Radiology-QA, a novel, high-fidelity dataset featuring 1,000 high-resolution chest X-rays with comprehensive annotations covering disease labels, quantitative measurements, and region-specific information. These multi-dimensional markers were created by synthesizing inputs from multiple expert radiologists to ensure consistency and depth. To validate our annotation strategy, we implemented and tested several state-of-the-art algorithms for quantitative feature extraction. Furthermore, we developed a unique projection technique that reconstructs our 2D radiographic images in 3D space using CT data to verify the anatomical and diagnostic accuracy of our measurements. We have made this dataset publicly available to encourage future research in radiographic analysis.

We establish a upper limit for the Euler characteristic of the Thurston norm unit ball's interior, which is intersected by the contact manifold $M$ carrying a tight contact structure that is non-divisible; this characteristic can be estimated using the sectional curvature of the manifold $M$. For the case of non-contact taut foliations, we demonstrate this same relationship, proving equality holds when the manifold $M$ is hyperbolic. On the other hand, regarding the lower bound of the Euler characteristic for such norms units intersecting $M$ with non-contact taut foliations, we utilize the Euler characteristics of the boundary components of $M$ to provide an estimate derived from the boundary data.

Microcavity lasers are renowned for their ultra-narrow spectral linewidth and high spectral brightness, making them indispensable in fields ranging from precision metrology and quantum information to biological sensing. Despite these advantages, their emitted light is typically confined to a limited solid angle, restricting their utility in applications demanding both directional propagation and small spectral angles. This work introduces an entropic gauge method to characterize and control the spatial coherence and entropy of microcavity output. We demonstrate that a simple structural modification can effectively enhance the entropy and direct the beam emission. Furthermore, the proposed methodology offers a versatile framework for analyzing and manipulating the characteristics of light sources.

This study evaluates the cost stability of major cryptocurrencies to determine their viability as a medium of exchange, ultimately concluding that Bitcoin surpasses its peers in this regard. The research employs two distinct approaches: first, it analyzes historical time series data using an Error Correction Model (ECM) to determine long-run cost stability, finding that only Bitcoin and Ethereum sustain stability over extended periods. Second, it calculates real-world cost volatility within cryptocurrency markets to assess cost risk, using this metric to explain why Bitcoin emerges as the clear leader due to its superior stability compared to other digital currencies.

Although the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation serves as a cornerstone model for random growth phenomena, its nonlinear nature has historically impeded analytical progress. Recently, a feeble noise theory was developed by Lin and Xu, enabling exact analysis of the equation under weak stochastic conditions. This study demonstrates that, by leveraging reverse time scattering within a Zakharov-Shabat system, one can generalize this approach. Specifically, noise strength in terms of larger but but still small is achievable. By utilizing an inverse scattering transform framework, exact solutions are derived for arbitrary times and spatial points, even when initial data exhibits randomness.

Compressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence has been identified in situ by the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MHS) mission within the solar wind, characterized by intermittent, large-amplitude compressive structures (CSs) that are often highly sheared. These features are hypoized to be solitons or shock waves, with their sheared boundaries triggering kinetic-scale interactions. This study examines the turbulent properties of these events using the MMS spacecraft's high-time-resolution electric potential measurements. We analyze the time-series data of the electric field parallel to the mean magnetic field ($E_{\parallel}$) and the local electron density ($n_e$) to determine the electric field component ($E_{\parallel}$) and electron density ($n_e$) along the mean magnetic field direction. The results indicate that the electric field parallel to the mean magnetic field ($E_{\parallel}$) and electron density ($n_e$) along the mean magnetic field direction. The generation of isolated attosecond pulses is essential for capturing electron motion on that timescale. A pulse is created by combining a few optical cycles of light with circular polarization in an elliptically polarized field; however, the resulting spectrum is typically symmetric, yielding a carrier-envelope phase (CEP) with low stability. Consequently, selecting a carrier cycle with inconsistent phase leads to an unpredictable spectral peak timing, resulting in a carrier with low stability. To resolve this, we propose a new approach: applying a slowly varying chirp across the spectrum using chirp tapering. This technique shifts the spectral peak to the chirped envelope's minimum, ensuring high stability. Our simulations demonstrate that even with a modest bandwidth of 10%, this method produces a spectral peak with over 90% stability.

The study examines a system of two parallel, optically thin layers of viscous incompressible fluids separated by an interface, subject to external periodic forcing. The analysis focuses on the conditions required for steady-state physical optics (PO) estimation to remain valid within this two-layer PO framework. It is demonstrated that within a specific parameter range, the standard PO assumption breaks down, necessitating a full wave-based approach. Conversely, the pure PO model remains appropriate beyond this threshold. A comprehensive and rigorous mathematical formulation is provided, accounting for both the linear and weakly non-linear regimes.

Gerrymandering represents a distortion of elections achieved through the manipulation of district boundaries. Although it is challenging to detect because the resulting district maps often appear plausible on the surface, a suitable algorithm for generating undistorted countermaps can effectively demonstrate such misconduct. Heating, a technique previously employed for near-optimal detection of overhangs, has been adapted here to produce simulated annealing. This modified process generates diverse collections of alternative districting scenarios. We have developed an outcomes-based metric evaluating the degree of Gerrymandering, utilizing these undistorted simulations to benchmark the performance of various existing and new undistorted map strategies. Furthermore, we present an improved algorithm for producing undistorted simulations and offer map-generated insights specifically for the 2012 election results in Pennsylvania.

Flaw identification in textile images is crucial for quality control within the industry. While human inspectors remain prevalent, their tendency toward fatigue-induced errors highlights the urgent need for automated alternatives. However, existing automated systems often struggle with the specific characteristics of textile images, particularly the high similarity between flaws and normal patterns, leading to subpar performance in current methodologies. To address this, we introduce a new Gabor-Haar cascaded Gabor pyramid (GHOG) descriptor that effectively captures local image features. Furthermore, leveraging the inherent low-rank structure of patterned images, we integrate this GHOG descriptor with a matrix completion approach for flaw detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms both traditional techniques and state-of-the-art solutions in real-world applications.

This research introduces a novel visual navigation framework that integrates reinforcement learning (RL) with an information-theoretic penalty to enhance navigation efficiency. Unlike standard RL approaches where agents learn a single policy per state, our proposed policy incorporates multi-step future planning. By dynamically adjusting the information-theoretic regulation of an agent's behavior based on remaining task steps, we achieve a uniform distribution of actions, thereby mitigating the tendency to settle into a local optimum. This mechanism boosts exploration and accelerates learning. Our approach was validated within the AI2-WebWorld environment, a text-based world with a fully observable Markov decision process (MDP). Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses several baseline techniques in both learning speed and final performance.

We establish a limit on the possibility of Bondi mass reduction. Consider any future-directed null geodesic originating from null infinity within an asymptotically flat spacetime. The corresponding component of the Bondi-Regge-Tamburini (Bondi) energy-momentum complex, evaluated along this path, remains non-negative. Consequently, the rate at which Bondi mass decreases over time cannot exceed a specific negative threshold.

We investigate binary black hole (BBH) mergers within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) of the first-generation stellar populations, focusing on systems where stars formed in dense clusters that subsequently migrated inward via dynamical processes. Our analysis covers BBHs of varying masses and initial formation times, examining their gravitational wave (GW) signals across a broad frequency spectrum. We find that the majority of these sources emit signals below 10 Hz, rendering them inaccessible to current detectors like LIGO and Virgo, and instead are best observed by future pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). We estimate the merger rate density to be between 10 and 1,000 Mpc$^{-3}$ Gyr$^{-1}$, with the bulk of events originating from systems formed more recently and possessing higher masses. This population offers a significant contribution to the stochastic GW background detectable by PTAs, potentially allowing for the identification of distinct peaks in the frequency domain that could serve as evidence for early-universe star formation.

This paper introduces a data-driven approach to identify incidents within distribution systems, specifically targeting the detection of issues such as tap changer malfunctions, line faults, and load shifts. The proposed framework relies on residual analysis, which measures the discrepancy between outputs from a data-driven model and actual field measurements. Specifically, a model utilizing synchronized voltage and current data predicts the expected current for various fault conditions. When significant deviations occur between these predictions and real-time readings, the system flags an incident. The strategy is validated using open-source measurement datasets, and the results are compared against a conventional method relying on zero-sequence current analysis.

The decay of $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi \delta$ is investigated within the framework of hadronic molecular model. The initial decay step, $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$, is analyzed using the mechanism of vector meson dominance, while the subsequent $1^{3}P_0$ annihilation of $\pi \gamma$ into $\pi\pi \delta$ is examined. The derived predictions for the differential and total decay distributions are compared with existing experimental data.

We present a categorical characterization of the Hom-worksheet for the Veronese embedding, $v_d:\mathbb{P}^{n} \to \mathbb{P}^{N}$, where $d\geq 2$ and $\mathbb{P}^n$ is governed by projective space. This study extends prior research by Buan and S\"{u}l{\uacute}k (2009), who provided a similar description for the quadratic Veronese map. Our findings further explore the global properties of these embedded projective spaces and their associated homogeneous ideals.

Text-based games like ALEPH, TW, andMW offer a proven platform for assessing and improving natural language agents. However, within this research, we present Express, a novel, high-speed environment for these text adventures. Express features two key components: a high-performance engine capable of executing 1,000 simulation steps per second using multi-threading, and an expressive language system that enables the creation of diverse customized tasks. This system utilizes byte-code compiled from a high-level pseudo-code to render these environments. The researchers evaluated Express by testing various state-of-the-art language agents on three specific benchmarks. The results indicate that the agents achieved higher success rates compared to previous performance on standard platforms. Furthermore, the agents demonstrated the ability to acquire transferable skills when introduced to similar customized environments. The source code for Express is publicly available at https://github.com/aleph-aiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaiaia

Topological Insulators (TIs) are a class of materials that support conducting surface states protected by a gap in their bulk. While flaws within TI materials can cause backscattering of surface states, they do not necessarily eliminate these states; instead, they may only localize them. Consequently, a long-range conduction mechanism should still exist across the surface. However, existing k-spatial approaches fail to capture this conduction because they rely on defining a local wavevector, which becomes undefined in regions of disorder. To address this limitation, we introduce a purely local formulation that circumvents the need for a wavevector. By applying this A-formulation to a flawed HgTe quantum well, we demonstrate a new long-range conduction mechanism, offering complementary insights to traditional methods.

We establish pointwise bounds for $p$-harmonic functions within planar sectors exhibiting power growth at infinity. For non-trivial cases where $p \neq 2$, these bounds rely on coefficients derived from positive one-dimensional hypergeometric functions. In our analysis, key coefficients for $p$-harmonic functions defined on planar cones are initially established, with special focus given to values of $p$ lying between $0$ and $2$.

This paper introduces a new multivariate spatial model designed to simulate extreme peaks of a Gaussian environment while respecting the unidirectional or multidirectional spatial dependence structures observed in real-world data. The proposed framework is grounded in a specific transformation of the standard conditionally spatial extreme peaks (CSPEP) model, which is applicable to univariate scenarios. We evaluate this model through simulations and apply it to analyze extreme wave heights within the North Sea.

We establish theorems analogous to Faltings's and Silverman's finiteness results regarding rational points, but for bounded non-constant maps from an fixed number field to an elliptic curve varying over a given base number field analogously, proving that any such map with an image height below a specified constant is non-constant only if it falls within a finite set; this generalizes previous rational function point results. Our strategy employs an adaptation of the "local height pairing" method pioneered by Bombieri and Pila, building upon foundational work by McQuillan and Zhang. As a corollary, our findings extend to prove the finiteness of rational equivalence classes of rational maps with a given height bound, thus providing a positive resolution to questions posed by McQuillan and Zhang in this context.

This study addresses robot operability assessment by adapting human operability metrics from one target to another. To achieve this, we introduce a human-robot specific domain adaptation method utilizing a pair of 3D motion datasets captured via an IMU-aided inertial measurement unit. First, we adapt the target domain by aligning its operability space with that of the source domain through parallel transport on a Grassmannian manifold. Second, we enhance this alignment using a manifold-aware Iterative Closest Point (ICG) algorithm. The concept manifold, representing operability space, is constructed by mapping IMU data onto a unit Grassmannian using Principal Component Analysis. During adaptation, parallel transport aligns the mean PCA subspace of the target domain with that of the source. Subsequently, the respective manifold data points are stochastically aligned through localized manifold ICP, employing Gaussian kernels to ensure smooth interpolation between discrete data points. Experiments involving operators with varying skill levels demonstrate that this two-stage approach significantly outperforms single-stage baseline methods in terms of Bland-Altman consistency and correlation.

This study examines the Standard Model Higgs boson pair production within the $\text{HH} \to \text{b}\overline{\text{b}}\text{W}\text{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC, employing both the matrix element technique and parton shower matching strategies. Utilizing Next2LeptonTools within MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, we generate next-to-leading order (NLO) corrections for the $\text{s-channel Higgs} (\text{H} \to \text{b}\overline{\text{b}})$ component of pair production alongside the relevant $\text{WW}^{*}\text{WW}^{*}$ processes. We further investigate the impact of parton shower matching on these $\text{H} \to \text{b}\overline{\text{b}}$ events. Additionally, we analyze the $\text{H} \to \text{b}\overline{\text{b}}$ contribution arising from $\text{s-channel H}(\text{s}=\text{channel H})$ processes alongside the $\text{H} \to \text{b}\overline{\text{b}}$ component from $\text{H} \to \text{H}^{*}\text{H}^{*}\text{H}^{*}\text{H}^{*}\text{H}^{*}\text{H}^{*}\text

We introduce Unintentional Turntables, a method for learning 3D object detection and pose estimation without requiring paired training images. This system utilizes large-scale image collections that contain natural camera movements resembling a table rotating an object in all directions. By analyzing these collections, we can train a 3D position and orientation estimator for an object class by detecting a single example of that class per image. To achieve this, the system employs a 3D position estimator trained on a generated "turntable dataset," where a single prototype object is rendered in various rotations against a uniform background. This estimator is then adapted to real-world scenes by identifying an image translation that maximizes the estimated 3D position of an estimated object. Experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively estimates 3D positions in data featuring single examples per image and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for multi-view stereo on standard benchmarks.

The ongoing global pandemic has intensified the need for widespread vaccination, a process complicated by misinformation that erodes public trust in vaccines and hampers adoption rates. This study introduces a novel framework to identify whether individuals accept, reject, or remain undecided about specific vaccine-related misinformaion. By leveraging dialogue data from Twitter, we developed three advanced neural network architectures designed to analyze the entire conversation context surrounding a misinformation post. Our results, presented as both qualitative and quantitative findings, offer new insights into the factors shaping public perceptions of misinformation and provide robust baseline performance.

Generating isolated attosecond pulses via High Harmonic Generation (HHG) offers a pathway to create electron tools with sub-cycle temporal and nanometer spatial precision, essential for characterizing and manipulating matter dynamics at electronic scales. However, achieving this traditionally demands the meticulous, field-by-field optimization of both amplitude and phase within the driving laser field. This paper introduces a robust alternative approach that minimizes pulse yield sensitivity to fluctuations in the driving field by employing coherent control strategies. Using a model system of attosecond pulse production, the method successfully produces isolated 200-attosecond pulses with peak intensity maximization while cutting the total number of required parameters from infinity to zero. This technique paves the way for more reliable and efficient electron manipulation, a critical requirement for advancing attoparticle physics and other emerging fields within ultrafast science.

The companion star of Algol was first identified in 1889, yet it was later discovered to be a detached eclipsing binary system. This study establishes that the entire Algol system comprises a tertiary star orbiting a tight binary pair, with the inner components separated by just 2.15 days and the outer star completing a revolution every 9.86 days. Utilizing high-precision data from the TESS mission, we have refined the orbital parameters for all three stars and modeled the light curve, which reveals the inner binary's components to be spectral types F5V and K0V. Furthermore, we confirm the tertiary is a K2V star. This discovery redefines Algol as a triple-star system, effectively eliminating recent candidate K-type stars proposed as the companion, as they are now known to be inner binary members.

We examine the nonlinear Schrödinger equation within the exterior region of a smooth, compact convex obstacle in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions and a specific power-type nonlinearity. By leveraging a variational framework, we establish the existence of a novel explosion solution characterized by zero magnetic flux and negative energy.

Residual Analysis for Neural Graphs (RANG) is a new method for dynamically creating mesh vertices in Neural Graph Animation (NGA). As a fully differentiable and adaptive approach, RANG assesses approximation accuracy within each mesh element and guides the placement of new vertices accordingly. This process enhances adaptive resolution specifically where neural network error is high. NGA leverages its inherent differentiability to optimize approximations across dynamically generated graphs; however, the rate and location of vertex addition can negatively impact this approximation quality. To mitigate these impacts, we introduced RANG under NGA. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed RANG improves both computational efficiency and solution accuracy. When compared against the existing state-of-the-art, NGA with RANG achieved a 3.25-fold reduction in training time and a 14.04% decrease in approximation error.

This research investigates multi-domain ferroelectric bodies within Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistors (FeFETs), utilizing a micromagnetic extension of the Poisson-Piezoelectric-Pomeranchuk (PPEP) model. The study focuses on non-hydrostatic states where out-of-plane mechanical constraints vary across the device, a condition that can generate an "Adverse Capacitance." In these scenarios, the local electric displacement field $D_z$ deviates from the internal electric field $E_z$, potentially triggering unexpected switching behaviors. We analyze FeFET structures with both pinned and anti-pinned boundary conditions for the polarization, demonstrating that Adverse Capacitance significantly influences switching dynamics in both cases. Furthermore, a simulation module written in Object-Oriented C++ is developed to experimentally verify these predictions.
