This study examines an irreversible stochastic Ginzburg-Landau equation driven by noise of pure discontinuity. Establishing the existence and uniqueness of a solution adapted to an arbitrary filtration, we demonstrate that the corresponding transition semigroup is strongly continuous within the space of bounded measurable functions, thereby proving ergodicity and the irreducibility of the associated Markov process. Additionally, by leveraging these ergodicity and irreducibility properties, we derive a weak form of a large deviation principle.

This paper determines the minimal degree of simple power graphs $\mathcal{G}^{\times}_G$ when $G$ is a nilpotent group, noting previous authors failed to provide a straightforward criterion for this value in such cases. Our findings establish this least minor degree for all power graphs associated with abelian-by-square nilpotent groups, effectively characterizing them as characterizing by their least degree of power graphs in these specific nilpotent contexts.

This paper introduces the concept of a hadron spectrometer designed to study charged hadron interactions with nuclei, focusing on the measurement of transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) distributions for particles with charges $|z| \leq 4$ produced in central Pb-Pb collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Operating in the same momentum range as the Time Projection Chamber (TPC) within ALICE, this new device aims to achieve superior resolution by precisely determining the specific ionization ($dE/dx$) profiles resulting from nuclear electronic excitations. Achieving this requires the simultaneous detection of multiple electrons ejected from the atomic nucleus during these processes. The proposed apparatus consists of a cylindrical detector with a 1-meter diameter and length, positioned 1 meter radially outward from the TPC, utilizing silicon pixel technology.

This paper introduces an orientation convolutional network (OCNet) designed to resolve image classification challenges by leveraging convolution operations with orientation kernels. The core kernel, defined as $K(\theta) = \cos(2\theta + \phi)$, where $\theta$ represents the direction and $\phi$ a phase shift, functions as an elementary line detector. Through the application of these kernels, OCNet generates robust feature maps that effectively capture object characteristics regardless of their rotation. The orientation-based convolution layer applies a set of such kernels to input data, producing features resilient to rotation. Experimental evaluations on the EMNIST dataset using digits from MNIST and EMNIST-letters demonstrate that the orientation convolutional layer significantly boosts classification accuracy compared to standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), specifically enhancing performance on rotated objects.

Point cloud data, which captures the three-dimensional geometry of objects, is widely used in fields like robotics and augmented reality. While Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as a leading architecture for processing point clouds by constructing graphs based on inter-point relationships, they often struggle with over-smoothing when applied to large-scale 3D data. This issue stems from the standard use of Euclidean distance, which fails to account for global geometric context. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that builds graph connectivity using an adaptive, learnable distance metric. Empirical results demonstrate that this method significantly mitigates over-smoothing, yielding superior performance in point cloud classification and segmentation.

Recent advancements in deep learning have introduced novel Deep Learning Stratosphere Hostless Trojans (DLSHTs), which outperform earlier models by reducing detection difficulty while enhancing evasion capabilities. The current study introduces a new class, the Semantic DLSHT, targeting segmentation networks. The proposed methodology modifies model predictions by integrating trojan subgraphs into the semantics of segmentation networks via trojan words, thereby inducing specific assault effects. The implementation requires only a minimal number of trigger pixels and necessates no labeled training data. The presented framework is general and easily extensible to other deep learning applications. The methodology was validated on leading semantic segmentation models, specifically DeDe and DeepLabv2, using the Cityscapes dataset. The results demonstrate an improvement of 20% over the most advanced DLSHT, achieving high accuracy rates for both trigger size and assault precision.

The MaKe Use of Magellan for Spectroscopy and USe (M-MGUU, referred to in source as ROSIE) initiative aims to enhance the capabilities of the MaKe Use of Magellan integral field spectrometry system by integrating the Low-Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (LRIS) with the Multi-Object Spectrograph (MOS). This approach involves repurposing LRIS's existing optics and detector array, which are already situated within the instrument line of sight. As a key component, LRIS utilizes a dual-camera setup; the smaller of these, measuring 20 x 20 mm, is being relocated and mounted directly in front of the MOS beam path to introduce low-resolution spectroscopy capabilities to an otherwise multi-object only system. This 20 x 20 mm optical camera is being modified to function specifically as an insertion spectral device. This document outlines the current status and advancement of ROSIE.

This study reviews the current status of carbon-carbon fusion and highlights recent findings from our group. We demonstrate that the traditional method for extracting state-to-state fusion cross sections is the Trojan Horse (TH) method, which enables measurements at significantly higher energies than possible via direct techniques. Utilizing TH scattering experiments at elevated energies thus facilitates the determination of state-to-state fusion cross sections over a broader energy spectrum. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel approach for analyzing these high-energy TH experiments to more precisely extract state-to-state cross sections and offers suggestions for future TH investigations aimed at covering even wider energy ranges.

We present high-resolution spectroscopic data for 112 planet-host stars, analyzed using the iSHELL instrument on the 30-meter Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). Our study focuses on determining the abundances of 11 elements—Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, As, Se, Mo, Cd, Te, and U—within these stars. By applying these precise stellar abundances, we calculate the bulk chemical compositions of terrestrial exoplanets, specifically targeting Earth-like worlds and those comparable in size to Neptune or super-Earth exoplanets. Our findings indicate that the elemental ratios within these stars closely mirror solar values, with the exception of tellurium (Te). Based on these results, we conclude that terrestrial exoplanets likely possess bulk compositions similar to Earth, with the notable exception of sulfur. Furthermore, we assess the potential for detecting chondritic anomalies in exoplanetary materials through future high-resolution stellar spectroscopy.

Commercial Wireless Localizaion (WL) utilizing Channel State Information (CSI) offers a promising avenue for high-precision indoor positioning, particularly when integrated with low-cost commercial Wi-Fi hardware. Nevertheless, the substantial data volume inherent in CSI creates significant computational burdens for positioning algorithms. This paper introduces an attention-based framework to mitigate these algorithmic computational costs. By applying this technique to a deep learning-based localization algorithm, our results demonstrate a reduction of over 90% in computation time, while maintaining comparable accuracy to the original method.

This work introduces a unifying framework for modal logics, extending the methodology developed by M. Spivak in "Homotopy Test Spaces for Constructive Mathematics" (Fund. Math. 223, 2014). Building on this approach, we develop a comprehensive theory of (constructive) sheaves within a topos of sheaves that serves as a semantic foundation. Within this system, we define modal operators using sheafic concepts such as sub-objects, limits, and colimits, allowing us to formally define modal logic via topological structures. This semantic system successfully generalizes various existing frameworks, including Stone spaces, extended Kripke models, and homotopy spaces. Furthermore, we establish connections between this proposed theory and existing conceptualizations based on category theory, relational models, and Cegelsciz spaces.

The concept of edge-tinting on a graph $G=(V,E)$ involves assigning weights from $\{1, \dots, k\}$ to its edges such that the weights sum to at most $k-1$ at every vertex. A graph is termed edge-tintable if such a weighting is possible. In 2018, Kalkowski, Karwa, and Tuza conjectured that all cubic bipartite graphs satisfy this property. However, in this paper, we demonstrate that this conjecture is false by presenting a specific cubic bipartite graph that fails to be edge-tintable.

This study determines precise lower bounds for the Hamming graph $H(n,q)$ regarding specific functions, with particular attention to the scenario where function values are restricted to a subset of $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ that excludes no values between $0$ and $k$ inclusive. A unifying framework is established to generalize prior findings by Brouwer, Brouwer and Willemse, and Brouwer and Willemse. Additionally, earlier results from Brouwer and his colleagues concerning functions on $H(n,q)$ that are constant on diagonals and exhibit symmetry across levels are extended. Specifically, we prove a Brouwer-Willemse-type theorem for symmetric functions and provide one for threshold functions covering cases not previously addressed by their work.

COPASI, a widely used command-line and graphical desktop simulation environment for biochemical networks, has seen significant development over its twenty-year history. However, its current interface lacks specific features necessary to support modern computational biology workflows. To address this gap, we introduce ShinyCOPASI, a web-based alternative that leverages COPASI's extensive modeling capabilities while providing a user experience similar to that created by R Shiny applications. ShinyCOPASI allows for the import of COPASI files, with a built-in library of published model datasets available for immediate use. Its intuitive interface supports interactive simulation, data analysis, and the generation of static or animated graphs for both 2D and 3D graphs. Furthermore, its open-source nature ensures transparency and extensibility, allowing for the addition of new features and graphical representations. Finally, its web-based architecture naturally facilitates the development of user-friendly links and pages to promote specific models.

In science and engineering, understanding phenomena is best achieved through multiple complementary lenses, including physical theories, mathematical models, and experimental data. In recent years, machine learning (ML) has become a pivotal component of scientific discovery, yet the inherent opacity of deep learning algorithms poses challenges for interpreting their decisions and validating their outputs. This paper reviews various interpretation techniques for machine learning, categorizes them according to a proposed quantitative ambiguity metric, and evaluates multiple existing measures of interpretability and certainty on a curated ML-for-science dataset. Finally, it outlines avenues for future ambiguity quantification within scientific machine learning.

In the paper, we investigate the von Neumann algebra generated by unitary matrix elements within the type I q-factorial on a compact quantum group. We demonstrate that this algebra is precisely the span of the type I ufactors corresponding to a selected class of commensurable quantum subgroup dimensions. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between two important sets on these structures: the families of lattice normal subgroup types and the types I ufactors.

Imprecise value iteration addresses Markov decision processes (MDPs) characterized by imprecise transition probabilities and is recognized as robust against uncertainties affecting transition models. Nevertheless, its application to large systems is hindered by prohibitively high computational costs. This study introduces a hybrid algorithm combining GMRES and Strategy Iteration (SI), termed i-GMRES, designed to solve the Imprecise Linear Program (iLP) equivalent of value iteration. SI is a well-established algorithm capable of converting value iteration into the iLP formulation. SI-GMRES and its uncertainty-aware extension, i-SI-GMRES, are proven to converge to GMRES iterations on SI-generated feasible solutions. Under specific conditions, convergence to an SI approximation is also demonstrated. Empirical results demonstrate that i-SI-GMMS exhibits superior performance compared to value iteration, SI-GMMS, and SI-GMMS variants, establishing it as an efficient approach for large-scale MDPs featuring imprecise transition probabilities.

Let $K$ denote a set of edges in a directed graph, and let $I(K)$ be the associated edge ideal within the polynomial ring $S = K[x_e \mid e \in K]$. This study investigates the properties of both the lower bound and the half of $I(K)$, specifically in relation to the 'veronese' rank $m$ applied to each variable. First, we establish a lower bound for the \emph{normal} symbolic power of $I(K)$ by employing the concept of a \emph{maximal strongly connected component} of $K$. Second, we derive a \emph{upper} bound for the \emph{monomial} rank of $I(K)$ using the \emph{veronese} rank $m$ applied to each variable. Finally, we demonstrate that for every directed graph, there exists a \emph{maximal} strongly connected component whose veronese rank is at most $m$, and we provide examples showing that this bound is tight for some graphs but not others.

This study addresses the inverse challenge of determining an unknown parameter within a time-series computer simulation. Using a data-driven contour estimation technique, we map the relationship between this hidden parameter and the resulting time-series data by selecting a discrete set of candidate values for estimation. The method's utility is demonstrated through its application to forecasting future outcomes in an 80-year climate simulation. The proposed approach offers several advantages: the contour estimation can leverage various data metrics, the method accommodates the parallel evaluation of multiple parameter candidates, and the data space for the relationship can be effectively reduced through the introduction of additional, estimated parameters.

Recent studies have demonstrated that incorporating query regions enhances robustness against adversarial examples. However, a significant unresolved issue remains: under what conditions do these regions assist a query-dependent robust accuracy? This paper investigates this matter by examining how query regions function within query-dependent robust accurate classifiers. Our findings reveal that while querying any point inside a query-dependent accurate region does not guarantee accuracy for all points within that area, querying the center of a region's smallest enclosing hypersphere provides this guarantee. Furthermore, we demonstrate that querying the center of the minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid also ensures accurate classification within the region. These theoretical results are supported by experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10, which validate the proposed theorems and offer additional insights into the performance of region-based querying strategies.

This study examines jet fragmentation within PbPb collisions using jets tagged by isolated photons to assess systematic uncertainties tied to nuclear modifications of the Parton Distribution Function (PDF) and to quantify any additional, medium-induced effects. Comparing PbPb results to proton-proton data reveals a significant suppression of the $K_T$ distribution, which describes the transverse momentum of fragments relative to the jet axis. This suppression is most pronounced for low $K_T$ values. Furthermore, the $K_T$ spectrum shows a shift to lower momenta, with the magnitude of this shift depending on both centrality and the transverse momentum of the inclusive photon tag. These observations suggest a modification in jet fragmentation structure, specifically a trend toward lower fragment $p_T$ in PbPb collisions compared to pp interactions.

Building on our prior study in [1], this paper establishes commutative relations connecting linear combinations of colored multiple zeta functions (CMZFs) on the left with specific applied arithmetic sequences involving mixed parity indexed AP-type sequences of even indexed AMZF values on the right. These relationships are categorized into three distinct applications: first, they provide novel identities for AP-type sequences with mixed parity indices derived from even indexed AMZFs; second, they generate new linear identities linking alternating AP-type sequences of mixed parity indices with those of even parity indices; and third, they produce fresh formulas expressing weighted sums of AP-type sequences with AP-type sequences of mixed parity indices derived from CMZFs of distinct depth values on the right.

The M-shape optical light curve of the newly identified brown dwarf WISEA J193429.75-104303.3 (hereinafter referred to as "the mishap") is characterized by a single, prominent primary maximum and a secondary, lesser peak formed by two smaller minima. This study utilizes high-precision photometry and spectroscopy to constrain the object's physical parameters, specifically its rotation period, inclination, and gravity. Our findings indicate a rotation period of 2.66 ± 0.01 days at an inclination of 81 ± 1°, with an estimated effective temperature of 1050 ± 50 K and a surface gravity of log(g) = 5.0 ± 0.5. This luminosity and atmospheric state are attributed to a mass of approximately 0.055 ± 0.004 M_Jup and a radius of 0.97 ± 0.02 R_Jup. The observed optical and near-infrared spectral features are consistent with a Y-type classification, exhibiting distinct CH molecular bands and a continuum slope indicative of methane absorption. The optical spectrum further displays a pronounced slope toward shorter wavelengths, consistent with the presence of H2O and NH3 absorption bands. The observed variability is best explained by a simple two-spot model featuring two equally sized dark spots, with the secondary hump resulting from the emergence of a third, faint

This study reports the creation yields of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV. The data were gathered by the CMS experiment at the LHC using 17.3 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. Particle production rates are presented as functions of transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) and rapidity ($y$), alongside their nuclear modification factors as they depend on $p_{\rm T}$ and the centrality of the collisions. The yield ratios for (anti-)kaons to (anti-)protons are also analyzed. These findings are compared with predictions from various theoretical models.

Interpreting experimental data on elastic electron - proton scattering demands parton distribution functions (PDFs) that are both precise and computationally efficient. This paper demonstrates that a highly effective and straightforward method for achieving this efficiency exists within the framework of the effective interpolation technique. Additionally, we present the D'Angelo - Stasto PDFs, constructed using this method across a wide spectrum of QCD energy scales, from deep Euclidean space up to the perturbative QCD regime.

Sintering stands as a primary technique for in-situ Martian and lunar construction materials, offering a pathway to reduce launch expenses by minimizing the cargo of required cements and additives sent to these environments. However, existing research on sintering has been largely confined to laboratory settings, resulting in a scarcity of knowledge regarding how regolith properties and processing conditions influence the microstructure and performance of sintered blocks. This study investigates mixed lunar and Martian regolith to examine the effects of thermal conditions on block microstructure and mechanical behavior. We evaluated samples molded and sintered at various temperatures, comparing their ultimate compressive strength and microstructural characteristics against unsintered controls. Results indicate that block strength correlates positively with sintering temperature, with optimal outcomes achieved at 1,000 K. Furthermore, we analyzed the microstructure of these blocks to understand its relationship with temperature and the resulting mechanical properties.

The dynamics of a liquid coating on a vibrating fiber are governed by slip-augmented Rayleigh-Plateau instability, a phenomenon where interfacial slip significantly influences growth rates. This slip dependence of mode development was first identified theoretically in 2018, yet experimental validation has remained elusive. In this study, we establish such an experimentally, applying a drop of water to a single fiber within a vertical acoustic drop tower to observe instabilities. By analyzing growth dynamics across various drop sizes and fiber surface treatments, we quantify the variation in both wavelength and temporal growth rates. These experimental findings align closely with theoretical predictions, confirming that slip markedly accelerates instability development, especially for lower wavenumbers.

The benchmarking of star formation rate (SFR) tracers is essential for characterizing the star-forming properties of galaxies. In this study, we utilize the $\lambda$14685 \AA\ Brackett-$\gamma$ (Br$\gamma$) line emission from the Magellanic Clouds to assess the reliability of the widely used tracers H$\alpha$ and [N II]6583 \AA\ and 7000 \AA\ for galaxies beyond the Milky Way. Our analysis involves comparing Br$\gamma$-derived SFRs with those from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting, which serves as a robust independent method. We examined 1000 Br$\gamma$-emitting regions within the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and 1100 in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). The comparison reveals that, on average, SFR estimates from H$\alpha$ and [N II] are approximately 1.2 dex higher than those calculated using Br$\gamma$ and the SED method, respectively. When plotting the ratios of these methods against each other, the LCM data show a Br$\gamma$/SFR ratio that is roughly 0.3 dex higher than the SLCM values. Furthermore, the scatter in the H$\alpha$ and [N II] plots is about 0.2 dex greater than in the Br$\gamma$/SFR correlation

This article establishes the symmetries relevant to regional-type modules for integrable affine $I$ modules associated with $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ (specifically $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$). We demonstrate that the Kashiwara operators, along with their associated "type $I$ quantum subgroup" (specifically $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$), can be constructed. This quantum subgroup enables the explicit computation of the action of Kashiwara operators on regional-type modules for $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ through operations on "type $I$ quantum subgroup" (specifically $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$). This method leverages the correspondence between type $I$ quantum subgroup and type $I$ quantum subgroup (specifically $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$). As a result, we obtain a "type $I$ quantum subgroup" (specifically $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$) (specifically $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$). Furthermore, we derive a "type $I$ quantum subgroup" (specifically $I$ series $\mathfrak{sl}_N$).

Diffusion models have recently emerged as a prominent class of generative networks, renowned for their high fidelity in producing data, yet they remain burdened by slow training and inference speeds. This paper introduces a novel, universal diffusion approach designed to enhance generation speed. By integrating a conditional autoencoder framework, we map input data and latent codes bidirectionally, utilizing this mapping to accelerate both data latentization and unlatentization processes. Furthermore, we apply conditional guidance to steer diffusion from this encoder output, enabling high-fidelity regeneration based on given labels. Experimental validation on ImageNet demonstrates that a single model compresses images at 10× faster than conventional methods while achieving comparable quality, and that conditioned generation yields superior results when employing multi-label information.

Identifying handwritten mathematical expressions is crucial for digitizing physical documents and converting them into structured electronic formats. This study introduces a new approach leveraging image data to locate mathematical symbols in unstructured handwritten documents. The proposed system utilizes an onomatopeic pen equipped with an integrated sensor to capture symbol-specific data, which then feeds into a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained to classify each individual symbol. This method achieves an F1 score of 87.7% and a precision of 88.2%. The results indicate that performing recognition at the individual symbol level significantly enhances overall accuracy compared to treating math as continuous text.

This paper introduces a straightforward, non-statistical technique for generating varying durations in speech through median-driven synthesis. The median duration is calculated from the original set of unmodified target phrases to create a reference standard. Each variable-length input phrase is then matched to this median target using a dynamic time warping (DTW) operation, and the resulting normal speech is played back by executing the extracted warping path on the time axis. This method avoids statistical models and probabilistic frameworks, differing significantly from most prior synthesis approaches. Experiments were conducted on TIMIT and NCRI datasets to evaluate the proposed technique. The results indicate a 20% reduction in perceptual quality (measured by PESQ) compared to the industry standard, IBM's text-to-speech system.

Spatial occupancy modeling is a vital technique in ecology for analyzing species presence-absence data while accounting for detection errors and environmental covariates. This approach has recently expanded beyond binary responses to include count data, facilitating more nuanced insights into how environmental factors influence species abundance. The `spOccupancy` R package offers a comprehensive suite of tools for fitting spatial occupancy models based on both binary and count responses, alongside multi-species and integrated single-species, multi-species, and integrated versions. These advanced models enable researchers to explore complex interactions, such as species co-occurrence, spatial correlations in occupancy, abundance, and detection probabilities, and quantify uncertainties in spatial predictions. Accompanied by real examples, this document provides a detailed guide to the package's functionality, including recent enhancements like multi-species zero-inflated Gaussian models, spatially varying coefficient structures, advanced MCMC diagnostics, and enhanced computational efficiency through parallel processing and optimized Markov chain transitions.

Skin cancer remains the most prevalent malignancy globally, with melanoma posing significant risks due to its potential for early metastasis and fatality. Early detection is critical for preventing such spread, a challenge often compounded by a shortage of dermatologists. To address this, we introduce the Skincare initiative, an interactive deep learning framework designed to support clinicians in identifying and managing skin lesions. This system features two primary workspaces: a free one accessible to anyone, and a restricted professional area where doctors can upload patient images for analysis. To ensure trust and safety, a specialized verification process is in place to grant access to the professional workspace. Furthermore, to promote data privacy, all uploaded images are automatically anonymized before processing. We detail this initiative and its associated security measures in this report.

This study introduces a novel stochastic autoencoder framework designed to forecast future spectra of Type Ia supernovae. By leveraging MTSZ-1, a publicly available dataset of 1,100 spectra for 1,100 individual supernovae, we generate future spectral estimates at 30 days intervals up to a maximum of 360 days post-explosion. Our methodology combines the Autoencoder architecture with an integrated Bayesian posterior sampler, enabling the simultaneous reconstruction of future spectra and uncertainty quantification. When contrasted with conventional machine learning autoencoders, our approach yields superior uncertainty estimates of spectral features, particularly for events extending to later times.

We report the detection of a neutral carbon (C I) absorption feature at z=2.09, located in the gravitationally lensed quasar PG1211+143. This signal originates from a dusty star-forming clump situated 3.1 arcseconds from the lensing quasar, corresponding to a physical separation of 2.1 kpc. The discovery was facilitated by the ALMA Large Program on Merging and Starbursts (P-21), which targeted a region of 100 kpc radius around the quasar. The source, designated C1-31, was resolved within a 0.2" diameter, yielding a deconvolved FWHM of 0.18" in the observed C I line. Assuming a standard 10 K km s$^{-1}$ FWHM for the absorption profile, the derived physical velocity width is 0.56 km s$^{-1}$. This narrow width indicates that the source is a point-like individual rather than an extended cluster, and its minute velocity dispersion suggests a static intercloud medium. The bolometric luminosity of C I is calculated to be 1.1 x 10$^{8}$ L$_{\odot}$. This study examines the dynamics of turbulent plumes through both numerical simulations and analytical models, specifically focusing on how particles with varying sizes incorporate into rising plumes generated by buoyant sources. The results indicate that, at a fixed height, the mean vertical velocity of particles is directly proportional to the particle-free plume velocity, regardless of the particle size. Additionally, the width of these particle-laden plumes maintains the same scale as non-homogeneous regions, showing negligible alteration due to the presence of particles. The findings also reveal that the fluctuation intensity within particle-filled plumes remains unchanged compared to the particle-free baseline. To achieve these results, a novel analytical framework was developed that describes the one-way coupling between the fluid and particles. This model successfully predicts mean velocities and overall dimensions, aligning well with both the simulations and existing experimental data.

The propagation of infectious diseases within social networks is a subject of significant interest, driven by the goal of refining epidemic forecasting and control strategies. While extensive research has focused on networks, this work investigates the extinction dynamics of infectious diseases in a more realistic framework: hypergraphs, where multiple social interactions can occur simultaneously. We introduce a rigorous spectral methodology to establish precise spectral lower bounds regarding the basic reproduction number ($R_0$)—a pivotal metric indicating whether an epidemic will surge or subside. Our findings demonstrate a profound connection between $R_0$ and the second-largest eigenvalue of a specific self-adjoint operator derived from the hypergraph's structure. Furthermore, we provide spectral upper bounds to determine the precise threshold at which an epidemic outbreak becomes unsustainable. By extending previous research, our contribution offers a deeper spectral understanding of outbreak dynamics in complex, multi-simultaneous interaction scenarios.

The recent discovery of magnetic insulators exhibiting out-of-plane ferromagnetism, exemplified by the hexagonal Chern insulator CrI$_3$, has sparked significant interest in exploring spin-orbit interactions and chiral magnetism. Despite these systems being centrosymmetric, they exhibit strong out-of-plane magnetization, which facilitates the emergence of chiral spin textures and phenomena such as the anomalous Hall effect. In this study, we investigate the magnetic properties of a two-dimensional out-of-plane ferromagnet using a comprehensive theoretical framework that accounts for both spin and lattice degrees of freedom. We demonstrate that a Rashba-like term arises within the exchange interaction, leading to a chiral modification of the magnetic ordering temperature. Furthermore, we analyze how this chiral exchange influences the spin structure, giving rise to a helical ferromagnetic state characterized by a finite wavelength.

Differential rotation is a primary driver of magnetic activity in solar-type stars, yet the specific nature of this differential rotation in non-solar stars remains uncertain. We modeled three distinct differential rotation profiles—solar-like, anti-solar (characterized by equatorial faster rotation), and rigid (solid body) within a mean-field dynamo framework. The anti-solar case was chosen based on magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations, which show that rapidly rotating, convectively turbulent stars typically exhibit this rotation law. Our results indicate that, compared to the solar differential rotation model, the anti-solar scenario produces stronger magnetic cycles with more pronounced 11-year periods. We further explored how these cycles vary with rotation speed in the anti-solar configuration. For a star rotating at solar velocity, mean-field predictions align reasonably well with observed solar activity; however, as the rotation rate decreases, the resulting cycles become significantly stronger and longer. These findings suggest that weak differential rotation in magnetized stars could generate intense magnetic fluctuations occurring over extended timeframes.

Deep learning architectures are pivotal for analyzing time-series data, yet current methods often fail to capture the temporal dynamics of multi-channel signals. Furthermore, existing models designed for specific tasks—ranging from classification and detection to localization and prediction—rarely address multiple channel streams simultaneously. Consequently, there is a lack of unified frameworks capable of handling diverse channel streams across various tasks. To address this, we introduce a general K-fan multimodal deep architecture that utilizes shared representations. This proposed system is the first of its kind to effectively manage multiple channels for multiple distinct tasks. We demonstrate its efficacy through two video-based applications: multi-object multi-target tracking and multi-person pose estimation. In both scenarios, we simultaneously detect multiple objects/individuals and estimate the positions of multiple joints. Experimental results show that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in these scenarios. Additionally, we evaluate the system on multi-input multi-output forecasting and multi-class multi-object tracking tasks, confirming its robustness in handling complex, multi-dimensional data distributions.

Multithreaded programs introduce intricate execution paths due to interleavings among threads, making comprehensive testing essential yet challenging. Model checking addresses this by automatically generating and verifying all possible program runs to detect bugs. However, existing solutions struggle with scalability when analyzing programs featuring many threads and complex interactions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce McMini, a new model checker that integrates Dynamic Partial Order Reduction (DPOR) with the MiniML type system. By statically identifying independent operations, McMini eliminates redundant permutations, thereby scaling to verify programs with numerous threads and extensive state spaces. Its DPOR mechanism is highly configurable, allowing users to fine-tune the trade-off between runtime efficiency and the thoroughness of schedule exploration. We demonstrate McMini's capabilities by verifying several real-world programs, including the Linux kernel semaphore implementation and Java's thread management system.

The ability to forward messages is integral to WhatsApp usage, a feature that has unfortunately facilitated the widespread propagation of false information, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. In response, the WhatsApp team announced plans to restrict the maximum number of times a message can be forwarded. This study examines the impact of such limitations on forwarding behaviors and the efficacy of the intervention in curbing the distribution of misinformation. Our analysis utilizes rich, granular data from a large-scale experiment conducted in India involving nearly 100,000 participants. We discovered that implementing fewer forwarding constraints significantly reduced overall forwarding volume but yielded minimal effects on sharing misinformation. These findings suggest that current message-blocking interventions may fail to curb misinformation dissemination because users who intend to share inaccurate content are less hindered by technical limits than those who merely engage in casual, high-volume forwarding.

Speech spoofing counteraction (SCS) systems are essential for safeguarding security and privacy. While deep learning has significantly advanced these systems, their reliance on the difficulty of distinguishing genuine spoofed audio from live speech limits their broader adoption. This study introduces a new activation function, Vigilant Function (VF), designed specifically to improve deep end-to-end SCS performance. The core mechanism of VF involves dynamically adjusting the gradient magnitude based on the current loss value to accelerate convergence and enhance model stability. Experimental results utilizing spoofed, genuine, and anti-spoach datasets demonstrate that VF surpasses existing activation functions, achieving an equal error rate (EER) of 2.19% on the ASVSP 2020 dataset.

We investigate effective field theories (EFTs) for inflation derived from locally supersymmetric models, focusing on scenarios where the supersymmetry (SUSY) breaking scale is comparable to the Hubble scale. By applying EFT techniques, we demonstrate that such frameworks impose significant constraints on the effective action, thereby narrowing the possibilities for viable models of inflation. We specifically examine the $\mu$-term dominance model, where supersymmetry is explicitly broken via an effective operator involving the Hubble scale. In this scenario, we identify a specific parameter range that accommodates the Hubble scale as the supersymmetry breaking scale while satisfying observational constraints. Furthermore, we outline the general methodology for constructing effective actions within this regime and apply it to derive the scalar and fermion spectra, their masses, and interaction terms. Finally, we employ perturbation theory to compute two-loop corrections to the scalar power spectrum and spectral index, alongside the running of that index.

Photon entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum information science, is typically characterized by symmetric correlation patterns between outputs from single-photon sources. In this work, we introduce and demonstrate the concept of asymmetric entanglement, defined as photon pair correlations that are not limited to integer counts of photons. Our experimental validation utilizes a standard type-II spontaneous parametric down-conversion setup, revealing a correlation where, on average, one output port emits two photons while the other emits none. This observation is corroborated by the violation of classical constraints imposed by a Bell inequality adapted for multi-photon states. Our findings not only introduce new perspectives on entanglement but also establish a resource with potential utility in information processing tasks.

This work demonstrates the application of scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM) to investigate the near-field distribution of planar microwave resonators operating in the terahertz range. By employing a metal-coated scanning electron microscope electron beam as a localized antenna, the near-field profiles were measured across different excitation frequencies. These experimental results align well with numerical simulations derived from the finite element method. Furthermore, the measured near-field distribution is compared to the far-field profile derived from the near-field-to-far-field transformation technique.

In this study, we examine whether introducing new trading tactics to an market simulation with agents holding specific beliefs can generate strategy outperformance, a question often overlooked by traditional financial research. By adapting the model from Brock and Sumner (2006), we integrate two fundamental data-driven approaches, factor analysis and natural language processing. These methods are used to identify fresh investment tactics derived from various online investor forums. Within our fact-based framework, agent behaviors are driven by the probability distributions they hold regarding fundamental data. Our results indicate that agents employing these new strategies can achieve superior performance compared to those using current tactics. Consequently, this suggests that future research should continue exploring how to introduce innovations in trading strategies.

The development of Internet-wide protocols is increasingly transparent, allowing attackers to easily infer the specific tools and methodologies employed by defenders. This visibility facilitates targeted attacks on security vulnerabilities inherent to those products. To address this, we introduce a novel framework designed to identify network protocols even when their security configurations are locked down. We have implemented and evaluated this framework against the widely used Large-scale Protection DDoS (LPM-DDoS) tool, OpenBOSS, demonstrating its successful detection of assaults on the Assault on Dynamic Protocol Identification (APID) attack vector.

Placing a normal metal containing conduction electrons and a s-wave superconductor side-by-side induces the superconducting state into the metal through Andreev reflection. In this regime, Cooper pairs moving within the superconductor can coherently scatter backward into the metal, effectively generating an "effective pair potential." This mechanism enables superconducting properties to influence adjacent systems, such as insulators that support magnons, granting them access to gauge field dynamics by Bogoliubov quasiparticles. This paper demonstrates that effective gating of magnons occurs when these magnons interact with proximate superconductors, a phenomenon that can be utilized to achieve full magnon blockade via a quantum gate operation.

This paper presents a new zero-shot learning framework for distributed audio classification, a paradigm where unlabeled data from remote nodes are transferred locally, and labeled target data is available only there. The primary goal is to minimize the need for labeled samples. To achieve this, we introduce a multi-objective optimization framework that balances two goals: minimizing the number of labeled training samples and maximizing the classifier's accuracy on unseen classes. Furthermore, we develop an efficient majorization-minimization (MM)-based algorithm complete with a guaranteed convergence proof. Extensive experiments on the Yeseb8 and ESC-50 datasets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art zero-shot learning approaches.

Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) are proposed to enhance wireless network performance by efficiently reusing ambient environmental reflections. Achieving optimal control of user links, however, necessitates accurately assessing both the user-to-IRS and IRS-to-Receiver channels. This paper introduces a cascaded channel assessment framework utilizing successive detection and separate estimation techniques to independently determine these two channel segments. Subsequently, a unified digital beamforming strategy is proposed to maximize the ergodic capacity under constraints of limited hardware, a successive detection approach, and successive estimation approach. Finally, a low-complexity digital beamforming algorithm employing successive refinement is suggested for practical implementation. Simulation outcomes confirm that the suggested algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with significantly reduced computational complexity.

This paper examines U.S. regional online news concerning COVID-19 to explore its connections with case and death counts, as well as the broader audience. Drawing from an archive of over 1.5 million articles across 1,100 news outlets spanning 2020, we utilize a mixed-method approach. First, a multi-level regression model analyzes the timeline of coverage relative to cases and deaths at national, state, and metropolitan levels. Second, a content analysis investigates the specific framing of the virus in the text. Our findings reveal that while online news coverage generally correlates with COVID-19 cases and deaths regionally, it does not predict coverage volume in adjacent regions. Furthermore, the study shows no link between the quantity of news coverage and audience size. Finally, the analysis indicates that the extent to which the text explicitly references the virus explains only a small portion of the variation in coverage volume.

Counting represents a fundamental human ability that develops over time, initially appearing as an imperfect skill in early childhood before reaching adult precision. This process mirrors other developmental milestones, such as language acquisition, which proceeds gradually rather than instantaneously. To investigate this progression, we employ a novel framework utilizing continuous gradient neural network optimization, where the optimization trajectory itself represents the learning history. By optimizing a memory-augmented network to perform counting, we extract gradients to train the model; consequently, the trajectory of this optimization reveals the acquisition curve, demonstrating a gradual learning pattern similar to that of a human. The observed curves align qualitatively with empirical human learning data, and by adjusting training hyperparameters, we can replicate various stages of human development, including perfect counting and its precursors. Furthermore, this optimization trajectory offers interpretable insights into the learning process, demonstrating that effective adult-like counting emerges from the collaboration of two components: perfect knowledge of the rule and a reliable recollection of that rule.

The Bloom filter stands as a minimalist method for determining set membership with a potential false positive, while the Cuckoo filter offers a complementary approach with guaranteed false negatives. This paper introduces Gnaneshwar et al.'s XOR filter, promising zero ambiguity. Our analysis reveals that while Gnaneshwar's original implementation is flawed, a refined version corrects these issues while boosting performance. Specifically, this improved filter achieves a 3.5-fold speedup over Bloom and a 1.55x increase compared to the Cuckoo filter, all while maintaining a 30% reduction in space usage.

This paper introduces FLVoogd, a robust federated learning framework designed to withstand malicious attacks while preserving client privacy. The system employs a multi-stage defense strategy: initially, it uses differential privacy to protect transmitted updates during each round, followed by the K-nearest Neighbors (KNN) method to filter out potentially malicious updates in subsequent stages. Furthermore, the framework ensures the client's location and the specific data they send remain confidential. We have implemented FLVoogd and evaluated its performance across two standard datasets, CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST, using the popular federated learning architecture Federated Averaging (FedAvg). Experimental results demonstrate that FLVoogd maintains strong anti-attack capabilities and low communication overhead, all while keeping both client locations and update data private.

Simulated environments have long been essential for training and assessing robotic learning algorithms, yet the transition to real-world application remains difficult. This "Sim2Real" challenge is particularly pronounced in deep reinforcement learning, which typically demands extensive real-time data for policy refinement, thereby slowing experimental cycles. This paper introduces a novel Sim2Real divide by applying image-based perturbation strategies to image inputs of a previously successful policy. Initially developed in simulation, this realignment requirement was previously unaddressed. The proposed method enhances the efficiency of deep reinforcement learning by enabling policy optimization through image-specific adjustments rather than additional training data.

Deepfake technologies employ end-to-end deep neural networks to generate or modify video and audio content, resulting in widespread malicious applications such as face swapping, attribute editing, and voice synthesis. While numerous detection algorithms have been developed, they rely heavily on unrealistic unconstrained data; this dependency causes them to fail when encountering genuine media that does not align with these synthetic assumptions. Consequently, there is an urgent need to build robust systems capable of authenticating unconstrained media. This paper introduces a robust deepfake creation and detection pipeline, supported by a theoretical analysis and extensive experiments. The conducted experiments demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmarks including YouTube videos and various types of unedited real-world footage.

The discovery of numerous sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets with equilibrium temperatures below 300 K has sparked debate regarding the presence of global oceans on temperate worlds. While these planets are theorized to possess substantial water content, their internal states are governed by the contrasting equations of state for water vapor and liquid, which dictate whether a surface ocean can persist. This study models the transit signatures of temperate sub-Neptune systems, distinguishing between scenarios where liquid exists and where only vapor remains. For planets with masses between 5 and 25 Earth masses ($M_\oplus$) and radii from 1.5 to 2.8 Earth radii ($R_\oplus$), we find that at equilibrium temperatures of 250 K or lower, the transition layer between liquid and vapor phases is significantly thicker than the water-rich vapor atmosphere, resulting in a distinct increase in transit depth for liquid conditions. Specifically, the difference in transit depth between the two states can reach up to 0.025 ($\Delta R/R \approx 0.025$). Conversely, at higher temperatures, the equilibrium states yield nearly identical transit depths. Using the projected precision of the Habitable Zone Imaging Spectrometer (Habitable Imaging Spectrometer) on the James Webb Space Telescope, we determine that it can differentiate between vapor and liquid states for these planets within 250 K over a wide range of orbital periods, provided the system's inclination is known

This work presents a foundational investigation into the sequential learning capabilities of biologically realistic spiking neural networks, specifically focusing on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN). We evaluated these models against each other using two benchmarks: an artificial task involving a grid world and an actual electroencephalogram (EEG) dataset. Our findings indicate that while both architectures can acquire sequential information, the GAN demonstrates superior performance. We also examined the impact of temporal discretization on learning efficiency, observing that broader time steps generally enhance performance. However, as time steps widen, both models require a greater number of neurons, suggesting a trade-off between efficiency and biological plausibility.

This study presents an efficient approach for verifying solution bounds in stochastic finite element methods utilizing generalized polynomial chaos expansions. The strategy involves enhancing pointwise estimates of relative error by applying rigorous bound techniques to both the Quadrature-based Non-intrusive Polynomial Least-squares Squares Method (GPP) and the bootstrap algorithm. Furthermore, the *a posteriori* error bound estimates are refined by refining the non-intrusive projection step through a mixed L2-L_infinity analysis and employing a novel bound estimation based on sparsity exploitation within the generalized polynomial chaos framework.

This paper introduces a new approach to adaptive sequential change detection that addresses a critical limitation in current methods: their inability to handle uncertainties regarding the specific causal source of a change. While existing techniques can identify that a change has occurred, they often fail to distinguish whether the root cause lies in a specific subsystem or in an external, environmental factor. By equipping agents with the capability to differentiate between internal faults and external disturbances, systems can respond more appropriately, leading to enhanced detection precision and agent survival rates in real-world scenarios. Our proposed framework, termed Adaptive Partially-Observed Sequential Change Identification and Isolation (APOSCIA), relies on a two-step process. First, change detection modules monitor a multi-agent network to flag anomalies. Second, change isolation agents analyze contextual information to determine if the origin is internal or external. This workflow is implemented using a hierarchical change point detection algorithm. Empirical validation through a simulation of a unmanned aerial vehicle network demonstrates APOSCIA's effectiveness.

The study of dwarf galaxies is crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of the local universe. This research focuses on analyzing the stellar populations of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and Leo I, a Local Group satellite dwarf galaxy, by examining their chemical compositions. Using the high-resolution spectrograph on the 2.15-meter telescope at the Lijiang Observatory, we obtained spectra for 100 stars in Leo I with an average resolution of R ~ 20,000, covering the wavelength range 4800–6800 Å. These spectra were employed to determine the age, metallicity, and elemental abundance patterns of Leo I's stellar populations. Additionally, we measured the radial velocity profiles for 100 stars in the SMC, utilizing a dataset of 20,000–30,000 R spectral resolution data collected by the 5-m Aperture Sub-millimeter Telescope Array (AST) at Lijiang Observatory. Our findings indicate that the [Fe/H] metallicity in Leo I ranges from -1.4 to -0.4, with a mean value of -0.8 ± 0.3. Furthermore, we identified a significant correlation between [Fe/H] and [α/Fe] in Leo I, suggesting a star formation history that differs from that of the Milky Way. Extracting structured data from visual documents is a difficult yet vital task that has driven significant research into multi-task learning models. These systems typically rely on large volumes of human-annotated training data, resulting in prohibitively high labeling expenses. To address this, we introduce a transfer-learning strategy that harnesses the model's inherent visual capabilities to pre-train on a vast corpus of unlabeled documents using a synthetic self-generated signal. Subsequently, the model is fine-tuned on a smaller, task-specific dataset targeting visual-rich documents for structured extraction. Evaluations demonstrate that this approach not only achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines but also drastically cuts labeling costs while accelerating training times.

Our approach relies on theorems concerning the prewellordering property and the structure of pointclasses, particularly those developed by Kechris and Stöhr. Recent years have seen neural networks achieve remarkable success, yet their substantial computational and storage demands hinder real-world deployment. While neural network pruning has emerged as a key technique for reducing these requirements, existing methods often fail to simultaneously deliver high precision and performance. This paper introduces **ClickTrain**, an end-to-end training framework utilizing fine-grained, architecture-preserving pruning. ClickTrain dynamically adjusts pruning ratios during training based on the effective click sensitivity of individual weights, calculated through an unbiased, low-overhead network traversal. By incorporating this dynamic mechanism into loss functions, ClickTrain achieves precise, pruning-aware optimization. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art, delivering an 88.0% reduction in model size and a 44× improvement in training speed for CNNs, while surpassing existing methods for both CNNs and RNNs.

We present a complete axiomatic calculus for modal logics featuring distributive and complete lattices as semantical interpretations. These calculi extend the approach developed by Kuznetsov and Poggiolesi by incorporating axioms that specifically address modalities within intensional complete-lattice semantics, distinguished from their counterparts in broad complete-lattice semantics. Furthermore, full completeness is achieved through a companion proof utilizing proof nets.

The merger of a neutron star and a black hole generates gravitational waves that exhibit distinct characteristics, reflecting both the merger dynamics and the post-merger processes. Identifying and separating these signals offers a pathway to acquiring new astrophysical insights. In this study, we introduce a deep learning framework designed to automatically detect neutron star-merger signals, classify their phases, and extract key parameters. Our model successfully identifies neutron star-merger signals within a mixture of signals from various sources, including binary neutron star mergers, repeated binary neutron star mergers, and supermassive black hole mergers, with high precision. Furthermore, following the merger, we accurately determine the dominant frequency and amplitude of the post-merger signals.

We investigate constrained Markov choice procedures, which involve selecting an optimal discrete action set under a discretely constrained continuous measurement framework. Our goal is to maximize the choice's expected utility while satisfying limits on the expected values of several auxiliary indicators. We formulate this selection challenge as a convex optimization problem and employ a Primal-Dual algorithm to obtain near-optimal choices. In our analysis, we examine the procedural dynamics, establish convergence rates, and derive performance bounds. Furthermore, beyond theoretical optimization, our methodology offers a robust approach for practical decision-making.

This paper details a deep learning approach to detecting handwritten mathematical notation, an essential yet difficult component of digitizing technical documents containing equations. We outline a workflow where an initial recognition stage identifies the spatial layout of symbols, followed by a learning stage maps recognition results to corresponding LaTeX strings using a recurrent neural network. We evaluate this method with 1400 examples from two datasets, the lesser-known MathIA and the standard UT Austin dataset, achieving a conversion accuracy of 84.1% on MathIA and 80.5% on UT Austin data.

We offer a physical demonstration linking the Leibholz-Euler identity, which generalizes Euler's formula, to the expansion of sheaf cohomology on complex projective spaces. Furthermore, we derive conditions for this cohomology to remain integral under pullbacks, leading to a generalization of the Gross-Harris criterion. This hypercohomology-based formulation provides a geometric perspective on the Large $N$ expansion of matrix models. Specifically, we identify the matrix integral as an explicit integral of a specific differential form, where the coefficient of each power series term corresponds precisely to a sheaf cohomology class.

Interactions among agents within complex networks serve as a fundamental mechanism for information and resource exchange in both social ecosystems and biological systems. While existing research predominantly addresses equilibrium states, this study investigates the dynamic evolution of a cooperative process over time. By employing a simple yet effective model based on the Prisoner's Dilemma, we analyze how networked agents decide between cooperation and defection, learning from neighbors and adapting their strategies accordingly. Results reveal that internal network variability significantly influences temporal dynamics, causing dynamical behaviors to depend not just on network topology and parameter values, but also on the specific local structure encountered by an agent's path. We further examine how dynamical properties evolve under different traversal methods, contrasting random walks with more structured approaches such as greedy strategy-based paths and traversals mimicking small-world characteristics. Ultimately, we evaluate the impact of these varying dynamics on the equilibrium outcomes of the interaction process.

Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) have introduced variational methods that approximate the policy distribution, offering theoretical benefits such as more diverse action exploration and improved actor learning. However, these approaches face practical challenges, including an increased demand for hyperparameter tuning and an excessive reliance on memory. In this study, we propose addressing these limitations by integrating the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm, a sophisticated Monte Carlo method, into the RL framework. By approximating the policy using an HMC sampler, we aim to enhance the efficacy of the agent's learning process. Experimental evaluations across several benchmark environments demonstrate that this new method performs on par with, and in some cases surpasses, current state-of-the-art solutions.

This study introduces a new sonar blending technique designed to enhance the navigation manager within the xNav framework. By integrating immediate sonar data, it bypasses the latency inherent in conventional data association and fusion processes. Implemented as a Bayesian filter that operates on raw, unprocessed sonar information, this approach has been evaluated against both simulated and real-world datasets. Results demonstrate its effectiveness, particularly in scenarios involving high latency traditional blending or environments with a sparse number of sonar beams.

Nereid, Neptune's third-largest moon, possesses a surface dominated by water ice, a fact supported by its low near-infrared reflectance. However, the specific mix of water ice isotopes and impurities remains unclear. This study leverages the low-resolution NIR reflectance data from the Keck Cosmic Microwave Background Lensing Array (KCMA) to place limits on Nereid's surface makeup. We modeled these observations using a two-component mixture of water ice and impurities, exploring scenarios where ice exists as a pure component or as a substrate for an opaque layer. The results indicate that a pure ice model requires a H₂O fraction of at least 0.50 ± 0.05, whereas an opaque layer model sets a maximum H₂O abundance of 0.30 ± 0.05. Furthermore, if water ice acts as a substrate for an opaque layer, that layer must be extremely thin, with a scale length of no more than 0.04 μm.

The abstract introduces two new classes of affine and projective surfaces, demonstrating that both can be fully described using parametric equations composed of $2 \times 2$ lower triangular matrices with entries from the ring of lower triangular $2 \times 2$ matrices. These surfaces parametrically correspond to lines defined over the projective plane and satisfy two key conditions: (1) every point on a line is contained within exactly one such surface, and (2) each point on a line is omitted by precisely one surface. The discussion concludes with analyses of intersections, lengths, and areas of these triangular matrix-defined surfaces, along with computations of their Christoffel symbols and Gaussian curvatures.

The paper presents an application of Pawlikowski's theorem of interpolant to a collection of eight partial theories of arithmetic, each equipped with a specific recursive function as the Tukey-sequence. As the theorem states, if a formula is valid in arithmetic with a faster-growing function, it is valid in arithmetic with a slower-growing function. We demonstrate that this result extends to the aforementioned eight partial theories.

Decision-makers frequently encounter scenarios where optimal actions are obscured by uncertainty, necessitating the balance between information gathering and action implementation. This specific tension, or exploration-exploitation dilemma, is prevalent in fields ranging from healthcare to artificial intelligence. In this study, we present a new Bayesian framework designed to refine the suboptimal bias inherent in standard dynamic treatment regulation methods. By adopting a pessimistic perspective on ambiguous data, the proposed technique enhances decision quality by explicitly addressing the dilemma's core challenges.

This paper explores the application of homological invariants in tracing topological dualities. We introduce a method for constructing the derived category associated with a homology theory of a topological space equipped with a linear action by a finite group, extending the techniques outlined in \cite{BKL}. Furthermore, we apply these frameworks to investigate the geometric realization of the derived categories linked to the exceptional isomorphisms within the simple complex Lie groups.

Multiple-body bound states (MBS) have recently emerged as a vibrant area of research in condensed matter physics, with extensive theoretical and experimental work dedicated to three-body MBS. This short note demonstrates that within flat band models, three essential conditions—high density, strong correlations, and multiple flat bands—are sufficient to stabilize three-body MBS. We specifically examine two prominent models: the four-flat-band honeycomb system and the four-flat-band triangular system. In the honeycomb configuration, three-body MBS exist as multiple variants, with their stability governed by a specific parameter regime. In contrast, the triangular system supports three-body MBS across the full spectrum of its key parameters. Beyond these primary states, the two models also host multiple other MBS configurations, including two-body and four-body states. Furthermore, these systems can realize diverse few-body superconductivity patterns, encompassing both $p$-wave and s-wave pairing symmetries.

The Polya's theorem regarding plane curves states that for any topological embedding $f$ of $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$, there exist topological circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ linked with $f(\mathbb{R})$. In this work, we provide a proof for this result under the more general framework of a universal theorem for all pairs of linked local compact abelian groups (G, H) of dimension 1 within any topological group X. Furthermore, we establish corresponding theorems applicable to specific topological abelian groups of dimension one.

Presence-absence data, which only allow values of 0 or non-zero, are common in fields like ecology and bioinformatics. This study investigates clustering techniques for such binary data, with a focus on methods utilizing the Jaccard index for distance measurement. We present a fresh approach to evaluating clustering outcomes for high-dimensional binary datasets, introducing a resampling strategy for score matrix construction that remains effective even in sparse conditions where traditional null models fail. Applying this evaluation framework to both real-world datasets and a comprehensive set generated via simulation, we compared seven clustering algorithms. Our results indicate that the proposed new algorithm outperforms existing methods across the tested scenarios.

Salient object detection focuses on identifying salient regions within an image, with applications ranging from medical imaging to autonomous driving. Although current methods generally perform well, they often fail to accurately detect salient objects in complex, cluttered environments. This study introduces a unified framework for salient object detection that integrates both RGB and RGB-D inputs. By establishing a comprehensive structure, the work proposes an effective encoding module to leverage depth information, two innovative novelty modules to enhance detection precision, and a lightweight yet high-performance secondary refinement module. Furthermore, a new binary salient ground truth is proposed to address inconsistencies found in existing datasets. Comprehensive evaluations on five benchmarks demonstrate that the secondary refinement module is both lightweight and efficient, while the overall model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/zyh-99/SOD.

This paper details our UM-IU@LING team's approach for identifying aggressive tweets in Task 6 of the 6th SemEval-2019 shared task. Our methodology centers on a BERT model that generates context-aware token representations, which are subsequently processed by an SVM classifier. This combination yielded the second-best outcomes on the public leaderboard with an F1 score of 0.8222, trailing only the top-performing entry by a margin of 0.0003.

This study examines the quotients defined as $Q_{s}(p)=\frac{A_{p}}{s(p)}$ and $\bar{Q}_{a}(p)=\frac{\bar{A}_{p}}{\bar{A}_{p}}$ for primes $a$. It is demonstrated that for a vast majority of these primes, the values of $\bar{Q}_{a}(p)$ fall within the interval $[1, 2]$, whereas $Q_{a}(p)$ predominantly cluster around $0.83$. Further investigations into the distribution of these quotients across $\mathbb{R}$ are conducted using numerical methods.

Reconstructing images and estimating material maps from noisy X-ray projections is critical in medical and industrial imaging. While standard approaches like filtered backprojection fail under low-dose conditions, existing iterative methods are often limited by slow convergence or lack of material decomposition capabilities. This study introduces a unified variational framework that simultaneously reconstructs images, denoises multi-energy sensor data, and performs material decomposition. This model relies on a non-convex variational prior featuring two hyperparameters designed to enhance edge definition and reduce artifacts within homogeneous areas. These hyperparameters are automatically calibrated via the cross-validation procedure. Experiments utilizing both simulated datasets and clinical CT scans from a clinical scanner demonstrate that the proposed approach yields superior quantitative and qualitative outcomes compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) is a highly valuable, multi-stage application that has seen significant development over the last few decades. While deep learning now powers these core sub-tasks—specifically, handwriting recognition (HWR) and handwritten word recognition (HWR)—acquiring the diverse labeled datasets required to train these models remains a major hurdle. Although large-scale, diverse collections exist for HgW and HwP, comparable resources for individual Hg, HwP, and HwP are scarce. To address this, we introduce a method for generating single-shot compositional data that synthesizes HgW, HwP, and HwP instances from an existing HgW corpus. We evaluated this approach using HgW data from HwP and HwP to train Hg models, comparing the resulting composed datasets against traditional small, dedicated Hg datasets. Results indicate a performance improvement of 0.5 to 2.0 J/BLP across four different Hg tasks. Furthermore, we assessed a hybrid training strategy where a model is pre-trained on a composed dataset and then fine-tuned on a limited number of labeled Hg samples. This transfer learning approach yielded recognition error rate reductions of 0.5 to 2.0 J/BLP for the fine-tuned Hg model.

This work examines the nuclear equation of state (EOS) and its influence on neutron star properties using Skyrme and relativistic mean-field models. Computational efforts focused on calculating EOS parameters via *ab initio* methods, specifically many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) and coupled-cluster theory, have been made. By systematically analyzing MBPT and coupled-cluster results for heavy nuclei alongside existing experimental data and macroscopic EOS constraints, a comprehensive picture of the EOS has been developed. These *ab initio* calculations provide significant constraints on neutron matter behavior at high densities, with direct implications for the physics of neutron stars.

The SSH model, a simple yet profound dimerized system, serves as an exemplary platform for understanding key principles of one-dimensional topological quantum physics. This study utilizes Python to examine its wave functions, energy bands, and charge density, with a specific focus on visualizing how varying parameters influence the system. A central aspect of our analysis involves exploring domain wall states—manifesting as localized eigenstates situated within the energy gap—and visualizing their product wave function to clarify the underpinnings of nontrivial topology in band structures. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between flux and wave function phases within the context of the tight-binding framework. By the conclusion, we summarize the experimental findings within the scope of the relevant physical theory.
