We derive the dual-loop supergravity S-matrix for Type IIB superstring theory on the AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ background using only its corresponding gauge theory data. This computation extends the established tree-level supergravity/CFT duality to the quantum level by obtaining the superstratum amplitude via a supersymmetric extension of the finite part of a hexagonal Wilson operator OPE, which is organized through the generalized amplitude representation. This representation constructs scattering amplitudes by summing over supersymmetric projections of Wilson coefficients associated with multi-particle operators defined by six-particle color-ordered tree amplitudes, known as the generalized amplitude function. Our findings indicate that at two loops, the superstrupted superstrupture tree-level results by incorporating BPS multiplet structure and accounting for bosonic and fermionic contributions.

Object-oriented development on GPUs has grown significantly, yet current allocators are constrained by their design for C-style programming, leading to inefficient memory management and high fragmentation. Furthermore, existing approaches fail to optimize the non-uniform access patterns typical of object-oriented paradigms, resulting in poor hardware utilization and low throughput. To address these limitations, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator engineered specifically for GPU object-oriented development. This system dynamically adjusts memory block sizes based on runtime allocation patterns and utilizes fine-grained locking to enhance the effectiveness of memory accesses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art allocators, delivering up to 2.4× improvements in allocated memory size and 1.6× fewer memory locks, along with up to 1.4× faster allocation times and 1.2× higher lock effectiveness.

We examine the origin of Standard Model $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetries within $SO(10)$ grand unified theories, specifically through subgroup chains that bifurcate following symmetry breaking. Our analysis reveals that three distinct $U(1)_X$ models emerge, each corresponding to a specific chain of subgroups. We analyze the phenomenological properties of these three models, focusing on the mass of the $Z'$ boson and the coupling strength of the $Z'$ to the Standard Model.

To evaluate the mechanical soundness of a straw container subjected to pressure, we applied pressurized air, generated by a jet of water falling into it, to the sealed straw whose cut end was wrapped in aluminum foil. By measuring the sound produced, we assessed when the foil seal breached. Our results indicate that the foil seal can withstand pressures up to approximately $40\text{ kPa}$ ($\sim 6\text{ psi}$). Once this threshold is crossed, the foil seal ruptures, and significant longitudinal stress develops along the straw. We estimate this resulting stress to be roughly $100\text{ N m}^{-2}$ ($\sim 1\text{ Pa}$, assuming a standard $1\text{ m}$ length). Consequently, the straws remain structurally sound and do not break under these conditions.

The probabilistic circuit (PC) representation has recently emerged as a powerful method for encoding probability distributions, offering efficient mechanisms for exact inference and learning. Concurrently, the credal Bayesian framework, which employs sets of probability distributions to represent uncertainty about model parameters, has gained significant traction. This study advances both areas by introducing a novel credal Bayesian framework that leverages PC representations. We propose an approach to compute guaranteed strength bounds for this framework, utilizing linear programming solved over exactly computable, linear structural constraints within the PC. Our results establish a soft constraint satisfaction problem applicable to various types of PC and demonstrate empirical applications of these strength guarantees across multiple domains.

We demonstrate that an accelerated frame induces an effective homogeneous blue shift in the two-dimensional excitations of a dilute quantum gas trapped in an anisotropic harmonic potential. This potential serves as an analog for a microcavity photonic crystal, where the resulting shift translates to a synthetic magnetic field. By modulating the potential, we can control the magnitude of this effective shift, thereby regulating the phase transition from a magnetically ordered state to a superfluid. Consequently, we propose a feasible experimental setup to observe the corresponding analogs of Landau and Zeeman oscillations.

In the general theory of metric spaces, a code is neighbor-transitive whenever its distance-neighborhood union equals the entire space minus itself. Within this framework, we investigate codes defined within generalized quadrangles (GQs), focusing especially on cases exhibiting high symmetry. Our analysis reveals that for a code to be symmetrically structured, it must either fail to be antipodal or assume an "almost 1-perfect" status relative to a specific GQ derived from its parameters. Furthermore, we examine the properties of 1-perfect codes in antipodal GQ configurations and present several examples of neighbor-transitive codes drawn from graphs that are not generalized quadrangles but are linked to them through their respective distance graphs.

The 2D correlation function (2D-CF) technique is employed to investigate the spatial arrangement of molecular gas within the Galactic Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). Leveraging high-resolution CO data from the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy (ATLAS3D), the study reveals that the 2D-CF is highly sensitive to anisotropic mass configurations. Specifically, the method successfully identifies the elongated structure of the molecular plane and detects a secondary, fainter elongation perpendicular to it, likely corresponding to the Southern Ridge. Furthermore, the approach quantifies the southern extent of the gas distribution, reaching approximately 300 pc from the galactic center. Although the primary elongation aligns with the molecular plane, the 2D-CF indicates a significant increase in the azimuthal variance of the standard deviation of molecular gas positions at latitudes exceeding $|b| = 1^\circ$. This finding suggests that the elongated nature of the gas is most pronounced in the southern CMZ, whereas in the northern region, the configuration is more isotropic.

We introduce a population rate framework to model the nonlinear absorption edges observed in recent x-ray absorption near-edge structure (XNES) experiments. This approach utilizes a set of rate equations describing the temporal evolution of electron populations in the valence, conduction, and core states. By solving these equations with a conduction band quasi-steady-state approximation, we derive analytical expressions for core and valence state populations. Our results indicate that nonlinear absorption arises from a reduction in core electron flux caused by the accumulation of electrons in both conduction and valence bands. We observe a power-law dependence of absorption on fluence, where the exponent is governed by the relative filling of conduction and valence bands. Furthermore, we identify that absorption reduction can be modeled equivalently as an increase in the material's effective edge absorption energy.

This research introduces a compact and cost-effective temperature sensor designed for the Internet of Things (IoT), utilizing a simplified approach to achieve high accuracy and low power consumption. The sensor's performance is evaluated through simulations and experimental testing using 0.18µm CMOS technology. Experimental results demonstrate an operating range of 0.6V to 1.8V, with a measurement resolution of 0.24°C, a temperature accuracy of ±1.4°C, a measurement range spanning -20°C to +100°C, and an average energy consumption of 1.06pJ per conversion.

We introduce a heralded method for generating polarization entanglement between two photons that possess unequal energies, utilizing a quantum scissors approach. This process involves passing entangled photon pairs with undefined energies through two spatial modes, each equipped with a mirror, concave lens, and lens system to selectively filter higher-energy photons down to pairs with undefined energies, effectively randomizing their exact energy levels. This setup produces robust, long-distance resilient entangled states that remain stable against decoherence. The resulting entanglement is verified through coincidence counting and quantum tomography, yielding a fidelity of 0.825. The proposed quantum scissors technique is applicable not only for generating entangled energies but also for manipulating the amplitude of already entangled photons.

Given a set of points in Euclidean space, the Euclidean spanner $S$ is $\epsilon$-stretch if every pair distance $d_S(u,v)$ satisfies $\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}d(u,v) \leq d_S(u,v) \leq (1+\epsilon)d(u,v)$. A virtual spanner is a metric defined over point pairs that remains within multiplicative factors of the original Euclidean distances but may deviate slightly from strict $\epsilon$-stretch. This paper establishes the existence of $\delta$-approximation virtual $(1.1)$-spanners with sparsity $O(n^{1+\delta})$ for any $\delta > 0$, applicable to datasets in $d$ dimensions where $d$ denotes Euclidean metric dimensions. Furthermore, we introduce an $L_1$-approximation virtual $(1.1)$-spanner of sparsity $O(n^{1+d/2+\delta})$ for $d$ dimensional points.

Feature extraction stands as a pivotal phase in machine learning workflows, where a subset of data is selected to construct a classifier. In the context of Internet of Things (IoT) device classification, this process is critical for effective operation. However, most existing methods overlook the associated data extraction costs, a factor that can be substantial in IoT scenarios due to the necessity of acquiring extensive datasets. This paper introduces an innovative, cost-aware framework for IoT device classification. It employs a genetic algorithm to autonomously identify the optimal feature subset, thereby minimizing the number of sensors required and the associated acquisition expenses. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques regarding accuracy, while also significantly reducing the cost of data collection by substantially shrinking the sensor footprint needed for classification.

G\"odel modal logics, which arise within the context of intuitionistic reasoning, hold significant value across diverse theoretical frameworks. This paper introduces algebraic models specifically tailored to these G\"odel modal logics and their extensions, alongside the corresponding relational structures.

This paper introduces a bilingual data-driven approach to aligning words within text. Our system takes text in one language and a corpus containing the target language as its inputs. Our methodology involves locating similar words by comparing the single-language text against this target language input. We demonstrate that this approach can successfully align words even with target language text that has never before been seen during training. Testing with extensive data from Wikipedia and the New York Times reveals results comparable to state-of-the-art statistical word alignment systems. Our findings also reveal a crucial requirement: a substantial amount of target language data is necessary to achieve high-quality alignments.

This work introduces a novel algorithm designed to generate Nash equilibria in general finite games, offering a computational complexity bound of $O(N^3)$ arithmetic operations, where $N$ represents the combined number of pure strategies across all players. Under the assumption that a game's Nash equilibrium possesses strict support, we demonstrate that our algorithm produces a $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium after $O(N^3/\epsilon)$ operations. Our approach leverages concepts from algebraic geometry and convex optimization, specifically utilizing the distorted Newton flow method. We establish the existence of our core technical tool, the distorted Newton flow, and demonstrate its utility by proving a key theorem regarding Nesterov's alpha-blend flow within an algebraic framework. Additionally, we establish an error estimate for the distorted flow that underpins our analysis of finite-game applications.

Primordial Black Hole Dark Energy (PBHDE) offers a promising alternative to the cosmological constant, derived from the assumption that energy emitted by astrophysical black holes influences cosmic expansion. This study advances the modeling of PBHDE by incorporating non-zero spin effects and conducting the first simulations of this model with primordial in-spin black spins within a cosmological framework. Leveraging Population Synthesis with Cosmology Evolution (PopSyCLE), a cosmology-enabled black hole evolution code, we performed simulations across a broad parameter space to calculate luminosity functions and expansion histories. Our findings suggest that current observational data can constrain the spin parameter space to approximately 0.2 precision. Moreover, we designed and implemented a novel machine learning approach to analyze expansion histories, which significantly enhances precision in determining spin and mass parameters.

This study examines how a rigid, asymmetric wedge penetrates into a granular medium, focusing on the initial penetration stage where the wedge angle is sufficiently large to cause the transition from friction-dominated to inertia-controlled dynamics. During this shift, the system enters an acceleration phase characterized by increased penetration velocity. We analyze how this acceleration stage evolves into a steady-state regime and report findings regarding the structure of stages observed during inertial acceleration. Additionally, we outline a method for estimating the time required to reach steady state.

We examine a spherical static random field that is Gaussian and invariants with respect to rotations, for which we derive one-step auto-regressive representations. The characteristic function of the associated marginal distribution fulfills an equation on the positive real axis that can be mapped to a condition concerning the parameters of the spectral measure. Leveraging this link, we demonstrate that a valid solution exists iff the spectral measure satisfies two specific criteria: it must be both "beakwise" and "log-convex." The article concludes with the presentation of several examples of measures that fulfill these requirements.

The interaction-free imaging technique, or "ghost" or "quantum" visualization, typically relies on high sample concentrations to register a signal, which results in substantial sample damage. This study introduces a method that eliminates the need for sample engagement and lowers the required concentration by several orders of magnitude. This approach utilizes a single pixel detector and does not rely on sample interference; instead, it identifies samples through changes in a globally entangled state triggered without direct particle-sample interaction. This capability allows for the detection of extremely delicate specimens, such as live bacteria, using merely thermal fluctuations.

The frictional behavior of complex fluids is significantly shaped by their microstructure. In this study, we demonstrate that adding a surfactant, specifically sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), to a glycerol-water mixture enhances the friction between sand grains. This enhancement arises because the addition of surfactant promotes the formation of a shear-induced, time-evolving microstructure within the soap solution's bubble networks. We quantify both the resulting increase in friction and the characteristic time scale of this microstructure by measuring the shear stress and rheology of the SDS-glycerol-water system. Subsequently, we integrate these findings with a frictional framework to model granular flow through an experimentally fabricated, textured channel composed of bubbles. Our results indicate that the frictional resistance experienced by the grains results from the competition between two opposing mechanisms: friction reduction due to frictional slip and friction increase from frictional hopping, the balance of which is governed by the texture's scale relative to the microstructural grain size.

Skin cancer is a prevalent and potentially fatal malignancy that necessitates early diagnosis for effective treatment. While deep learning has achieved significant advancements in image classification, it often falters when dealing with classes containing outlier samples. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework for identifying skin carcinoma that integrates deep learning with multi-scale entropy to detect anomical data. Specifically, the proposed approach first generates an entropy map representing local heterogeneity within the carcinoma regions. Subsequently, these maps are utilized as inputs for a classification model, which has been trained using the weighted loss function to mitigate bias inherent in imbalanced data distributions. Experimental evaluations conducted on the ISIC 2019 dataset demonstrate that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We report on measurements of electron quasi-particle lifetimes in sodium, a nearly free-electron metal, utilizing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy with photoelectrons possessing kinetic energies between 0.6 and 2.8 eV. By measuring photoemission intensity as a function of the detector's acceptance angle, we observed that the measured scattering rates align with theoretical predictions based on Fermi's golden rule, which employ a constant matrix element. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the non-dispersive quasi-particle lifetime at the Fermi surface correlates with kinetic energy following an inverse proportionality to that energy's cubic power.

This paper presents a new technique for analyzing any symplectic map by employing paths within the Hamiltonian framework. The primary objective is to link an arbitrary symplectic map to a specific Hamiltonian system, thereby facilitating the examination of phase space structures and volume changes over time while revealing critical regular and chaotic motion dynamics. Furthermore, it elucidates how a specific path integral can be reconstructed from a corresponding symplectic map, a capability that proves especially beneficial for understanding concepts in symplectic transport. The study also investigates the significance of trajectory dependence in this restoration process and demonstrates how trajectory selection can be optimized to minimize error accumulation during long-term phase space evolution. The remainder of the work focuses on the free expansion scenario, where the trajectory selection strategy is optimized to achieve the simplest possible Hamiltonian system.

We calculate the coefficients for integrals of link and curvature graphs at a singular point of symplectic leaf within a deformation of a Poisson structure. We demonstrate that these coefficients—referred to as "link weights"—possess a universal nature, independent of the specific underlying structure. "Curvature," referring to weights assigned to general graphs, was previously defined and computed by the second author in collaboration with M. Markwig for complex projective spaces; these results have now been generalized to all complex manifold dimensions and extended to the real domain. Link weights were subsequently computed for specific configurations of symplectic leaves exhibiting various singularity types. Additionally, we provide evidence supporting the conjecture that the resulting link weights correspond to a subset of the "Milnor weights" identified in works by D. Dostrovsky, P. E. Dey, and others.

This study examines nonlinear traveling waves within one-dimensional granular chains, focusing on non-dispersive nanoptera situated near non-degenerate linear eigenmodes. By applying a singular perturbation technique to the weakly nonlinear equations of motion, we derive expressions for the amplitudes of these waves, finding them to align with the singular limit of the classic Duffing oscillator. Numerical simulations confirm these theoretical findings and reveal the coexistence of dual types of non-dissipative, non-dissipative nonlinear waves: (i) spatially periodic nanoptera anchored to degenerate linear modes, and (ii) spatially modulated nanoptera based on non-degenerate linear eigenmodes. For systems supporting two transverse eigenmodes, our theory predicts a specific ratio between the amplitudes of the resulting nanoptera, a result that numerical verification supports. Furthermore, we identify the existence of diatomic granular-optera, characterized by an asymmetric, non-symmetrical spatial profile.

Features known as "primal" arise from analytic continuation in the conformal collider model, which we investigate within the framework of a single field coupled to gravity in two spatial dimensions. We demonstrate that a Primal S-matrix exists for this system and can be explicitly constructed and explicitly verified to satisfy Primal Feature Unitarity. This approach allows us to derive leading-order differential equations governing correlation functions by applying the conformal collider method to cosmology, solving them using an initial condition set by Primal Feature Unitarity. The resulting two-point function exhibits a power-law behavior, while the three-point function displays a leading term that mirrors the structure of a standard single-field inflationary interaction.

This paper introduces a method to demonstrate that specific acyclic acyclic graphs (bipartite graphs) are actually cycles by leveraging "accordion charts." While the technique was initially developed by Chudnovsky, Thomassé, and the others for showing the non-existence of certain structures in graphs without cycles, we adapt it here to prove graph cyclicity. As a direct result of applying this proof, several families of accordion graphs are shown to possess a polynomial number of cycles. Additionally, we establish a striking isomorphism between two distinct classes of acyclic graphs: "circulants" (a type of regular graph with high symmetry) and those generated by applying our theorem to accordion graphs.

We investigate the dynamical scaling behavior of state distributions arising from three-state quantum walks on the one-dimensional lattice, with a specific focus on how initial momentum influences these dynamics. When initiated with a narrow wave packet centered at zero momentum, the position probability density follows a $1/t$ decay, while non-zero momenta induce a distinct power-law decay of $1/t^2$. Consequently, the global evolution exhibits classical dynamical scaling, $f_t(x) = t^\alpha F((x)/t^\beta)$, where $F$ is a universal function, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are scaling exponents, and the global distribution converges to a stationary distribution $F$ in the long-time limit. However, when considering very broad wave packets with non-zero momentum, classical scaling breaks down, replaced instead by anomalous scaling characterized by $\alpha \neq 0$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this momentum-dependent power-law decay originates from the singular nature of the Fourier transform of the stationary distribution $F$.

Self-distillation has emerged as a key method for enhancing deep learning model accuracy. In the context of self-guided Vision Transformers (ViTs), property tokens are utilized to facilitate knowledge transfer among transformer blocks, resulting in a unified model with improved performance. Nevertheless, current strategies for self-guided ViT development suffer from suboptimal knowledge propagation and require manual tuning of numerous hyperparameters. To address these challenges, this work introduces a self-distillation framework that utilizes auxiliary properties as internal signals to orchestrate knowledge distillation. By integrating property tokens with an adaptive-fusion mechanism, a dynamic knowledge-graph is established to manage information flow between adjacent blocks, allowing a more comprehensive understanding of visual features. Furthermore, a cross-attention-based adapter module is introduced to refine the interaction between knowledge graphs and subsequent vision transformers. Experiments across multiple image classification benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method, named ViT-Kit, achieves a 2.5% absolute improvement in top-1 accuracy compared to existing self-guided ViT approaches, all while eliminating the need for hyperparameter adjustment.

This study introduces a dissipative dark fluid model incorporating both dark matter and dark energy components, with dark energy fluid exhibiting non-zero pressure, viscosity, and an equation of state (EOS) parameter $\omega$ ranging between $-1$ and $-1/3$. Adopting an LRS Bianchi type-I metric, we derive the corresponding field equations and solve them using a Hubble-depending expansion scalar $\theta = n\dot{n}/\nolimits + \dot{\gamma}$, where $n$ represents scale factors. Our findings indicate that this dissipative dark fluid model provides a more accurate description of the universe's evolution compared to non-dissipative dark fluid models. Furthermore, we analyze the physical characteristics of these fluids and their impact on the overall dynamics of the cosmos.

An alternative demonstration of ill-posedness for the $d$-dimensional incompressible Euler equations in critical Sobolev spaces $W^{2,p}(\mathbb{T}^d)$ is presented, for $1 < p \leq \frac{d}{p-2}$. This approach relies on the established method by Kato and Témam, employing an argumentative framework similar to that used by Kato in his proof of the Navier-Stokes equations' local well-posedness.

Recent advancements in text-to-image generation models have produced photorealistic and visually captivating images; however, generating high-fidelity images that strictly adhere to textual semantics remains a significant hurdle. To address this, we introduce the "Steady Creator," an architecture designed to enhance meaningful statistical correlations between text semantics and visual elements within latent spaces through guided diffusion. Initially, we develop a shared steady-state diffusion framework capable of producing high-resolution imagery from image-text pairs at accelerated rates. Subsequently, we advance this model with two specialized components: a guidance module within the generator to refine internal text-semantically-based statistical distributions, and a cross-attention mechanism leveraging pre-generated image banks to further boost visual semantic accuracy. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate superior performance in both quantitative and qualitative assessments compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/lyl-lyl/Steady_Creator.

Recent advancements in Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) have demonstrated their efficacy in uncertainty estimation for computer vision tasks. This paper introduces a novel application of BNNs for reversible data concealment, a process recently gaining attention for securing sensitive image data through encryption or watermarking without irreversible modification. By leveraging the inherent probabilistic nature of BNNs, we successfully train a lightweight neural network capable of both encoding and decoding images. Our proposed method is straightforward and achieves a substantial enhancement in the fidelity of the final watermark, while also allowing watermarks of greater bit-depth than current standards.

This study investigates the significance of $J/\psi\to (\gamma + ){\rm invisible}$ decays in light of current experimental data. We demonstrate that this process imposes stringent constraints on both neutrino and dark energy effective field theories. Specifically, it establishes tight bounds on the scale of the neutrino Fermi surface, $E_{\rm F}$, yielding $E_{\rm F} > 10^{10}~{\rm GeV}$, surpassing previous limits by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, it reduces the viable parameter space for neutrino interactions by roughly two orders of magnitude. In the context of dark energy, assuming a neutrino mass of $m_\nu \sim 0.1~{\rm eV}$, our results narrow the scale of neutrino Fermi surface, $E_{\rm F}$, to $E_{\rm F} > 10^{10}~{\rm GeV}$, significantly exceeding prior limits of $E_{\rm F} > 10^{8}~{\rm GeV}$. Consequently, this process restricts the parameter space for dark energy models by approximately 30%.

Magnetic bright spots (MBS) are regions of intense magnetic fields where solar faculae appear brighter than the surrounding light. Drawing on 15 years of Big Bear Solar Observatory (BBSO) data, we demonstrate that the distribution of MBS intensity relative to the background is inherently two-part. This distribution is defined by a narrow peak near an intensity ratio of 1.0, followed by a broad secondary distribution that peaks around 1.3. This broad component is consistently observed across all three wavelength bands analyzed (4156 Å, 6176 Å, and 8542 Å). We propose that the narrow distribution corresponds to facular elements with field strengths below approximately 1.5 kG, while the broader distribution corresponds to MBS with strengths exceeding 1.7 kG.

Current identification models are typically benchmarked using long video sequences, which often results in performance metrics that do not reflect real-world scenarios. To address this discrepancy, we introduce the Human Minimal Clips (HMC) benchmark, consisting of brief 1-second clips designed to evaluate model performance in realistic settings. Our analysis reveals a significant performance gap between models that excel on long videos and those that excel with HMC data, indicating that existing models struggle to identify human actions effectively in short durations. Furthermore, we examined the impact of frame sampling strategies on performance and tested several alternative approaches—including clipping via random crops, iterative random crops, and random trajectory sampling—to improve short-video recognition. Ultimately, the best results were achieved by integrating our proposed method into the Video Transformer architecture.

Observations indicate that galaxy fields endure for hundreds of millions of years, implying that shadow matter must dissipate at a rate exceeding 10$^{-13}$ yr$^{-1}$. We demonstrate that this constraint relaxes to approximately 10$^{-17}$ yr$^{-1}$ if a fraction of the shadow matter consists of milli-magnetic monopoles. These monopoles interact with baryonic matter through the universal ISO(3) gauge symmetry, causing them to rapidly lose kinetic energy and become trapped within galactic disks. There, they annihilate slowly with ions due to their exceptionally small cross-sections, leading to an even slower disappearance of trapped monopoles. Consequently, we derive an upper bound on monopole abundance of roughly 10$^{-17}$ relative to the disk's baryonic density.

Accurately predicting future spatiotemporal climate patterns is vital for sustainable development and ecological security. Deep learning methods have become popular tools for this task, yet existing approaches often rely on fixed window partitions that ignore global context, while also facing computational bottlenecks when processing high-resolution grids. This study introduces STTra-X, a novel Transformer model designed for efficient and accurate forecasting of climate variables. The architecture utilizes 2D position embeddings to encode high-resolution spatial data, employs shuffled intra-attention to capture local features within windows, and adopts shuffled inter-attention to integrate global context across adjacent blocks. Additionally, a channel mixing module enhances the representation of multi-dimensional channel information. Experimental results demonstrate that STTra-X significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two standard datasets: the Climate Simulation Data (CSD) and the Precipitation Dataset (PD). Specifically, on the PD dataset, STTra-X reduces Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) by 10.6% and 13.0% for short-term and long-term predictions, respectively, surpassing the leading current model, LSTNet.

We examine scalar dark matter models featuring two Higgs-doublets, which are equivalent to three-doublet theories with $S_3$ symmetry where the lightest particle remains stable. In this scenario, the mass matrix of charged components is generally non-diagonal, resulting in eigenstates that are linear combinations of the original fields. The first model, corresponding to a dark matter candidate that decays into photon pairs, imposes the mass matrix to be real and its eigenvalues real as well, forcing the lighter charged mass eigenstate to be a symmetric combination of the original fields. The second model, applicable to dark matter that annihilates into both photon pairs and W-boson pairs, utilizes a complex mass matrix where the lighter charged mass eigenstate is an antisymmetric combination of the original fields. The article analyzes the annihilation and decay cross-sections for both scenarios, specifically focusing on the impact of CP violation on these interactions.

We demonstrate that the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis holds true within the $3 \times 3$ quantum system. Previously, our research outlined four distinct scenarios for entangled states in this $3 \times 3$ system, with the second scenario consisting of states PPT-convertible to those in the first. While the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis had been proven for uncutably entangled states in scenario one and separable states in scenario four, it remained unaddressed for scenarios two and three. In this paper, we establish that for pair-wise entangled states in scenario two, the PPT boundary is defined by NSEPs (non-separable states with minimum trace). Furthermore, we confirm that the NSEPs remain PLOT (PPT orthogonal locally trace) when transitioning to separable states. Consequently, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis is verified for all $3 \times 3$ quantum systems.

In this study, we formulate a mathematical model to simulate how astrocytes regulate ion and substance transport within the brain's extracellular space (ECS). The proposed framework utilizes a gradient diffusion coefficient to simulate pericyte-mediated pore constriction in glial cells, thereby regulating transport within astrocytes. To capture pericyte responses to specific pathophysiological conditions, the concentration of those conditions serves as an input signal that controls the constriction of circular smooth muscle cells surrounding the pericytes. The resulting co-culture system of astrocytes and ECS is governed by a set of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). To assess whether targeted physiological states can be achieved through appropriate pericyte modulation, the PDEs are embedded within an optimization objective that seeks to minimize discrepancies between simulated and target concentrations. The paper introduces the weak and strong formulations of the optimization problem and presents an algorithm based on the adjoint method to solve it. The optimization task is solved using the interior-point approach via the IPOPS software, and the implementation is validated through numerical simulations comparing ion concentrations during healthy conditions and ischemic events. The results demonstrate that selective constricting of pericytes effectively regulates ion levels in the ECS during both normal and pathological scenarios.

This study introduces a novel, unsupervised approach to the field of fraud detection, designed to identify concealed money laundering patterns within transaction networks. By leveraging network motif analysis, the method automatically discovers the structural characteristics of transaction networks and locals areas exhibiting significant similarity to known money laundering networks. Key contributions include a detailed analysis of transaction network structure, the identification of a new, effective network motif, and the successful identification of transactions linked to money laundering. Experimental results indicate that this technique outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, thereby extending the reach of motif analysis into the money laundering domain.

When a white dwarf spirals into a black hole, it releases electromagnetic radiation across the spectrum, from radio waves to X-rays. Because these signals can be partially obscured by interstellar dust, it is vital to distinguish the source's intrinsic emission from the foreground interference. This study models the electromagnetic output generated by the disruption of the white dwarf and calculates the foreground radio noise using standard power laws. By comparing these two profiles, we determine the conditions under which foreground emissions dominate over those from the accretion event.

We have calculated the form factors for semieeetronic $\tau$ decays into three-body nonleptonic final states, assuming a vector or axial-vector baryonic current. The computation employs a form factor basis and utilizes quark-hadron duality to determine their shapes. This analytical framework yields predictions for branching ratios and ratio of form factors that can be compared with experimental data.

The study introduces a parametric family of Tversky metrics governed by a single real parameter $\alpha \in [1,3]$, with the classic Jaccard distance corresponding to $\alpha=1$. While the distance at $\alpha=1$ measures pure set overlap, the distance at $\alpha=3$ evaluates the overlap relative to the symmetric difference of two sets' cardinalities. We demonstrate that this framework bridges the gap between the Jaccard distance and a metric derived from the normalized information distance, as recently defined. Furthermore, we analyze key properties of these Tversky metrics and investigate their applicability within a range of practical domains.

Deblurring degrades image quality, causing issues with downstream tasks like recognition and reconstruction. Although various deblurring techniques exist, they often fail to deliver satisfactory results for dynamic scenes involving moving people or objects. This paper introduces a new approach to deblurring static images within these dynamic environments by leveraging a pseudo-blur generator. This unsupervised component creates paired datasets by selecting frames from video sequences, where one is treated as a reference and the other as its corresponding blurred variant. Using this synthesized training data, a convolutional neural network is employed to deblurred specific movements. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior visual quality and significantly lowering Mean Squared Error (MSE) on both MSDR and MGBE datasets.

**Objective:** The primary aim of this research is to investigate the extent to which a system employing discrete chemical reactions can replicate the behaviors of a single spiking neuron. To achieve this, the work examines the capacity of chemical reaction networks (CRNs) to emulate specific neuronal models, specifically the Izhikevich model, when equipped with programmed molecular components.

**Methodology:** The investigation utilizes a hybrid simulation framework that couples chemical reaction solvers with biologically grounded neuron models. This approach tests whether CRNs can accurately represent fundamental neuronal functions, including spike generation, response to varying input strengths, and the adaptation phenomenon observed in specific neuron types.

**Key Findings:** The study demonstrates that specialized molecular parts can be synthesized to drive individual CRN species to replicate distinct features of the Izhikevich model. Collectively, these findings indicate that a chemical-based system utilizing these discrete components is entirely capable of mimicking the overall dynamics of an Izhikevich neuron.

**Implications:** The research supports the hypothesis that chemical reaction networks programmed with synthetic molecular parts offer a viable alternative to traditional electrical wiring for connecting simulated neurons. This has significant potential for the field of molecular computing, suggesting that future processors based on chemical reactions could be designed to replicate biological neurons with remarkable fidelity.

Let $(A,\le)$ represent a partially ordered set (poset) equipped with a sequence of intervals $\{I_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$. The construction builds the corresponding ordered structure $\prod_{\mathfrak{U}}(A,\le)$ by defining an ultrapower based on the cardinality of these intervals. Specifically, the resulting poset consists of equivalence classes derived from the filter $\mathfrak{U}$ on $\mathbb{N}$ containing all co-finite sets. The study examines the properties and characteristics of this poset, with a specific focus on its completeness attributes.

Although significant research has been dedicated to profiling neural network architectures, there is a notable absence of similar investigation into profiling neural network architectures, there is a notable absence of research into profiling specific datasets to inform model selection. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a comprehensive analysis of how different datasets vary in their impact on architecture performance. We examine a wide variety of classification tasks, including image, audio, and natural language classification, utilizing multiple popular datasets within each domain. Our investigation reveals that dataset characteristics profoundly influence how well an architecture functions, a effect so strong that it can even overshadow the inherent properties of the architecture itself. These data-specific variations offer critical insights into what an ideal classifier ought to achieve, thereby establishing rigorous benchmarks that any new classifier must meet. Finally, we propose a rigorous methodology for evaluating new classifier architectures that explicitly accounts for these dataset particular variations.

Hadwiger's well-known conjecture posits that any graph exhibiting a connectivity of $k$ necessarily admits a $k$-contractible complete subgraph. In this study, we assume a graph $G$ possesses an average degree exceeding 2.5; this condition guarantees that if $G$'s chromatic number is no greater than 4, it contains a Hamiltonian cycle. Furthermore, if $G$ is 5-chromatic, it contains a subgraph $H$ belonging to a specific class that facilitates 4-contractibility. Notably, $H$ also satisfies two key properties: it possesses an average degree exceeding 1.5 and its chromatic number exceeds 4.

Our results show that this scheme successfully surpasses this threshold using fewer than ten atoms. The strategy involves first generating a specific entangled state through spin-squeezing, followed by customized measurements on the resulting ensemble. Recently, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCN) have gained significant traction for processing graph data, primarily due to their ability to perform convolution operations that respect the inherent topology of graphs. However, the fundamental principles behind GCNs remain somewhat opaque. This study offers a clear understanding of the core mechanics of convolution by introducing Graph Convolution as a direct application of matched filtering. Using this framework, we derive the formal definition of the Graph Convolution operator and subsequently prove that the widely adopted diffusion-based GCN model constitutes a legitimate graph convolution method. Furthermore, we demonstrate mathematically why the widely adopted diffusion-based GCN model qualifies as a valid form of graph convolution. Additionally, we establish mathematically that the commonly used diffusion-based GCN architecture represents a valid form of graph convolution. Through these mathematical demonstrations, we further elucidate why the diffusion-based GCN design is effective. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through numerical experiments.

Automated data collection and labeling are essential for training high-quality contextual models, yet they are costly and labor-intensive. This paper introduces a cost-effective, end-to-end auto-training framework designed to mitigate these expenses. The system employs active learning to generate high-priority context subsets and applies weak supervision to create training data efficiently. Furthermore, it fine-tunes BERT using a domain-specific data subset selected by active learning. Validated through a dependency analysis task, the proposed method outperforms models pre-trained on web corpora and surpasses weak supervision-only approaches.

The semi-inclusive weak decays $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ are examined using a model of semiquantitative light-front quark framework. In this study, light-front wave functions for the $B$ and $D$ mesons are derived by enforcing quark model wave function continuity. The form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_0(q^2)$ are subsequently determined, and the differential decay rate $d\Gamma/dq^2$ as well as the ratio $f_0(q^2)/f_+(q^2)$ are computed. The calculated differential decay rate $d\Gamma/dq^2$ aligns well with experimental measurements, while the form factor $f_+(q^2)$ shows satisfactory agreement with existing data. The behavior of the ratio $f_0(q^2)/f_+(q^2)$ is consistent with phenomenological expectations.

In the context of the categorical logic of non-reversible processes, we introduce a comprehensive theory of membrane structure. Our work extends the established theory of membranes found in the reversible setting, where types are organized into a locally cartesian closed positively-graded family functor. Crucially, our system allows membranes to separate processes belonging to distinct temporal orders, such as activation from deactivation. We demonstrate that this theory forms the foundation of the type structure underlying the linear lambda-cube designed for non-reversible symmetric processes.

The study examines the complexity of graph isomorphism within specific polynomial-size symmetric networks under bounded amplitude and width constraints when operated by a group of polynomial amplitude. It establishes that for any polynomial $f$, there exists a family of undirected graphs $\{G_n\}$ such that standard polynomial time computability in symmetric networks of amplitude $O(\log n)$ and width $f(n)$ holds if and only if computability in $f(n)$-amplitude networks over $g(n)$ nodes with width $o(n)$ (for some function $g$) is also true for all $f$. This equivalence mirrors the relationship between standard and logarithmic amplitude computation. The research further demonstrates the existence of an isomorphism family $\{H_n\}$ where deciding isomorphism for $f(n)$ nodes using networks of amplitude $f(n)$ and width $o(n)$ ($g$) requires width $\Omega(f(n))$ ($h$), thereby extending the Cai-Immerman-Invitation (Cai-Furer-Invitation) result. We conducted valence band X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS) on Eu$_{1-x}$Bi$_{x}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$ to examine the impact of Bi substitution on the electronic structure. As x increases, the valence band top shifts upward, approaching the Fermi level, while the lower binding energy region remains largely unchanged. This upward movement correlates with a transition from an insulating to a metallic ground state. We attribute this shift to a reduction in the effective Ir valence, resulting in an expansion of the 5d orbital width and enhanced bandwidth. These findings are consistent with first-principles calculations, which indicate that the top of the Ir $t_{2g}$ orbitals rises with increasing Bi content.

This study examines the properties of finite-dimensional set-valued mappings, with a specific focus on those ranging from 2 to N dimensions. The research centers on the fundamental nature of 2-dimensional (Y, N)-spherical mappings and explores their interplay with broader mapping classes. It also addresses robust conditions ensuring the existence of single-valued selections for Lipschitz continuous set-valued mappings. Furthermore, the paper introduces straightforward algorithms designed to generate specific selections from mappings with limited dimensional ranges.

Our analysis demonstrates that it is impossible to simultaneously satisfy $\text{pr}(A > B) = \text{pr}(B > C)$ and $\text{pr}(B > A) < \text{pr}(A > C)$, thereby proving the impossibility of circularity under these specific constraints while offering a broader perspective on nontransitive events. Sub-GeV dark matter remains a significant focus in current research. However, detecting the recoil signals from such lightweight particles in nuclear experiments is exceptionally difficult because nuclear recoil generates negligible signals compared to backgrounds from nuclear reactions. This study demonstrates that nuclear recoil interactions actually produce distinct electron emissions, whereas nuclear fragment recoil does not. By targeting these specific electrons, we can substantially lower background noise and directly observe dark matter signals. Using this strategy, we derive novel nuclear recoil limits for dark matter interactions that extend well beyond existing direct detection bounds up to 100 MeV. These new constraints cover dark matter masses up to 10 MeV, a region previously largely unexplored.

We examine two variations of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, investigating energy exchange oscillations, entanglement dynamics, and photon transmission coefficients. It is observed that both configurations exhibit oscillatory energy exchange, and their capacity to generate entanglement reaches a constant maximum during these fluctuations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the photon transmission coefficient equals unity whenever oscillatory peaks for energy or entanglement occur.

This study introduces a new method for estimating Inter-Beat Intervals (IBIs) using the Tiramisu model, which offers a distinct approach compared to the conventional autoregressive (AR) model. The goal is to achieve more precise heart rate variability (HRV) analysis by generating Inter-Beat Interval (IBE) estimates with higher fidelity. The proposed method involves fitting the ECG signal to Tiramisu to derive Instantaneous Phase (IP) estimates, from which IRBs are subsequently calculated. To validate its efficacy, Tiramisu-based IBI was compared against AR-model-based IBI using the NN dataset from the MIT-PTB Database. The outcomes demonstrate that Tiramisu yields superior performance, as evidenced by lower error metrics: the standard deviation of the error decreased from 0.078 (AR) to 0.043 (Tiramisu), the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) dropped from 0.103 to 0.057, and the Root Mean Cubic Error (RMCC) improved from 0.133 to 0.064.

Active matter systems are defined by their self-propulsion, a characteristic driven by a combination of self-generated forces and internal memory. Within this framework, Labor (the work performed by active agents) serves as a key metric for quantifying self-propulsion. This study examines two mathematical formulations of active self-propulsion: one utilizing an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AUP) framework and the other based on an effective stochastic first-order equation. By analyzing labor in both models, we identify a fundamental discrepancy in their predictions. Specifically, we demonstrate that an apparent contradiction in labor values arises from a non-physical singularity present in the stochastic integral defining the AUP framework. Furthermore, we propose a refined mathematical formulation that resolves this issue and aligns labor calculations across both the AUP and first-order stochastic equations.

Capturing human gestures is essential for advancing research in computer vision and graphics, yet existing public datasets are often limited in size, lacking natural variation, or omit robust evaluation protocols. Introducing HUMBI, a new multiview dataset containing 1,000 distinct gestures recorded from 20 actors across 12 camera angles, this work provides high-quality gesture capture at an unprecedented scale. To address varying research requirements, HUMBI offers three specific sub-collections: one for large-scale synthesis evaluation using state-of-the-art methods, another for fine-grained gesture recognition, and a third for synthesis tasks driven by an innovated "InGesture" benchmark challenge. Empirical evaluations on all three subsets using leading techniques demonstrate significant room for improvement, underscoring the potential of HUMBI to drive future breakthroughs. Humble data can be accessed at https://humbi.cs.cmu.edu.

Task embeddings, which utilize neural network representations to encode tasks, have emerged as a promising technique for transfer learning. However, existing methods are constrained by specific frameworks, demanding the retraining of embedding layers whenever a new task or transfer scenario arises. In this study, we introduce a simple yet potent approach that generates task embeddings via a single multilingual BERT model, eliminating the need for embedding layer retraining across different tasks or transfer setups. To avoid introducing new linguistic biases, we ensure BERT sees no task names during training. Instead, we leverage the "instruction tuning" paradigm, where tasks are encoded by their instructions themselves. Empirical results demonstrate that these derived embeddings achieve performance on par with previous state-of-the-art methods across multiple down-stream tasks. Furthermore, we illustrate how this methodology enables effective, feeble-supervised, independent-model cross-lingual transfer.

Anchoring on the paradigm of anisotropic alignment and propagation employed in BasicVSR for anisotropic video super-resolution, we introduce two key enhancements. First, we develop bidirectional propagation with a novel symmetric design that supersedes the unidirectional approach in BasicVSR; this new method simultaneously performs forward and backward spatial propagation, effectively mitigating propagation errors and significantly boosting super-resolution quality. Second, we integrate a multi-scale feature alignment strategy to refine the anisotropic alignment process. This approach adaptively fuses features from various scales, ensuring precise anisotropic registration even in regions with rich details. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in anisotropic video super-resolution.

In modern Reinforcement Learning (RL), the complexity of real-world applications often exceeds human capacity to design effective reward functions. Concurrently, the community is increasingly addressing multi-task learning to enable agents to acquire related tasks simultaneously, thereby enhancing sample efficiency. However, simply transferring acquired skills can be counterproductive, as inappropriate actions may degrade performance. This paper presents a solution by decomposing tasks into modular components, allowing agents to master each module independently and selectively apply them based on the current situation. We demonstrate this approach using two prototypical scenarios: the "modulated continuous control" task, which requires context-aware choices between two actions, and a "modulated navigation" task involving distinct goal-pursuit behaviors. Our results indicate that models employing module-based decomposition achieve a 40% reduction in sample requirements compared to single models handling multiple tasks without modular structure.

We investigate a quantum thermal engine operating over a finite duration, where the system's evolution is constrained by a limited set of unitary operations. These engines achieve power output by converting thermal energy from a hot reservoir into work, with the maximum power determined by the specific unitary operation selected from the allowed集合. This selection process constitutes a non-equilibrium thermodynamic optimization problem. For a two-level system interacting with a heat reservoir at inverse temperature $\beta$, we identify an optimal unitary transformation that maximizes power. Furthermore, we demonstrate that as the temperature of this bath approaches zero, the maximum power scales with a factor of $1/4$ relative to the square of the characteristic energy scale divided by the square of $\tau$.

This study introduces a spatiotemporal model designed to evaluate the impact of hurricanes on the power grid, specifically by analyzing the interplay between storm wind forces, wind speed variations, and the varying intensity of storm surges on substations. The research further develops a specialized optimization framework aimed at enhancing the resilience of these localized areas against hurricane threats. Notably, the proposed optimization problem is reformulated into a solvable linear programming model. The validity of this approach is confirmed through case studies utilizing real-world hurricane data, which effectively demonstrate the system's applicability.

This work establishes an "three spheres" theorem for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator within Clifford-valued functions. For these functions, the mean square value over a sphere is governed by a specific combination of values evaluated at three strategically selected nested spheres situated inside it. This finding serves as a powerful tool in proving uniqueness results and three related theorems regarding zero distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a broad class of finite zero polynomials for Clifford-valued Dirac operators' eigenfunctions.

For dynamical systems defined on graphs, the topological entropy $h_{\rm top}$ serves as an upper bound for the specific entropy $h(\mu)$ of any invariant probability measure $\mu$, establishing that $h(\rm top) \ge \max_\mu h(\mu)$. This work introduces two systems on graphs that violate this inequality, demonstrating that specific entropy can drop as much as $1/e$ below the system's topological entropy. The first example consists of a directed circle map, which generates a heterochaos system featuring both a positive Lyapunov exponent and a zero-specific entropy; this system also exhibits a non-maximally entropic Baker diagram. The second example is the heterochaos-driven Dyck system on an infinite binary tree, where the failure of the system to reach maximum entropy provides a clear mechanism for this phenomenon.

The recent LHC findings have established that the Higgs boson's properties are largely consistent with Standard Model predictions, yet significant deviations remain possible. The next generation of experiments at the LHC and future colliders aims to scrutinize these potential deviations with greater precision. This review examines extensions of the Standard Model featuring enhanced scalar sectors, with a specific emphasis on models predicting additional light states. We analyze upcoming detector capabilities to highlight how they can distinguish between these various theoretical frameworks.

This study introduces Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), a novel pitch-conditioned audio synthesis system designed to produce raw waveforms. To address the limitations of standard waveforms in capturing long-term dependencies, the model employs a QP-Dilated Convolutional Network (QP-DCCN). This architecture integrates two parallel dilated convolutional branches: one utilizes standard dilation, while the other implements quasi-periodic dilation. The latter applies dilation factors that are dynamically calculated based on the fundamental frequency ($F_0$) and harmonic structure of the input pitch contour. This mechanism allows hidden features to be expanded at a rate corresponding to the spacing of the source's quasi-periodic waveform, effectively modeling the fundamental tone and its harmonics over extended temporal ranges. Empirical results demonstrate that QPNet achieves rapid synthesis speeds with high efficiency. Furthermore, when compared against the WaveNet architecture, QPNet delivers comparable or superior quality in synthesis while offering significantly faster generation times.

This study investigates how solar magnetic activity affects the spectral line shapes of the Sun, utilizing high-resolution, disk-integrated spectra from the HARPS-N telescope. We analyzed spectral line profiles across 1000 Å to 1000 nm to detect activity-induced variations, employing both established markers (S-index, G-index) and newly proposed markers (H-index, N-index). Our findings indicate that activity-related spectral changes are most prominent in the 400 nm to 450 nm range, specifically targeting the wings of strong lines. We correlate these variations with solar activity markers and compare the resulting relationships to model predictions. We also examine how the connections between spectral line shape alterations and magnetic activity vary across different levels of solar activity.

Distinguishing Majorana zero modes from conventional zero-energy states remains a significant hurdle in confirming non-Abelian topology within nanowires. This difficulty arises primarily from the presence of spurious zero-energy peaks caused by flux leakage and proximity effects from ferromagnetic materials. To address this, we offer an innovative strategy involving tunneling spectroscopy with a resistive tip, operated under conditions of Ohmic (or exponential) dissipation. Our analysis reveals that, unlike other zero-energy features, the true Majorana signature exhibits a distinct shift away from zero bias when the system undergoes adiabatic, slow measurement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a dual-tunneling spectroscopy setup can reliably separate Majorana modes from remaining spurious peaks.

In the context of bicategory theory, a shadow functions as a kind of "trace" that elevates a bicategory to an ordinary category. We provide a comprehensive and elevated examination of shadows utilizing the language of profunctor categories and, most significantly, the concept of spaned categories (or bicatic spans). This approach extends the established idea of double-cated spans found in the literature. We further explore the connection between bicategory shadows and triple-cated spans by demonstrating that every triple-cated span can be viewed as a bicategory equipped with a specific shadow.

This document outlines the specifics for the Long Video Anonymization for Vulnerable and Exploited Children (LOVEU) AQTC Challenge. It begins by detailing the contest background and objectives, then describes the data sets and evaluation metrics. Following this is an overview of the AQTC pipeline and guidelines for submitting entries. The final section provides essential information regarding the contest schedule and the official website.

Accumulation plays a critical role in the performance of optical systems, particularly for telescopes and imaging instruments in atmospheric turbulence, where snow poses a significant threat. This study presents the inaugural experimental proof that snow particles exhibit a preferential selection during accumulation, influenced by their fall velocity and size. The research utilizes a dual-beam trap to capture individual particles in flight, measuring both their sedimentation velocities and diameters while determining their approach velocity toward a collection surface. The resulting probability density functions demonstrate that larger particles settle faster and are more likely to be trapped, whereas smaller ones are less likely to accumulate. The authors also provide a model that characterizes this preferential selection as stem-cell-like, wherein particles with higher fall velocities tend to land in flow stagnation zones, whereas those with lower fall velocities navigate deeper into the trap volume. These findings offer novel insights for developing effective snow removal strategies to maintain atmospheric turbulence optical systems.

This paper introduces the principles of active inference and its recent advances, demonstrating their successful application in autonomous navigation for both single robots and multi-robot systems. We restructure the core concepts of active inference, emphasizing the primate-inspired free energy minimization process that guides agents to perceive and act within their environments. Additionally, we address computational challenges related to the high dimensionality of state spaces, which can hinder inference; we resolve this by approximating probability distributions using the variational approach. Finally, we outline our most recent developments, including a deep-learning-based approximation scheme and a mechanism for hierarchical policy selection, before validating the entire framework through experiments. These experiments involve a novel, lightweight robot navigating unknown environments, confirming both the theory and the empirical evidence.

Addressing the exponential growth in data volume from large-scale particle physics experiments, this paper introduces a new end-to-end data compression framework for Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) that relies on sparse 3D effective coordinates. The proposed method employs a dual Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) to process these effective coordinates, treating them as letter-like input to generate a reconstructed "alphabet" of patterns for comparison. To enhance the model's interpretability, we integrate a decision tree to classify the 3D events into distinct physical processes before the compression stage. Furthermore, an improved unsupervised pre-training technique for dual CAEs is implemented to accelerate convergence and boost compression performance. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves superior statistical fidelity and significantly higher compression ratios compared to existing solutions.

The Finzi gravity model offers a novel framework of self-gravitating systems that extends the Mielschke model by allowing the high-density state to remain stable. In this study, we statistically characterize clusters of galaxies using the Finzi model. Specifically, we examine the radial distribution function $g(r)$, the mean squared displacement $\langle r^2(t) \rangle$, and the two-point correlation function $\xi(r)$. Our results indicate that Finzi gravity yields a $g(r)$ profile consistent with observational data, while $\langle r^2(t) \rangle$ and $\xi(r)$ align well with simulations of $\Lambda$CDM.
